articles.title: With US-Iran talks stalled, diplomatic efforts expand to unlikely European players
articles.body:
With US-Iran talks stalled, diplomatic efforts expand to unlikely European players
WASHINGTON (AP) — Faced with an increasingly bellicose Iran as talks to end the war have stalled, the Trump administration appears to be reaching out to a broader swath of countries that might be able to help pressure Tehran or ease its hardline position where traditional mediators have not succeeded so far.
While discussions between Iran and Oman, as well as between Iran and Pakistan, Turkey and Qatar, persist at an uneven and unpredictable pace, the U.S. administration quietly has expanded its outreach to include perhaps unlikely interlocutors in Europe.
Just this week, Secretary of State Marco Rubio met in person in Washington with the foreign minister of Austria on Tuesday and held a call with the foreign minister of Greece on Wednesday.
Those interactions were not notable beyond the normal course of relations between the U.S. and two close European allies. The official State Department readouts of the discussions were bland and vague and did not mention Iran by name as a topic of conversation.
But it then emerged that both foreign ministers — almost immediately after their talks with Rubio — spoke Thursday with Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi.
The apparent new tack to break the negotiation logjam comes as the U.S. and Iran are both pushing for control of the Strait of Hormuz, the crucial oil shipping corridor. President Donald Trump faces little wiggle room in his next steps as the economic fallout from the war and dwindling stockpiles of key weapons pose political problems for Republicans ahead of November’s midterm congressional elections.
A desperate push is on to break the diplomatic logjam between the US and Iran
The entry by Austria and Greece is likely less of a formal mediation attempt, analysts say, and more reflective of a desperate push to halt the conflict because of the impact it has on an increasing number of countries, beyond those in the Middle East.
“Everyone is just urging both sides to stop this reckless game of chicken,” said Ali Vaez, Iran project director at the International Crisis Group.
It also shows how much Iran’s effective closure of the Strait of Hormuz has forced countries, which otherwise were neutral bystanders to the larger conflict, to exercise any diplomatic sway they may have on their Iranian and American counterparts to kick-start a lasting resolution.
Mona Yacoubian, director of the Middle East Program at the Center for Strategic and International Studies, warned that any efforts by Greece, Austria or any other non-mediating country could prove to be futile.
“While the calls to both sides may entail encouraging both Iran and the U.S. back to the negotiating table, such efforts fall short of mediation, which is a very complex endeavor and requires trust to be built by the mediator with both sides,” Yacoubian said.
She added that it’s not something that any country can “just jump into.”
Rubio discussed Iran with his Austrian and Greek counterparts
The State Department said Friday that it could not comment on the timing of calls by other countries’ foreign ministers and maintained that Rubio had made no requests of either to get in touch with Iran or pass messages to Araghchi.
One European diplomat, who was briefed on the matter and spoke on condition of anonymity to detail sensitive diplomatic conversations, said the timing of the calls was not an accident.
The State Department did allow, however, that Iran had been a topic of conversation in Rubio’s discussions, which occurred as Trump is facing serious political headwinds over a war for which he has offered shifting objectives.
No longer purely about making Iran incapable of producing a nuclear weapon, the immediate goal has become reopening the Strait of Hormuz, where a fifth of the world’s oil usually passes through and which was open before the U.S. and Israel launched attacks on Iran on Feb. 28.
“That’s goal number one: keep oil and gas cheap for Americans all over our country,” Vice President JD Vance said in an interview Thursday on Fox News Channel. But he did not say anything about the strait being open and toll-free for transiting ships, as he had in the past.
The second goal, Vance said, is to ensure that Iran will never get a nuclear weapon.
The two European countries have key connections to the war’s fallout
Austria and Greece may not be obvious choices to assist on the Iran portfolio, but Vienna is home to the International Atomic Energy Agency, which will play a key role in any resolution to the Iran’s nuclear program, and hosted the final negotiations that resulted in the 2015 Iran nuclear deal. Greece is a major maritime nation in the Mediterranean and has significant shipping interests in the Strait of Hormuz and the Red Sea.
In statements from the Austrian, Greek and Iranian foreign ministries, it was clear that Iran had been a top topic in all of the conversations this week.
The Greek foreign ministry said Foreign Minister George Gerapetritis had been briefed by Araghchi on “regional developments, and in particular on the ongoing talks regarding the Strait of Hormuz.” It said Gerapetritis “underlined the importance of freedom of navigation and maritime security.”
The Austrian foreign ministry offered Austria’s services as a venue for further potential talks with Iran and said Foreign Minister Beate Meinl-Reisinger had stressed to Araghchi “the urgency of restoring stability in the region through serious diplomatic efforts.”
“There can be no military solution,” it said. “A diplomatic solution remains possible. Our priority is to safeguard freedom of navigation through the Strait of Hormuz.”
Iran’s foreign ministry, expectedly, took a different tack in explaining the calls.
It said Friday that in Araghchi’s calls with his European counterparts they discussed “mechanisms for the future management of the Strait of Hormuz,” which he said had been disrupted by the “unlawful aggression by the United States and the Israeli regime against Iran.”
In both calls, he accused the U.S. of violating the interim deal signed by both sides in June to end the immediate hostilities and begin broader talks to end the war.
___
Amiri reported from New York. Associated Press writers Derek Gatopolous in Athens and Claudia Ciobanu in Warsaw, Poland, contributed to this report.

articles.title: Ukraine attacks Russia’s Samara industrial site as Kyiv ramps up long-range strikes
articles.body:
Ukraine attacks Russia’s Samara industrial site as Kyiv ramps up long-range strikes
A large-scale Ukrainian attack struck industrial infrastructure in Russia’s southwestern Samara region Saturday, a Russian official said.
Ivan Noskov, head of the region’s capital, Samara, said air defense forces had repelled a “massive” missile attack, with “localized damage” to the city’s industrial sites. He also said that medical assistance has been provided to those injured in the attack, but did not give further details.
Ukraine has stepped up its long-range aerial attacks on Russian military industries and energy facilities, aiming to cut Moscow’s revenue for the war and make Russians feel the consequences of the invasion, now in its fifth year.
Zelenskyy says need for peace has to be felt in Russia
Writing on social media, Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said that Kyiv’s forces had carried out a strike against Samara’s Progress Center, which operates under Russian space agency Roscosmos and is involved in producing rocket technology and electronics.
He said that the strike used Ukraine’s domestically produced Flamingo missiles to hit the site, which is approximately 900 kilometers (560 miles) from the Ukrainian border.
Zelenskyy also said Russia’s Savasleyka air base, some 700 kilometers (430 miles) from the front line, had also been hit.
“Peace is needed, and this must be evident in Russia — through concrete damage to specific facilities,” Zelenskyy wrote.
While most of Ukraine’s strikes have a range of less than 200 kilometers (125 miles), its longer-range attacks have increased dramatically this year. It launched three times as many of those strikes in July as it did in January, according to data from ACLED, an independent conflict monitor. Repeatedly hitting deep into Russia has forced its military to stretch air defenses over a larger area.
Russia’s Ministry of Defense said Saturday that it had shot down 598 Ukrainian drones over 19 Russian regions, as well as the Black and Azov Seas and the annexed Ukrainian peninsula of Crimea.
Separately, two people, including a nine-year-old child, were wounded when a Ukrainian drone attack hit a private home in the town of Shatura in the Moscow region, local Gov. Andrey Vorobyov said.
Child killed in drone strike
Elsewhere, a Russian strike on an apartment block in southeastern Ukraine Saturday killed a three-month-old baby and wounded 11 people, local officials said.
Drones hit the building in the town of Marhanets, said Oleksandr Hanzha, head of the Dnipropetrovsk Regional Military Administration.
Russia’s Ministry of Defense also said that it had targeted warehouses and infrastructure at the Ukrainian ports of Odesa, Izmail and Yuzhnyi.
Ukraine’s Air Force said that Russia launched 152 drones over the country Saturday, of which 124 were destroyed.

articles.title: Ukraine reportedly strikes Russian military airbase behind ballistic missile attacks as rockets target Samara
articles.body:
Ukraine hits key Roscosmos facility with Flamingo missiles, strikes Savasleyka airbase, Zelensky says
Editor's note: This is a developing story and is being updated.
Ukrainian forces struck Russia's Savasleyka military airbase and a key Roscosmos facility in Samara Oblast using domestically produced Flamingo missiles, President Volodymyr Zelensky confirmed on Aug. 15.
"The Savasleyka airfield, where the carriers of Russian missiles that strike our cities and villages are based, was also reached by our long-range sanctions," Zelensky said. "It is about 700 kilometers from Ukraine," he added.
MiG-31K fighter jets capable of carrying Kinzhal ballistic missiles have previously been stationed at the airfield.
Explosions were also reported in the Russian city of Samara, where Ukraine struck the Progress Rocket Space Center, one of the key enterprises belonging to Russia's state space corporation Roscosmos.
"The progress center, which was involved, among other things, in producing electronics, was hit. Flamingo missiles were used — a good achievement," Zelensky said.
Samara Oblast Governor Vyacheslav Fedorishchev earlier said that missiles had struck an "industrial facility" in the region without identifying the site. Authorities were still determining whether there were casualties or additional damage, he added.
Zelensky said the progress center lies around 900 kilometers (560 miles) from Ukraine's border, while the Savasleyka airbase is approximately 700 kilometers (435 miles) from Ukraine.
The extent of the damage could not be independently verified by the Kyiv Independent.
Russia kills Ukrainian civilians in recurring attacks launched from its many airbases and military sites.
On Aug. 11, Russian forces struck Zaporizhzhia and Kyiv using North Korean ballistic missiles and Zircon cruise missiles, authorities reported. The attack killed seven workers of the Zaporizhstal steel plant and injured a total of 24 in Zaporizhzhia. One more civilian was injured in Kyiv.
A Russian ballistic missile attack on Aug. 8 killed four, including a three-year-old child, in Ukraine's capital and Kyiv Oblast. Another ballistic missile attack on Aug. 5 killed 17 people.
Ukraine regularly strikes military infrastructure deep within Russia and the occupied territories in an effort to diminish Moscow's ability to continue waging its war.
Overnight on Aug. 14, Ukrainian forces struck the Ust-Luga port in Russia's Leningrad Oblast, damaging two processing plants and sparking a fire, Ukraine's General Staff said.
The site is one of Russia's largest ports on the Baltic Sea and holds an oil terminal that serves as a major hub for the export of crude oil and petroleum products.
The Gazprom Neftekhim Salavat oil refinery complex in Russia's Republic of Bashkortostan was struck by Ukrainian forces the night prior on Aug. 13, the General Staff said.

articles.title: Putin Ordered Kremlin to ‘Destroy NATO and EU From Within’ – NYT
articles.body:
Russian President Vladimir Putin has reportedly ordered his intelligence services and military to work toward “destroying NATO and the EU from within” in 2026, with Moldova emerging as a key target in the Kremlin’s strategy, The New York Times reported.
Friday’s report, based on officials from two countries familiar with a secret December 2025 meeting, says Moscow is pursuing the strategy on at least two fronts: testing NATO’s willingness to defend its members and destabilizing Moldova.
JOIN US ON TELEGRAM
Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official.
US intelligence has assessed that Russia could seek to test NATO’s resolve as early as this fall through a limited attack on an alliance member.
Possible scenarios range from cyberattacks and sabotage to operations involving unidentified armed groups or a limited incursion into a NATO country on the alliance’s eastern flank.
But Moldova could offer Moscow a different route to destabilizing Europe.
Why Moldova matters
Western intelligence officials told the NYT that conquering Ukraine remains Putin’s top priority, while establishing control over Moldova is reportedly second.
Moscow’s strategic goal, according to the officials, goes beyond political influence in Chisinau. Putin is still believed to want to seize southern Ukraine and create a land corridor connecting Russia to Moldova.
That would put Moldova – a small country of about 2.4 million people wedged between Ukraine and NATO and EU territory – in an extremely vulnerable position.
Poland Uncovers Russian Plot to Kill US-Ukrainian Citizen in Warsaw
Moldova also has the Russian-backed separatist region of Transnistria on its territory, where Russian troops have been stationed for decades. That gives Moscow an existing military foothold just across the border from Ukraine and within striking distance of Moldova’s capital, Chisinau.
Control over Moldova could therefore give Russia another platform for pressure on Ukraine while placing the EU and NATO’s eastern flank under additional strain.
Moscow already has pressure points
Russia does not need an open invasion to destabilize Moldova.
In March, a Russian strike on a Ukrainian hydroelectric plant triggered an oil spill that polluted the Dniester River and disrupted water supplies in Moldova, including the country’s third-largest city.
Russian drones later struck a high-voltage line in western Ukraine that supplies Moldova with a large share of its electricity, exposing how closely the country’s infrastructure is tied to the war next door.
The pressure is also political. Moldova has been moving decisively toward the EU, while Moscow has repeatedly sought to exploit political divisions, disinformation and economic vulnerabilities to weaken that shift.
“Hybrid attacks every day”
German Chief of Defense Gen. Carsten Breuer has warned that Russia is already conducting hybrid operations across NATO, particularly on the eastern flank.
Poland and the Baltic states are now increasing security around dams, power plants, gas facilities and other critical infrastructure amid fears Russia could stage a false-flag attack using Ukrainian-made drones.
A Baltic intelligence official told Reuters that such an operation could be designed less to cause physical damage than to create political chaos inside NATO – forcing Washington and European capitals to debate whether Russia was responsible and whether the alliance should respond.

articles.title: Ukraine says it has struck Russian 'rocket and space' centre
articles.body:
Additional strikes were carried out on Savasleyka air base - which Ukraine said housed aircraft used for missile attacks - and an oil facility in Ust-Luga, per Zelenskyy.
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy announced on Saturday that Ukrainian forces had struck the Progress Rocket and Space Centre in Russia's Samara region, a facility involved in the manufacturing and operation of space launch vehicles.
In a post on X, Zelenskyy said Ukraine hit the centre with FP-5 Flamingo cruise missiles, describing it as one of Russian space agency Roscosmos' "key enterprises" and saying it was involved in "electronics production".
Additional strikes were carried out on Savasleyka air base in the Nizhny Novgorod region - which the Ukrainian leader said housed aircraft used for missile attacks on Ukraine - and an oil facility in Ust-Luga, close to the border with Estonia, per Zelenskyy.
He shared video footage on X appearing to show the aftermath of some of the strikes. Large columns of black smoke and flames can be seen at sites in the distance.
"Our plan of long-range sanctions against Russia for this war is being implemented, and it is important that Russia’s war potential be reduced," Zelenskyy wrote.
The General Staff of the Armed Forces of Ukraine has since shared more details on the operation as well as its intelligence on the targets, confirming hits were recorded at both the Progress centre and the air base and that a fire had broken out on the facilities' grounds.
It added that the launch vehicles produced at the Progress centre were used to "place Russian military, reconnaissance, and communications spacecraft into orbit."
The Savasleyka air base, the General Staff added, is used to operate MiG-31K fighter jets, which it said were used to carry Kh-47M2 Kinzhal ballistic missiles.
Ukraine's 'long-range sanctions' and Russian strikes
Ukraine has repeatedly hit targets deep inside Russia in an effort to increase pressure on Russian President Vladimir Putin and the country's military capabilities and to squeeze the Russian economy.
Kyiv has in particular sought to home in on energy facilities across Russia as part of this strategy, striking oil refineries, terminals, and depots across the country. The attacks have led to fuel shortages across parts of Russia and Russian-occupied territories.
The Ukrainian air force said on Saturday that Russian forces had launched 152 drones and loitering munitions at Ukraine overnight.
"According to preliminary data, as of 9 am, air defences had shot down or neutralised 124 enemy UAVs," it said, adding that strikes had been recorded in 16 locations.
Russian attacks on the Kherson region in southern Ukraine over the past day injured 28 people, including a child, according to Oleksandr Prokudin, the head of the Kherson Regional Military Administration.
A child was also killed and 11 people were injured in a series of strikes on the Dnipropetrovsk region in southeast Ukraine, per regional governor Oleksandr Hanzha, while four were injured in Sumy Oblast in the country's north.
A further nine people were injured across the regions of Donetsk, Zaporizhzhia, and Kharkiv, per local authorities.

articles.title: Japan’s Defense Minister Koizumi prays at shrine seen by neighbors as symbol of Japanese militarism
articles.body:
Takaichi skips controversial shrine visit on 81st anniversary of country’s World War II surrender
TOKYO (AP) — Japanese Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi avoided Tokyo’s controversial Yasukuni Shrine, apparently to prioritize diplomatic relations with China and South Korea, as Japan marked on Saturday the 81st anniversary of its surrender in World War II.
However, she did not mention her country’s wartime past in Asia or show remorse over it in her address.
The Yasukuni Shrine, which commemorates over 2.4 million people who died in wars, became controversial after including 14 convicted World War II Japanese war criminals. China and South Korea say visits by Japanese officials to the shrine show a lack of remorse over Japan’s wartime atrocities.
Takaichi mourned the victims of major devastation in Hiroshima, Nagasaki and Okinawa, as well as those who perished in overseas battlefronts, and thanked them for their sacrifice as the “foundation of Japan’s peace and prosperity today.”
“Japan, since the end of the war, has consistently contributed to global peace and prosperity. We will never let the tragedy of the war be repeated,” she said in her address at Budokan Hall, a walking distance from Yasukuni.
Takaichi said Japan can play a key role in addressing global challenges as “a dependable nation” in the region.
China and South Korea protest shrine visits
Japanese Defense Minister Shinjiro Koizumi, three other Cabinet ministers and three executives from Takaichi’s governing party showed up at the shrine earlier Saturday. A nonpartisan group of dozens of lawmakers also prayed there.
China’s Foreign Ministry protested to Japan over the visits, saying that Japanese politicians’ true intentions were to “change the verdict on the war criminals, cover up Japan’s war crimes, distort the historical facts and pave the way for accelerating militarization.” It urged Japan to do “serious soul searching” on history and make a clean break with militarism.
Tensions between Japan and China escalated in November when Takaichi said a Chinese attack on Taiwan could constitute “a survival-threatening situation” for Japan requiring the use of force. The comments enraged Beijing.
South Korean President Lee Jae Myung, in his speech Saturday marking the 81st anniversary of Korea’s liberation from Japanese colonial rule, said that his administration used “pragmatic diplomacy centered on national interests” and will broaden cooperation in shared interests to resolve common challenges. “Korea-Japan cooperation is now more important than ever.”
“The new bilateral relationship we are building must warmly illuminate those who are still suffering from pain in the shadows of history,” he said.
Attention this week was on whether Takaichi, who has repeatedly said she would pray at the shrine on Aug. 15 despite the controversy, would keep her pledge and show up at Yasukuni.
Defense minister prays at Yasukuni
Koizumi has regularly visited the controversial shrine on Aug. 15 and other occasions. But as a defense minister pushing to increase Japan’s military capability and weapons sales under Takaichi’s hawkish government, his visit is seen as more contentious.
The previous shrine visit by a defense minister was in 2024 by Minoru Kihara, the current chief secretary and top government spokesperson for Takaichi’s government.
Japan’s Defense Ministry prohibits group visits by service members of the Self-Defense Forces, on grounds of constitutional separation of religion and state. Koizumi said in October it is natural for anyone in any country to pay respect for those who sacrificed their lives for their nation.
Hours after his Yasukuni visit, Koizumi said on X he paid respects to the war dead for their sacrifice for the country. “I renewed my war-renouncing resolve and will continue to fulfill Japan’s postwar responsibility as a peace-loving nation.”
He is the son of popular former Prime Minister Junichiro Koizumi, whose 2006 Yasukuni visit as a serving leader outraged China.
Party executives make up for Takaichi’s absence from the shrine
The three executives from Takaichi’s governing Liberal Democratic Party prayed together Saturday at the shrine and brought offerings in a rare joint visit on the prime minister’s behalf, seen as a move to make up for Takaichi’s absence and appeal to her right-wing supporters.
Party secretary-general Shunichi Suzuki told reporters he prayed while keeping in mind the prime minister’s thoughts for “the spirits of the war dead” and that he brought Takaichi’s cash offerings in her capacity as party leader.
For Takaichi, appealing to right-wing voters is key at a time when her support is seen as falling rapidly, presumably over delayed economic measures to address rising prices, as well as scandals including alleged negative election-campaign videos and unpopular revisions to Japan’s imperial family succession rules.
Takaichi has not visited the shrine since taking office but has sent offerings twice for the shrine’s biannual festivals. On Saturday she prayed remotely toward Yasukuni from the Budokan parking lot before the ceremony, NHK television reported.
Japanese emperors have shunned the shrine
Japanese emperors have shunned Yasukuni since its 1978 inclusion of the war criminals as “martyrs,” and have expressed regrets over Japan’s wartime past, though in a nuanced way.
Emperor Naruhito, in his address Saturday at the ceremony, said he hopes the ravages of war will never be repeated while “reflecting on our past and bearing in mind the feelings of deep remorse.”
“It is my sincere hope that we shall continue to pass down the memories of the sufferings endured during and after the war.”
Pushback against remembering Japan’s wartime history
Takaichi has resisted acknowledging Japan’s wartime aggression and atrocities, and denied that coercion was used against Korean laborers and women held as sex slaves for Japanese troops. She was previously part of a campaign to remove references to wartime sexual slavery, known as “comfort women,” from school textbooks.
She has said she is from a postwar generation that bears no responsibility for Japan’s past actions and has no intention of apologizing.
The country has faced revisionist pushbacks since the 2010s under nationalistic former Prime Minister Shinzo Abe, who pushed to correct a “self-deprecating view” of Japan’s wartime history and regain national pride. Takaichi considers Abe a mentor.
Since 2013, Japanese prime ministers have stopped apologizing to Asian victims for wartime atrocities, under a precedent set by Abe.
Last year, however, former Prime Minister Shigeru Ishiba expressed “remorse” over the war and called it a mistake, though he fell short of mentioning Japan’s aggression across Asia or apologizing.
People at Yasukuni remember relatives lost in the war
At Yasukuni, some of those queuing up early Saturday were descendants of the war-dead, and for them Yasukuni is a place to remember their relatives.
As a child, Mariko Shinoda, 56, whose grandfather died as a Kamikaze pilot, came to Yasukuni with her mother every year on Aug. 15. Kamikaze pilots departed on their one-way missions saying, “Let’s meet at Yasukuni,” her mother told her.
“To me, Yasukuni is where every spirit gathers, and that’s where you get to see them on Aug. 15,” Shinoda said.
Masashi Ichimura, 48, whose grandfather went to war, often heard from his father about harsh wartime living conditions, including starvation.
“There is nothing good about the war, win or lose,“ he said. “But those who died in the war only fought for our country, and I just want to thank them for the sacrifice.”
___
Associated Press writers Hyung-jin Kim in Seoul, South Korea, and Kanis Leung in Hong Kong contributed to this report.

articles.title: What to Know About the Growing Concerns Over Conditions on the Long-Deployed USS Abraham Lincoln
articles.body:
The USS Abraham Lincoln has been at sea in the Middle East for months, and with no clear end in sight for the war in Iran, concerns for those aboard the aircraft carrier—and for the vessel itself—have mounted amid a series of troubling reports.
Another aircraft carrier, the USS George Washington, had begun making its way towards the Middle East as of Thursday to replace the Lincoln, multiple news outlets reported. President Donald Trump appeared to confirm the reported ship swap on Friday, saying that the Lincoln "is moving right now, or very shortly and is being replaced with another very similar ship.”
The Washington’s deployment comes as reports have emerged in recent months recounting worsening living conditions, mental health concerns, and supply shortages on board the Lincoln.
Trump seemed to deny the reports on the state of the Lincoln and its crew on Friday, responding “No, they’re not,” in response to a reporter saying that families of the crew members are worried about conditions on board. He also said, when asked if the carrier has been deployed for too long, that it has been deployed “not nearly long enough.”
Defense Secretary Pete Hegeseth on Thursday called the reports of dire conditions on the Lincoln “completely misrepresented.”
“We make sure that every ship, every crew, every captain has everything we can provide them at every single moment. Some deployments are longer than others. I have more respect and gratitude for those sailors than anybody,” Hegseth, with a hand to his heart, told reporters. “I want them home as soon as everybody else, too.”
The Defense Department did not immediately respond to TIME’s request for comment.
Here’s what to know about the USS Abraham Lincoln, the concerns that have been raised over conditions on board, and the burgeoning calls for its crew to return home.
What is the USS Abraham Lincoln, and how long has it been deployed?
The Lincoln is in its ninth month at sea and has been deployed for more than 260 days.
The vessel works as a mobile airbase and command center with its own defense systems. It’s the length of more than three football fields and has a crew of roughly 5,000 when fully deployed.
It departed from San Diego in November on an alternate deployment, but was redirected towards the Middle East in January to provide tactical support to U.S. forces ahead of the war in Iran, which began with an initial wave of American-Israeli strikes at the end of February.
The Lincoln has played a key defensive role in the war against Iran, having shot down “hundreds and hundreds of missiles” and drone attacks that targeted the vessel, according to Hegseth.
“Every single one of those shots, easily shot down miles and miles away from the Abe Lincoln,” he said in April. “They were blowing ammo into fantasy land.”
The ship has also had a part in enforcing the U.S.’s blockade of Iranian ports.
The Lincoln’s deployment was expected to end in May, but was extended indefinitely.
The reported ship swap with the Washington comes as Trump has reinstated a blockade against Iran in the Strait of Hormuz and peace talks have stalled between the countries.
Reports of issues on board the carrier
Several reports have detailed poor conditions aboard the Lincoln. According to MS Now, which interviewed a dozen family members of crew members, those aboard the ship have been dealing with moldy showers and running out of key toiletries, such as toothpaste, deodorant, and soap. The outlet was also told that crew members are working grueling shifts with limited days off and that there are holes on the Lincoln’s flight deck, where pilots take off and land.
A spouse of a service member on the Lincoln also told CBS News that sailors had previously experienced food shortages. Another report from USA Today contained photos of rationed meals served to crew on board the carrier.
Adm. Daryl Caudle, chief of naval operations, pushed back against reports of food shortages back in April. “In no way, shape or form, has there been a time where in, at least in this deployment, where they’ve not met the nutritional requirements of our menu,” Caudle said.
As the deployment has stretched on and living conditions on board have allegedly deteriorated, the crew of the Lincoln has also reportedly struggled with increasing mental health concerns. The Navy Times and Stars and Stripes reported several instances of crew members on the vessel attempting to jump overboard.
An unnamed U.S. official confirmed to CNN that a crew member went overboard and was rescued last month, an event that was viewed as a mental health incident by the Navy, according to the outlet.
More than 200 families of crew members attended a meeting in San Diego last week with acting Secretary of the Navy Hung Cao. Many of the families raised a litany of concerns at a later virtual meeting, including about the crew’s mental health, safety, a lack of supplies and food, and water contamination, according to MS Now, which reviewed recordings of the meeting.
Cao was unable to specify during the meeting when the crew on the Lincoln would return home, according to the outlet.
The U.S. military has strongly pushed back against reporting about mental health concerns regarding the Lincoln’s crew.
“We have not observed an increase in suicidal ideations or attempts aboard the ship,” a U.S. official tells TIME. “Adapting to life at sea can be difficult, so we've learned how to provide resources and help Sailors with these transitions. We are not experiencing an uptick in mental health issues aboard Abraham Lincoln.”
The official says that “religious, medical and mental health professionals” are aboard the Lincoln, including five chaplains, a psychologist, a social worker, three "behavioral health technicians,” and a service dog “to support crew morale and emotional welfare.”
The official did not provide information regarding the ongoing deployment of those aboard the Lincoln “due to operations security.”
“The Sailors and Marines of the Abraham Lincoln Carrier Strike Group remain resilient and resolved after more than 260 days at sea, 10,000 aircraft flights, and 1.5 million pounds of ordnance expended,” U.S. Central Command posted on X on Thursday. “No service members aboard the aircraft carrier have died, and the one Sailor who fell overboard Aug. 3 was quickly and safely recovered.”
Democrats push for answers
The reports about conditions on board the Lincoln have sparked calls from several Democrats urging the Defense Department to remedy the situation.
In a letter to Hegseth and Cao, Sen. Richard Blumenthal of Connecticut, a member of the Senate Armed Services Committee, noted that the vessel’s crew members have not been to a port in a record-setting 200-plus days and demanded answers to a series of questions about the crew and the state of the ship.
“There have been widespread reports of shortages of basic supplies, water contamination, plumbing issues, deteriorating mental health, deck safety concerns, and disruptions in the mail system,” Blumenthal wrote. “These reports warrant immediate attention, but they also raise a broader question: whether the Navy can sustain the operational tempo now being demanded of its carrier force, particularly as this Administration repeatedly commits U.S. forces to conflicts of its own choosing and increasingly relies on aircraft carriers to sustain those operations.”
He also noted that the long deployment of the Lincoln is not an isolated incident, “suggesting that extended deployments may be becoming a feature rather than an exception of the Navy's force-generation model.” The USS Gerald R. Ford, used for the U.S.’s military operation in Venezuela, spent 326 days at sea before its return in May, Blumenthal wrote, which he noted was “nearly twice the length of a traditional six-month carrier deployment and the longest modern U.S. carrier deployment since the Vietnam era.”
Sen. Ruben Gallego requested an oversight visit to investigate the reports.
“Unlike Donald Trump, I've seen active duty,” Gallego wrote on X. “The way he's treating our service members as he carries out this illegal war is not just disgusting; it’s dangerous. These sailors are owed a sense of when they will go home.”
Gallego referenced the reports of crew members threatening to jump overboard, shifts lasting as long as 16 hours, rationed meals, and moldy showers, which he called “a frightening alarm bell.”
Rep. Sara Jacobs of California, who has introduced a War Powers Resolution to restrict Trump’s authority to continue the conflict in Iran without congressional approval, said that the Lincoln’s crew was “going through hell” and called for an end to the war. She described the reported poor conditions on the carrier as “a personnel issue and a national security risk.”
Sen. Mark Kelly of Arizona, a Navy veteran, has also taken to social media to call for accountability.
“Our servicemembers deserve better than this,” he said in a video posted to Bluesky. “There needs to be an investigation.” Kelly also blamed Trump having “no way out” of the war with Iran for the extended deployment of those aboard the Lincoln.
Rep. Mike Levin, who represents part of the San Diego region where the Lincoln was deployed from in November, took jabs at Hegseth’s comments downplaying the reports about the carrier.
“When families first raised the alarm back in April, Pete Hegseth called it fake news,” he wrote on X. “These men and women signed up to serve their country. The least their country owes them is hot water, a working toilet, and a real meal. Hegseth cannot even manage that, and he has the nerve to look their families in the eye and call them liars.”
A number of other Democrats have also joined the chorus of concerned voices over the Lincoln, including Rep. Jason Crow of Colorado; Rep. Seth Moulton of Massachusetts; and Sen. Chris Coons of Delaware, the top Democrat on the Senate Defense Appropriations subcommittee.

articles.title: Zelenskyy announces new sanctions rounds against Russian defence industry, financial sector, intermediaries
articles.body:
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy announced new rounds of sanctions against the Russian military-industrial complex, the financial sector, and intermediaries.
"Today, Ukraine has a sanctions package targeting companies and ships that are transporting grain and other goods stolen from Ukraine's temporarily occupied territories. We are preparing new sanctions packages against the Russian military-industrial complex, financial networks, and intermediaries," he said in an evening video address on Friday.
According to him, there are still a significant number of Russian enterprises working for the war effort. "This must be addressed during August and September. We will speak with leaders at all working levels. The Ukrainian diplomatic service has a direct task: in the world's major jurisdictions, sanctions must be imposed on those Russian companies and individuals, as well as those who help Russia, whose influence genuinely matters in terms of prolonging this war and producing Russian missiles and drones," Zelenskyy said.
Zelenskyy also outlined the immediate tasks for the Defense Forces in the context of Ukraine's long-range sanctions. "Thanks to all the decisions made last autumn – political decisions, financial decisions, and the technological choices we made a year ago – we were able to transition to a significantly more technologically advanced defense system this winter and this spring. The long-range sanctions plan is being carried out, along with an increasing number of our mid-range strikes. In fact, we have succeeded in blocking Russia's south, and we are expanding this strategic operation – quite justifiably – in response to Russian strikes on our ports and our cities," he said.
The President of Ukraine said every level of pressure on Russia "must lead this country, and its society, above all, to the desire to end their war. "Our sanctions against Russian oil refineries and their facilities in the Russian oil sector, our strikes against Russian military logistics, and our operation in the Black Sea and Azov Sea, all of this works to limit Russia's war potential."
"It is important to continue this effort with more active political and legal measures as well," he said.

articles.title: Russia, Ukraine trade overnight drone strikes targeting port, industrial facilities
articles.body:
Burc Eruygur
15 August 2026•Update: 15 August 2026
- Zelenskyy says key enterprise within Russian space agency Roscosmos in Samara region, air base in Nizhny Novgorod region hit by Ukraine overnight, while Moscow yet to comment
Russia and Ukraine on Saturday renewed accusations against each other concerning overnight drone strikes, which have targeted port infrastructure and industrial facilities.
In Russia, Samara Governor Vyacheslav Fedorishchev said on Telegram that Ukraine launched a missile strike on an unspecified “industrial facility.”
“An emergency response team has been formed. All emergency services are on the ground,” Fedorishchev said, noting that authorities are assessing the situation, including with regard to casualties.
Samara Mayor Ivan Noskov wrote separately on Russian social media platform Max that the city’s industrial infrastructure sustained “localized damage,” adding that medical assistance has been provided to those injured.
“In Russia’s Samara region, one of the key enterprises within (Russian space agency) Roscosmos – the Progress Center, which was involved, among other things, in electronics production – was hit. Flamingo missiles were used,” Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said in a statement shared on US social media platform X.
Zelenskyy further claimed strikes on the Savasleyka air base in Russia’s Nizhny Novgorod region, adding Kyiv also received confirmation on damage it aimed to inflict at an oil facility in Ust-Luga, situated in the country’s northern Leningrad region.
Russian authorities have not yet commented on Zelenskyy’s remarks, though the country’s Defense Ministry claimed its air defenses shot down 598 Ukrainian drones overnight across 19 regions, as well as over the Black Sea, the Sea of Azov, and Crimea, which Moscow annexed in 2014.
The ministry later claimed that, since Friday evening, the Russian military hit a warehouse in the port of Pivdennyi, a patrol boat and warehouse in the port of Odesa, and infrastructure in the port of Izmail, which it alleged are “involved in supporting the Ukrainian Armed Forces.”
In Ukraine, Odesa Governor Oleh Kiper said that strikes in his region hit the grounds of a shoe factory, damaging warehouses and a canteen, as well as causing fires.
“There were also fires on the territory of a non-working enterprise and an abandoned private residential building. Rescuers have now extinguished all fires,” Kiper further said, noting that there are no casualties based on preliminary information.
Zaporizhzhia Governor Ivan Fedorov said that a shopping center and an unspecified industrial facility were targeted overnight by Russian drones. He later reported that five people were injured during morning strikes.
Meanwhile, Dnipropetrovsk Governor Oleksandr Hanzha said that a 3-month-old baby died and 11 others were injured following a drone strike on a multi-story building in the city of Marhanets.
Ukraine’s Air Force claimed that the country’s air defenses downed 124 out of 152 drones launched by Russia overnight.
Moscow and Kyiv have increasingly targeted each other's logistics centers, as well as port and energy infrastructure, during the ongoing war.
Both sides deny deliberately targeting civilian infrastructure, maintaining that their strikes are directed at military targets or facilities linked to military activities.

articles.title: Ukraine’s Flamingo Missiles Strike Russia’s Soyuz Rocket Factory Behind Its Starlink Rival
articles.body:
- Category
- War in Ukraine
Ukraine’s Flamingo Missiles Strike Russia’s Soyuz Rocket Factory Behind Its Starlink Rival
Ukraine’s Flamingo cruise missiles struck the Progress Rocket Space Centre in Samara overnight on August 15, hitting the factory that produces Soyuz-2 launch vehicles used to deploy Russian military satellites and the Rassvet low-Earth-orbit network—Moscow’s answer to Starlink.
The apparent confirmation that Flamingo cruise missiles were used in the attack came from Fire Point co-founder Denis Shtilerman, who shortly after the strike posted nighttime footage showing the launch of the Ukrainian-made missile.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
Samara regional governor Vyacheslav Fedorishchev confirmed that a missile strike had hit an industrial facility in the city but did not identify the target. Samara Mayor Ivan Noskov described the attack as a large-scale missile strike.
Local residents reported explosions shortly after a missile alert was issued in the region. Videos published from Samara showed a large fire and a column of smoke rising from an industrial area occupied by the neighboring Progress Rocket Space Centre and Aviakor aircraft plant.
According to Defense Express on August 15, available imagery indicates that the strike may have hit Progress, one of Russia’s key producers of space launch vehicles. The outlet said satellite imagery would still be required to confirm the precise impact point and determine the extent of the damage.
Progress is one of the central enterprises in Russia’s space-launch industry and manufactures the Soyuz-2 family of launch vehicles, including the Soyuz-2.1b.
The Soyuz-2.1b is used to place Russian government and military spacecraft into orbit and has also been used to deploy satellites for Rassvet, a planned Russian low-Earth-orbit communications constellation often described as Moscow’s counterpart to Starlink. On March 23, 2026, a Soyuz-2.1b launched 16 satellites associated with the Rassvet system.
According to Defense Express, the Samara plant represents a particularly concentrated point in Russia’s Soyuz production chain. The enterprise consists of an interconnected industrial complex roughly one kilometer long where launch vehicles pass through successive stages of assembly.
The outlet assessed that the reported strike may have affected the western section of the complex, where later stages of Soyuz production are believed to take place.
Defense Express reported that Russia has conducted approximately six to eight Soyuz-2.1b launches annually since 2022, with the rockets supporting military, government and other space missions.
Soyuz remains one of Russia’s primary methods for placing military satellites into orbit, meaning disruption at Progress could also affect reconnaissance, communications and other space programs beyond Rassvet.
Vadym Skibitskyi, deputy chief of Ukraine’s Defense Intelligence, previously said Russia was developing the satellite system faster than initially expected. The constellation is intended to provide broadband communications from low Earth orbit and could support both civilian and military users.
The Progress and Aviakor facilities are located roughly 850–950 kilometers from Ukraine’s state border, placing the industrial complex deep inside Russian territory.
Earlier, Russia’s Rassvet satellite network was reported to face a major launch bottleneck because its satellites rely on Soyuz-2.1b rockets produced at the Progress Rocket Space Centre in Samara. Russia needs at least 18 Soyuz-2.1b launches to deploy the planned 288-satellite constellation, while only six to eight such rockets are typically launched per year.

articles.title: UFORCE promotes Magura combat record for U.S. bid
articles.body:
- UFORCE is promoting Ukrainian Magura drone strikes in Crimea ahead of a Pentagon prize challenge for drone-launching naval vessels.
- GUR confirmed strikes on two S-400 launchers, an Orion antenna, and a Pantsir-S1 system worth roughly $15 million.
UFORCE, the London-headquartered maker of Ukraine’s Magura naval drones, is touting a series of Ukrainian strikes on Russian air defenses in Crimea as evidence for its pitch to the Pentagon, days before the deadline for a Defense Innovation Unit prize challenge seeking naval drones that can launch their own aircraft.
Ukraine’s Defense Intelligence agency, GUR, said its Group 13 special operations unit destroyed or damaged Russian equipment in occupied Crimea in early August using Magura naval drones to carry smaller FPV drones toward the coast before launching them at targets on land. GUR said the unit hit two launchers from a Russian S-400 “Triumf” air defense battery and an antenna used to control “Orion” drones. In a separate strike the same week, GUR said Group 13 destroyed a Pantsir-S1 air defense system valued at roughly $15 million, along with a military crane. GUR’s own public statements put the total cost to Russian forces at tens of millions of dollars, without giving a more precise figure.
UFORCE said the value of destroyed equipment topped $80 million, a figure not confirmed in GUR’s own public statements.
“From now on, our Maguras threaten the Russian occupiers on land as well, a fundamental shift in the battlespace,” said the commander of Group 13, who uses the callsign “Thirteenth.”
“What we are seeing in Crimea is exactly the fight UFORCE was built for. The Magura isn’t just a one-way-attack naval strike drone, it’s crossing hundreds of kilometers of open water and putting aerial drones on targets inland,” said Oleg Rogynskyy, chief executive of UFORCE. “That’s long-range strike effect at a fraction of what high-end systems cost. And nothing about it is specific to the Black Sea. Any contested waters, same logic. The future is battle-proven systems that work together and give operators options no single platform can.”
UFORCE said the operation showcases the same capability the Pentagon is now soliciting. The Defense Innovation Unit opened its Suitable Warfighting Adaptive Payloads (SWAP-USV) challenge in late July, offering $100 million in prize money for mature unmanned surface vessels integrated with at least two market-ready aerial drones able to detect and strike targets, with a Sprint 1 submission deadline of Aug. 10 and a further $200 million budgeted for follow-on production contracts. UFORCE has separately signed a memorandum of understanding with Alaska-based RECONCRAFT to build Magura vessels in the United States.
UFORCE’s release describes Magura’s hull as modified with hatches that open at sea, letting onboard FPV drones launch and fly toward nearby targets rather than being flown from shore, extending their range and reducing the time they spend exposed to jamming.
The company says it consolidated nine Ukrainian defense-technology developers, including the teams behind Magura and its Nemesis strike drone line, which includes a Magura-launched variant called SEASTRIKE. UFORCE’s statement did not specify whether Nemesis or SEASTRIKE, rather than the FPV drones GUR described, were the aircraft used in the Crimea strikes.

articles.title: Zelensky Signals More Deep Strikes as Ukraine ‘Blocks Off Russia’s South’
articles.body:
Ukraine has “succeeded in blocking off Russia’s south” and is expanding its operations in response to Russian attacks on Ukrainian ports and cities, President Volodymyr Zelensky said Friday.
Ukrainian strikes on Russian oil refineries and other facilities, alongside military operations in the Black Sea and Sea of Azov, are aimed at limiting Moscow’s capacity to continue the war.
JOIN US ON TELEGRAM
Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official.
“The long-range sanctions plan is being implemented, and there are more and more of our mid-range strikes as well,” Zelensky said in his evening address on Aug. 14.
Kyiv describes the campaign as “long-range sanctions” – combining deep military strikes with economic and legal pressure on the infrastructure and networks sustaining Russia’s war.
On Friday, Zelensky signed sanctions targeting individuals and companies involved in the illegal export of Ukrainian grain from Russian-occupied territories, as well as vessels used in those operations.
Ukraine has also prepared new sanctions packages targeting Russia’s military-industrial sector, financial networks and intermediaries helping Moscow sustain its war.
Zelensky called for Ukraine’s measures to be replicated by major international jurisdictions, arguing that Russian companies, individuals and those assisting them should face broader restrictions.
The president also renewed calls for frozen Russian assets to produce tangible benefits for Ukraine.
Zelensky: Ukraine Expects 30,000 Russian Occupiers to Be ‘Eliminated’ in August
Zelensky has repeatedly described Ukrainian deep strikes as a tool for forcing Moscow toward peace.
The message behind “long-range sanctions” is straightforward: as long as Russia continues its occupation and attacks on Ukraine, the infrastructure supporting Moscow’s war will remain under pressure.

articles.title: Putin’s recruiters scramble to avoid second mass mobilisation as Ukraine losses mount
articles.body:
In kitchens and Telegram chats across Russia, the same question is being asked with growing frequency: will Vladimir Putin order another mobilisation?
Nearly five years into the war, Russia is scrambling to find enough soldiers to replenish its ranks, as voluntary recruitment slows and its forces suffer heavy losses on the battlefield in Ukraine.
With Putin showing no sign of abandoning his far-reaching territorial demands, even as Russia’s summer offensive stalls, the Kremlin faces a growing manpower headache.
“The problem for the Kremlin is that it is getting much harder to find people willing to fight, even for crazy money,” said Aleksei Tabalov, a human rights activist and director of an organisation that helps Russian conscripts.
Putin last resorted to mobilisation in September 2022, when a series of dramatic battlefield setbacks forced the Kremlin to call up 300,000 reservists to stabilise the front.
Since then, Moscow has avoided another deeply unpopular call-up by relying largely on high paid voluntary contracts to fill the ranks with roughly 1.3 million contract soldiers Russia has recruited since.
Men, particularly from Russia’s poorer regions, have been offered life-changing signing bonuses and salaries on open-ended contracts amounting to several years of local wages, alongside substantial payouts to their families if they are killed.
But Russia’s heavy losses mean it must continue finding new soldiers at a high rate.
Western estimates put Russian casualties at more than 30,000 killed and wounded a month, a toll that reflects the army’s attritional “meat grinder” tactics, in which troops are repeatedly sent forward in small assault groups despite heavy losses.
Moscow, meanwhile, now recruits roughly 1,000 soldiers a day, according to calculations by Janis Kluge, a Russia expert at the German Institute for International and Security Affairs, which means most new recruits are used to replenish depleted units rather than expand Russia’s offensive capacity.
That has once again raised the prospect of mobilisation.
Top Russian officials have dismissed reports of an impending call-up, with former president Dmitry Medvedev describing them as “nonsense” and a “lying provocation” by Ukraine.
Two people familiar with discussions in Moscow also said there was no indication that Putin had decided to order another mass mobilisation. A senior western official likewise said there were no signs that a decision had been taken.
But fears that another call-up may be on the way have nevertheless increasingly entered everyday conversations.
In Telegram chats used by local sports teams, work colleagues and groups of friends, Russians swap rumours about a possible mobilisation and share advice on securing exemptions or avoiding the draft. Some speculate that a new call-up could come after September’s elections to the Duma.
“It’s guesswork right now whether mobilisation will actually happen,” said Ivan Chuviliaev, a spokesperson for Get Lost, a group that helps Russian soldiers desert.
But he said the renewed speculation was already being exploited to boost recruitment.
“The panic around mobilisation is being used by officials to pressure men into signing contracts,” Chuviliaev said. “The message is: mobilisation is coming anyway, so you might as well sign a contract now and get a payout before you’re forced to fight.”
For now, people familiar with the Kremlin’s thinking say the authorities appear determined to strong-arm more men into signing contracts rather than risk another mobilisation.
Over the summer, lawyers and activists have documented increasingly coercive recruitment tactics in several regions, with men detained on the street by police, taken from workplaces or summoned to stations – before being brought to military recruitment offices and pressed to sign contracts.
“It has turned into a hunt for people,” said Tabalov. “Under various pretexts, through deception, blackmail, violence and threats, they are forcing them to sign contracts.”
Tabalov said recruiters were increasingly targeting what he described as “socially marginalised” men, including those with debts, criminal cases or other vulnerabilities that could be used to put pressure on them to enlist.
In the southern Penza region, where some of the most aggressive draft methods have been reported, videos posted online have shown men being driven away in vans as relatives protested outside recruitment offices. Activists say some have been threatened with prosecution or beaten until they agreed to sign.
The search has widened elsewhere too. Universities, technical colleges and vocational schools have been encouraged to recruit students into newly formed drone units, offering another source of manpower for the military. Putin recently signed a law expanding the pool of convicted prisoners eligible to sign contracts with the army, including people convicted of “serious and especially serious crimes”.
Much of the responsibility for finding soldiers has been pushed down to Russia’s regions.
Governors and local administrations are expected to meet recruitment targets set by Moscow, giving the Kremlin some distance from the drive while leaving regional officials responsible for finding enough men in their own territories.
Around that system, a lucrative recruitment industry has emerged. Regional governments offer thousands of dollars not only to soldiers who sign contracts but also to those who find them, with “bring a friend” schemes paying residents for every person they persuade to enlist.
Private recruiters and public-sector employees scour social media for candidates, while advertisements for military contracts have become ubiquitous online. Russian regions have paid recruiters at least 7.7bn roubles ($96m) since such schemes were introduced, according to the independent Russian outlet IStories.
One recruiter in central Russia, speaking to the Guardian on condition of anonymity, said his organisation was expected to find between 20 and 30 men each month, with bonuses for exceeding the target and penalties for falling short.
“It was easier last year,” the recruiter said. “Now it is getting harder.”
The recruiter said mobilisation was also being discussed in his office, but that there had been no orders or indications that a new draft was imminent.
Another mass call-up, however, would carry significant political risks for the Kremlin.
The 2022 call-up triggered one of the biggest episodes of domestic disruption since the invasion began, prompting a mass exodus of Russians and a sharp drop in Putin’s approval ratings.
It would also come at a potentially sensitive moment. Recent polling suggests confidence in the course of the war is weakening, with the share of Russians who believe the campaign in Ukraine is going well falling to its lowest level since April 2022.
For now, analysts say Moscow is more likely to step up recruitment efforts through higher bonuses, pressure on regional officials and increasingly coercive tactics.
Whether that will be enough could ultimately determine if Putin resorts to another mobilisation, said Tabalov, the activist.
The options before the Kremlin, Tabalov said, could range from another mass call-up to a more selective mobilisation, sending existing conscripts to the front or quietly calling up reservists for frontline service.
“I don’t think they’ll be able to recruit enough people under the current system,” Tabalov said. “Then they’ll be faced with the question of what form mobilisation should take.”

articles.title: ‘We’ll Warm Ourselves With the Fire of Russian Oil Refineries’: Ukraine Hits Back at Russia
articles.body:
Ukraine’s Armed Forces responded to a Russian defense ministry post that appeared to threaten intensified attacks on Ukrainian energy infrastructure this winter with a warning about strikes on Russian oil refineries.
On Friday, the Strategic Communications Department of the Armed Forces of Ukraine published an image on Telegram showing a fire at an industrial facility with the caption: “We’ll warm ourselves with the fire of Russian oil refineries.”
JOIN US ON TELEGRAM
Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official.
The post appeared to be a response to a message published earlier by Russia’s defense ministry featuring Shahed attack drones and the caption: “Like snow on your head.”
The Russian message appeared to hint at further attacks on Ukraine’s energy infrastructure during the winter, when Moscow has repeatedly targeted power generation and heating infrastructure.
The reference to “freezing” also comes amid renewed discussions about a possible halt to hostilities. However, the Russian post appeared to suggest that Moscow could instead continue or intensify attacks on Ukraine’s energy system.
However, Ukraine’s Armed Forces responded with a direct warning aimed at Russia’s oil industry.
The image posted by the Strategic Communications Department showed a large fire at what appears to be an industrial facility, alongside the message about “warming” with the fire of Russian oil refineries.
The Ukrainian military did not provide details about any planned strikes or identify specific potential targets.
‘Only a Madman’ Would Say Sending Patriots to Ukraine Weakens Poland, Polish Minister Says
Russia rejects ceasefire efforts
The exchange came amid renewed discussions about possible limited ceasefires and restrictions on attacks against civilian infrastructure.
Reuters recently reported that Ukraine had proposed to Russia, through a third party, a mutual halt to attacks on civilian targets in the Black Sea. Russian officials said they had not received any formal proposal.
Turkish Foreign Minister Hakan Fidan has also called on Ukraine and Russia to develop a mechanism for a moratorium on attacks against ships in the Black Sea, according to Ukraine’s FM Andrii Sybiha.
However, on Friday, Russian Foreign Minister Sergey Lavrov rejected a halt to fighting along the current line of contact. Lavrov also threatened to make Russia’s approach “harsher,” saying Moscow would seek to destroy what he described as everything supporting Ukraine’s military machine from the West.
The latest statements from both sides come as Ukraine and Russia continue to signal that energy and other critical infrastructure could remain central targets as the war enters another winter.

articles.title: Ukraine strike hits Russia’s main space rocket maker
articles.body:
- Russian officials confirmed a missile strike on an industrial facility in Samara overnight Aug. 15, without naming the target.
- Ukrainian open-source analysts identified the likely target as Building 106A of the Progress rocket-space center.
Ukrainian long-range strikes hit an industrial site in Samara, Russia, overnight into Aug. 15, triggering a regional air raid alert and a series of explosions residents reported hearing across the city, according to Russian officials and Ukrainian open-source monitoring of the aftermath.
Samara region governor Vyacheslav Fedorishchev confirmed that a missile struck an industrial enterprise in the region, saying emergency services and an operational headquarters were on site and that details on casualties were still being clarified. He did not name the facility. Samara Mayor Ivan Noskov later said a “massed attack” by enemy missiles caused localized damage to the city’s industrial infrastructure, adding that Russian air defenses had intercepted part of the attack. Neither official specified how many missiles were involved or which weapon system struck the ground.
The Ukrainian open-source analysis group CyberBoroshno, which has previously published satellite-imagery assessments of Flamingo missile strikes inside Russia, said the strike most likely used a Ukrainian FP-5 “Flamingo” cruise missile and identified the impact point as Building 106A at the Progress facility, geolocating it to coordinates 53.217623, 50.303163.
Ukrainian commentator Oleh Ponomar separately reported the same conclusion, citing the group’s “GEOINT collective” analysis. Neither Ukraine’s military nor Progress itself had publicly confirmed the specific building as of this writing, and the claim rests on CyberBoroshno’s imagery review rather than official acknowledgment from either government.
According to CyberBoroshno’s assessment, Building 106A is part of the production complex for the Soyuz launch vehicle family and operates as a cleanroom facility, where onboard electrical systems, instruments and circuit boards are installed. The group described the building’s function as producing the rocket’s guidance and control systems, cable network and instrument compartment, work that must be completed before a rocket can be considered finished even after its airframe and fuel tanks are built. CyberBoroshno said a neighboring structure, Building 106B, serves as the final assembly point for completed rockets and may also have been damaged by the blast.
Progress, formerly known as TsSKB-Progress, has produced Soviet and Russian launch vehicles since the 1950s, including the R-7-derived rocket that carried Yuri Gagarin into orbit in 1961. It is Russia’s only facility that performs series production of the Soyuz-2 family of launch vehicles, used both for crewed and uncrewed missions and for placing military and commercial satellites into orbit. The plant also builds electro-optical reconnaissance and Earth-observation satellites.
CyberBoroshno said the facility’s significance lies in that exclusivity. The group said Soyuz-2 rockets built at Progress launch and replenish Russia’s military satellite constellations, including the Liana network used for signals intelligence and targeting and the Persona and Razdan optical reconnaissance satellites, as well as the Rassvet broadband satellite constellation operated by Bureau 1440, a Russian company building a domestic answer to Starlink. Public launch records reviewed independently show that Bureau 1440’s Rassvet satellites, including test and commercial batches launched in 2023 and again in March and July 2026, have so far flown exclusively aboard Soyuz-2.1b rockets from the Vostochny and Plesetsk cosmodromes, a pattern consistent with CyberBoroshno’s characterization, though it could not be independently confirmed that no other launch vehicle has ever been used or is planned.
CyberBoroshno assessed that recovery from fire and firefighting water inside a cleanroom facility would take considerably longer than a conventional industrial repair. The group said restoring the site would require reclassifying clean-room zones, recertifying the manufacturing process and re-testing for airborne particulate contamination, work it estimated in months rather than weeks. The group also said Soyuz onboard electronics depend on imported components subject to export restrictions that Russia cannot currently readily replace, though it did not provide further detail on which specific components would be affected.
The FP-5 Flamingo, built by the Ukrainian company Fire Point, is a ground-launched cruise missile with a published range of up to 3,000 km (1,860 miles) and a warhead of roughly 1,000 to 1,150 kg (2,200 to 2,540 pounds). Ukraine first used the missile in combat in August 2025 against a Russian security service facility in Crimea, according to Ukrainian officials at the time. Fire Point told the Associated Press in 2025 that it aimed to raise production from an initial 30 units a month to 210 units a month by October of that year, though independent verification of actual output has remained limited. CyberBoroshno has previously attributed Flamingo strikes to attacks on the VNIIR-Progress electronics plant in Cheboksary, a separate facility from the Samara center that manufactures satellite-navigation receivers and antennas, and on the Antipinsky oil refinery in Tyumen in July.
The scale of damage at the Samara site remains unresolved.

articles.title: Leaked Files Reveal How Russian Missile Giant Uses Front Brands to Bypass Sanctions
articles.body:
- Category
- World
Leaked Files Reveal How Russian Missile Giant Uses Front Brands to Bypass Sanctions
Internal procurement documents from Russia’s Khrunichev Centre—a key state enterprise behind the Angara launch vehicles—reveal how the country’s military-industrial complex bypasses international sanctions by utilizing front companies and rebranded foreign machinery, according to an investigation by Dallas Analytics, posted on August 13.
This scheme fits a broader pattern of restricted dual-use technology powering Moscow’s defense industry. Western-made computer numerical control (CNC) machine tools from American, European, and Japanese manufacturers continue to reach Russian weapons facilities—including plants producing the nuclear-capable Oreshnik missile—through third-party supply chains and Chinese intermediaries.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
While the documents list planned equipment purchases as domestic or originating from China, an analysis by Dallas Analytics shows that Russian “import substitution” relies heavily on relabeling industrial machine tools manufactured in Taiwan, China, and Japan.
The rebranding strategy: “Russian” umbrella brands
Russian companies presenting themselves as domestic machine-tool manufacturers frequently act as importers for foreign equipment, concealing the actual producers to insulate both themselves and their suppliers from international sanctions.
Dallas Analytics highlighted three key brands used in Khrunichev’s procurement plans:
- ProTech: Classified in the internal documents as Chinese, the brand’s most expensive listed item—the PFG-50150AHR surface grinder—is actually produced by PERFECT, a Taiwanese firm. PERFECT stated it officially ended its relationship with ProTech in March 2024 and did not supply that specific model directly. However, it acknowledged that global distributors could be circulating its products. The Russian legal entities tied to ProTech—JSC ProTekhnologii and LLC ProTekhnologii—remain unsanctioned by major Western jurisdictions.
- F-tech: Advertised as a manufacturer of CNC machining centers, F-tech lists a partner office in Shanghai that could not be verified in public databases. However, Russian regulatory filings tie the brand to F-TECH CNC LATHE in Anhui Province, China, sharing an address with machine-tool builder WMT. F-tech’s affiliated Russian legal entities, TD VtorTsvetMet LLC and ChVCM-RESURS LLC, are currently not designated under US, EU, or UK sanctions, Dallas Analytics wrote.
- Finist: Marketed by the Russian Finval group, the brand’s FF-38BSY machine tool is a direct rebrand of the SZ-386F manufactured by Chinese firm Shenzhen SOWIN Precision Machine Tool. While SOWIN is sanctioned by the UK and Ukraine, it is not subject to EU sanctions. Finval is sanctioned by the US, but the specific entity named in the Khrunichev procurement files—Finist Machinery Co., Ltd.—is not listed under any international sanctions regime.
Silence and gaps in enforcement
When contacted by Dallas Analytics regarding their supply chains to Russia, most Chinese manufacturers—including Anyang Forging Press, Ningbo Chuangji Machinery, and SOWIN—did not respond.
Taiwanese manufacturer Goodway Machine Tool Group similarly did not comment on findings indicating that its division, AWEA, may be the origin behind Khrunichev’s planned DYNO SEIKI imports.
Japanese manufacturer Sodick responded directly, stating that it halted trade with Russia in 2022 and conducts end-user verification. Dallas Analytics noted that the company stated that monitoring does not extend to equipment sold before 2022, despite current advertisements for Sodick tools continuing to circulate on Russian industrial websites.
The findings demonstrate that private-sector oversight and current end-user tracking mechanisms remain insufficient. Closing these loopholes will require government intervention from Taiwan, Japan, and Western nations, alongside fuller utilization of EU market access leverage to hold foreign suppliers accountable.
This flow of restricted industrial machinery parallels Russia’s illicit acquisition of Western microelectronics. According to another recent investigation, a massive, structured international supply system continues to channel high-reliability electronic components from major Western firms into Russia’s arms industry.
Through industry trade shows like ExpoElectronica, hundreds of Chinese distributors and Russian intermediaries—such as the unsanctioned supplier LifeElectronics—openly facilitate deliveries of restricted microchips to Russian defense contractors for the production of glide bombs, missiles, and other state defense orders.
