articles.title: Ukraine’s quiet counteroffensive took 745 square km. Russia’s dead Starlink is how
articles.body:
- In six months of unheralded advances, Ukrainian forces liberated a wide stretch of the southeast
- The collapse of Russian communications turned a local push into a six-month advance
- Now the Russians may mobilize yet again, so the Ukrainians are digging in and consolidating their gains
The scale of Ukrainian forces' counteroffensive in southeastern Ukraine early this year is finally becoming clear. In six months of maneuver starting on 29 January, a clutch of Ukrainian units, including the 78th, 79th, 80th, 82nd, and 95th Air Assault Brigades and the 1st and 425th Assault Regiments—tens of thousands of troops, in all—marched through gaps in Russian defenses and, according to Ukrainian officials, liberated around 745 square km and 26 settlements. Mostly in Dnipropetrovsk Oblast but also in neighboring Zaporizhzhia and Donetsk Oblasts.
That is Kyiv's own accounting, and it is the high end. The Institute for the Study of War, which maps control from geolocated imagery, put the figure at roughly 627 square km across the Oleksandrivka direction and the northern Hulyaipole direction—while noting its own conservative method probably undercounts. Either number describes the largest Ukrainian territorial gain since 2023.
The Ukrainian gains helped to offset Russian gains around the last few free cities in eastern Ukraine's Donetsk Oblast. Between the start of February and the end of July, Russian regiments captured a net total of just 260 square km of Ukrainian soil, according to a tally by the Black Bird Group. It would've been more than 1,000 square km if those air assault and assault units hadn't been busy clearing the Russians from a wide swathe of the southeast.
The Ukrainian counteroffensive kicked off on 29 January. Three days later, Elon Musk's Starlink bricked Russia's thousands of smuggled and stolen satellite terminals. Practically overnight, the Russians lost their best method for controlling small drones and guiding assault units across the disputed gray zone. Drones couldn't fly. Troops couldn't navigate.
Ukrainian commanders surely knew their communications advantage wouldn't last: the Russians would eventually adapt with new methods of command and control. Seizing the opportunity, Ukrainian paratroopers and assault troops pressed the attack. And in stark contrast to the usual assault tactics for both sides, the Ukrainians attacked in tanks and other armored vehicles, counting on the Russians' connectivity problems to clear a path for heavy forces.
The blackout was not the only thing working in Ukraine's favor. ISW credits the gains to five reinforcing factors: better operational planning, a campaign to suppress and destroy Russian air defenses, deeper strikes on Russian logistics, Ukrainian drone superiority at the tactical level—and the Starlink cutoff. But the cutoff is the one that arrived all at once, and it arrived just as Ukrainian armor was starting to move.
Mechanized assaults
Not all the vehicles got through. The assault troops lost one up-armored M-1 Abrams tank in early February. But by March, other assault forces M-1s were engaging Russian troops at point-blank range with their 120-mm main guns. After clearing a few disputed villages along a 45-km front between Dobropillya and Zelenyi Hai, the Ukrainians focused their maneuver and firepower on Komar, 12 km southeast of Zelenyi Hai.
The Ukrainians "started a slow and quiet offensive, with very few videos and small teams, during April and May," mapper Clément Molin recalled. The strict information security obscured the Ukrainian moves for all but the closest observers, allowing Ukrainian commanders to press their attacks without drawing too much attention—and risking a Russian countercounteroffensive.
By summer, the Ukrainians were within mortar range of Komar. Embarrassed Russian commanders resorted to sending out small teams on virtual suicide missions to plant Russian flags in disputed territory. The flags could create the impression of Russian control on terrain that, in fact, neither side controlled. "Russia is trying to intoxicate us with flag videos, which are meant to hide the real situation to both us and their command," Molin wrote.
The reality was that the Ukrainians had gained ground. A lot of it.
Trending Now
Announcing the results on 12 August, Ukrainian officials also claimed 9,550 Russian troops killed and more than 6,600 wounded—figures no independent body has verified. Former commander in chief Oleksandr Syrskyi, who planned the operation, said it proved the Ukrainian army "is capable not only of steadfastly holding its defences, but also of launching offensives, seizing the initiative, and liberating Ukrainian land."
But the momentum was unsustainable. As the Russians gradually restored command and control through the summer, the Ukrainians encountered more resistance. Now the gray zone is stabilizing again. Observer Moklasen predicted new Ukrainian commander in chief Maj. Gen. Mykhailo Drapatyi will order his corps and brigade commanders "to dig in positions, consolidate and strengthen more army corps" instead of continuing to attack.
After all, the Russians are pushing hard in Donetsk, and the resources the Ukrainians had devoted to the southeastern counteroffensive could boost the defensive effort in the east. Moreover, there are worrying signs the Kremlin may attempt another mobilization soon, potentially surging hundreds of thousands of fresh troops into Ukraine.
The Ukrainians may soon prioritize holding over attacking.

articles.title: Japan Weighs New Russia Sanctions After Putin’s First Visit to Disputed Kuril Islands
articles.body:
- Category
- World
Japan Weighs New Russia Sanctions After Putin’s First Visit to Disputed Kuril Islands
Japan is weighing additional sanctions on Russia after the Russian leader, Vladimir Putin, traveled to the disputed Kuril Islands on August 13, his first visit as the leader.
A senior Japanese Foreign Ministry official told reporters that Tokyo is "considering what step to take going forward," Kyodo News reported on August 14.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
Putin traveled to Iturup, known in Japan as Etorofu and the largest of the four Russian-held islands Tokyo claims, days after overseeing Russian Pacific Fleet exercises in the Far East. According to the Russian government, he visited a fish-processing plant, a hospital and a school and met with local residents.
Tokyo summoned Russia's ambassador, Nikolay Nozdrev, and lodged a formal protest, calling the visit "totally unacceptable." Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi declared the islands "an inherent part of Japanese territory both historically and under international law."
The Institute for the Study of War (ISW) assessed that the Kremlin is likely using the visit to deter Japan from adopting a more assertive defense posture. The move also aims to discourage EU seizures of Russian shadow-fleet vessels, tying the island dispute to the pressure campaign around Moscow's war against Ukraine.
Russia and Japan have never signed a peace treaty to end World War II, a stalemate entirely rooted in the Kurils. Soviet forces seized the four southernmost islands—Iturup, Kunashir, Shikotan and the Habomai islets—in the war's final weeks, expelling the Japanese residents. Japan calls them the Northern Territories and has never dropped the claim.
The visit lands as Tokyo's posture toward Moscow hardens. Japan's 2026 Defense White Paper, published earlier this month, named Russia among the country's principal threats. Putin criticized the paper on Wednesday, asserting the islands became Russian territory "as a result of World War II" and accusing Japan of imposing "unprovoked sanctions" over the war in Ukraine.
The trip closes even the pretense of a diplomatic thaw. Under former Prime Minister Shinzo Abe, Takaichi's political mentor, Japan met Putin 27 times in pursuit of a peace treaty. In 2018, the two sides agreed to accelerate talks on a 1956 declaration that envisaged returning Shikotan and the Habomai islets after a treaty was signed. Russia's full-scale invasion of Ukraine froze those negotiations in 2022.
The visit is not without precedent. In 2010, then-President Dmitry Medvedev became the first Russian head of state to visit the islands, traveling to Kunashir, a move that drew a formal protest without severing bilateral contact. Putin's trip arrives as a harder marker, set against Russia's sustained war footing rather than a peacetime dispute.
Ukraine has staked out its own position in the row, aligning with Tokyo against Moscow. Kyiv's parliament recognized the islands as Japanese territory in 2022, and President Volodymyr Zelenskyy signed a decree affirming Japan's sovereignty over its Northern Territories.
The protest has drawn a combative response from Moscow, where Security Council deputy chairman Dmitry Medvedev warned that Tokyo's insistence on its historical claim would change nothing and threatened grave consequences should Japan continue to press it. He dismissed Takaichi's position outright, asserting the islands had always been and would remain Russian territory.

articles.title: US maintains 400-plus aircraft build-up around Iran
articles.body:
More than 200 US aerial refuelling aircraft and upwards of 230 combat jets have been tracked across the Middle East and the wider network supporting American air operations in the region, according to open-source analysis compiled by UK Defence Journal Senior Editor Jon, known as DefenceGeek on X, alongside the Military Air Tracking Alliance.
The assessment draws together aircraft movements, unit deployments and other publicly available information to provide a snapshot of the scale and geographical spread of US air power positioned across the US Central Command area and supporting locations in Europe and the Atlantic.
A fast-jet order of battle published on 10 August placed the deployed force at around 237 aircraft, covering F-15E Strike Eagles, F-35A and F-35C Lightning IIs, F-16 Fighting Falcons, A-10C Thunderbolt IIs, EA-18G Growlers and F/A-18C/D Hornets.
US ORBAT – Fast-Jets – 10/AUG/2026 #IranWar
So as promised, here’s the slightly more detailed US Orders of Battle for fast-jets in CENTCOM available in case of further conflict with Iran. Due to the fact my list of airframes is over 250, I am not going to list individual… pic.twitter.com/59enR8x6m1
— DefenceGeek 🇬🇧 (@DefenceGeek) August 10, 2026
The largest individual contingent listed is the F-15E force, with 64 aircraft associated with deployments from the 4th Fighter Wing, 366th Fighter Wing and the RAF Lakenheath-based 494th Fighter Squadron. The figure includes two aircraft recorded as unidentified combat losses.
A further 55 F-35As are listed, including aircraft from the Vermont Air National Guard’s 158th Fighter Wing, Hill Air Force Base and RAF Lakenheath. Fifteen F-35As from Lakenheath’s 495th Fighter Squadron were recorded as deploying in July.
The F-16C/CM force is placed at 61 aircraft, with deployments involving units associated with South Carolina, Shaw Air Force Base, Spangdahlem, Aviano and Misawa. Eleven additional aircraft were recorded at Spangdahlem but excluded from the forward total because they had not deployed into the CENTCOM area.
Thirty A-10C Thunderbolt IIs are also listed across deployments involving the 107th Fighter Squadron, 124th Fighter Wing and units from Moody Air Force Base. The figure includes one aircraft recorded as an unidentified loss.
Naval and Marine Corps aircraft add another layer to the force. Twelve F/A-18C/D Hornets from VMFA-312 and ten F-35Cs from VMFA-311 are included, alongside six EA-18G Growlers from VAQ-135.
Another six EA-18Gs from VAQ-138 had previously been tracked at Lajes in the Azores and were initially excluded from the forward total. US imagery dated 3 August subsequently showed a VAQ-138 Growler operating in the CENTCOM area carrying an AN/ALQ-249(V)1 Next Generation Jammer Mid-Band pod, indicating continued movement through the wider deployment network.
The scale of that network becomes clearer when the tanker force is considered. A separate assessment dated 13 August records 209 US aerial refuelling aircraft across locations stretching from the United Kingdom and continental Europe to the Gulf and Indian Ocean. The total consists of 33 KC-46A Pegasus aircraft, 152 KC-135Rs, 23 KC-135Ts and a single KC-135RT.
Of the 209 tankers, 107 were placed in the assessment’s red zone closest to the principal area of operations. Another 48 were in the orange zone and 37 in the green zone farther west. Sixteen were recorded as having returned to the United States during the previous two weeks, with one aircraft listed as being at another or unidentified location.
The accompanying map shows tanker locations across a broad chain of bases. RAF Mildenhall is marked in the United Kingdom, with Lajes in the Azores, Avord and Istres in France, Stuttgart in Germany, Bucharest and Mihail Kogălniceanu in Romania, Bezmer in Bulgaria, Sigonella in Sicily and Souda Bay in Crete also forming part of the tracked network.
Farther east, tankers are shown at locations including Ben Gurion, Ovda and Ramon in Israel, Prince Sultan Air Base in Saudi Arabia, Al Udeid Air Base in Qatar and Al Dhafra Air Base in the United Arab Emirates.
Al Udeid and Al Dhafra had both returned to use by the tracked tanker force by 13 August after previously dropping out of the observed deployment pattern. Diego Garcia is also marked on the map as part of the wider support architecture. The British Indian Ocean Territory facility has long been used by the United States to support military operations across the Middle East and Indo-Pacific.
Aerial refuelling is central to sustaining combat air operations over the distances involved. Tankers allow fighters, electronic warfare aircraft, surveillance platforms and other assets to remain airborne for longer, while also supporting the movement of aircraft from bases in the United States and Europe to forward locations.
The numbers are based on open-source tracking rather than an official US military order of battle, and individual aircraft can move between locations without appearing on publicly accessible tracking systems. They therefore represent a snapshot of observable deployments rather than a definitive real-time inventory. The data shows a US combat-air presence numbering well above 200 fast jets backed by a tanker network of more than 200 aircraft distributed from Britain and the Atlantic through Europe and into the Middle East.

articles.title: Why Moldova is second on Putin’s list: what The New York Times learned the Kremlin’s plan to ‘collapse’ NATO and the EU from within
articles.body:
Why Moldova is second on Putin’s list: what The New York Times learned the Kremlin’s plan to ‘collapse’ NATO and the EU from within
Vladimir Putin gathered his military commanders for a briefing in late 2025 and set a goal for 2026: “the collapse of NATO and the EU from within,” The New York Times reported, citing officials from two countries familiar with the details of the meeting.
Moldova is central to those plans, according to the newspaper’s sources. Western intelligence officials say the Kremlin’s top priority is subjugating Ukraine, followed by taking control of Moldova. Around the same time, though — at a meeting of senior Defense Ministry officials — Putin publicly criticized European leaders for “stoking hysteria” over the threat of a Russian attack. “I’ve said this many times: it’s a lie, it’s nonsense, sheer nonsense — this talk of some imagined Russian threat to European countries,” he said.
Moldova would make an ideal staging ground for further Russian aggression against both Ukraine and the West, The Times’s sources said. They also said Putin still hopes to seize territory in southern Ukraine to create a land corridor linking Russia to Moldova.
To that end, Russia tried, among other things, to interfere in Moldova’s parliamentary elections, held on September 28, 2025, using cyberattacks, disinformation, vote-buying, and canvassing.
Moldovan priests were also enlisted in the Kremlin’s campaign. They traveled to Russia, where they were given Promsvyazbank debit cards. Back in Moldova, they were to be paid $1,000 to persuade parishioners to vote against the referendum on joining the European Union and to speak out against the country’s pro-Western policies. The elections were called “historic” at the time, with observers saying the future of Moldova’s European integration hinged largely on the outcome.
In the summer of 2025, a training camp was set up in Serbia. Its participants — most of them Moldovan citizens — were taught to use rifles, break through police lines, and set buildings on fire. They were paid $400 for a three- to four-day course. The instructors were operatives linked to Russian military intelligence — the GRU — and the camp was meant to build a cadre of fighters trained to disrupt elections, Western intelligence officials said.
A similar camp was held in Bosnia, and another outside Moscow. Moldovan prosecutors said more than 100 young Moldovans attended the Moscow camp and were taught to make and use incendiary materials and improvised explosive devices, and to handle drones “with special attachments for explosives or arson.”
Stanislav Secrieru, Moldova’s presidential adviser on national security and defense, said Russia wants to use Moldova “as a springboard for hostile activities against Ukraine as well as its main defense and financial supporter, the EU.” “For these reasons,” he said, “Russia allocated over the last few years unprecedented resources.”
Moldovan authorities, however, were prepared, according to The Times. In the weeks before the vote, police searched hundreds of homes and detained people who had trained at the camps. Moldova’s cybersecurity specialists, backed by Western allies, fended off the cyberattacks. President Maia Sandu’s party held on to its parliamentary majority. “We won the battle,” said Mihai Lupașcu, the director of Moldova’s Agency for Cybersecurity. “But we did not win the war.”
At Meduza, we are committed to transparency about our use of artificial intelligence in the newsroom. The story you’re reading was written by one of our living, breathing journalists and translated from Russian using an AI model configured to follow our strict editorial standards. This translation process is the result of extensive testing and refinements to ensure our English-language coverage is timely and accurate. A Meduza editor reviews every draft before publication.
If you find any errors in this translation, please contact us at [email protected].
To read Meduza’s exclusive content in English, please subscribe to our newsletter.

articles.title: Russia plans to remove border zones separating Russia from occupied Ukrainian territories
articles.body:
Russia’s Federal Security Service (FSB) plans to abolish special border zones along several boundaries with Ukrainian territories occupied by Russia, according to draft orders reviewed by the Russian outlet Agentstvo.
The proposed changes would remove restrictions that currently treat movement between Russia and occupied parts of Ukraine much like crossing an international border. The FSB says the move follows Russia’s claimed incorporation of the occupied Ukrainian territories into Russia.
FSB seeks to remove border zones
The draft orders, as reported by Ukrainska Pravda, would invalidate previous FSB orders establishing border zones along the boundaries between Russia’s Rostov and Voronezh oblasts and the occupied territories of Ukraine.
A similar change is planned for occupied Crimea, where the current border zone along the boundary with occupied Kherson Oblast would be abolished.
The existing rules effectively impose additional controls on people entering and leaving the occupied territories, making movement subject to procedures similar to those used at Russia’s state border.
In the draft orders, the FSB justifies the changes by referring to the alleged “admission into the Russian Federation” of the occupied parts of Donetsk, Luhansk, and Kherson oblasts.
Russia illegally claimed to annex those territories, along with Zaporizhzhia Oblast, in September 2022. The move has been rejected by Ukraine and the international community, and Russia does not control all of the territory it claims to have annexed.
Border zone would remain around Crimea's islands
The FSB proposal would not completely eliminate the border zone in occupied Crimea.
A restricted zone would remain “within the boundaries of the Black Sea islands belonging to the Russian Federation,” according to the draft. The FSB’s regional directorate would determine where and when people could enter the zone and would install warning signs.
The proposed changes would remove the existing border zones along Russia’s boundaries with occupied Ukrainian territories, while retaining a border zone around certain Black Sea islands in occupied Crimea.
Russia treats occupied territory as part of its territory
The planned changes reflect Moscow’s effort to incorporate occupied Ukrainian territories into Russia’s administrative and legal system.
In September 2022, Russian President Vladimir Putin signed so-called “accession treaties” claiming to incorporate Donetsk, Luhansk, Kherson, and Zaporizhzhia oblasts into Russia. Russia’s parliament subsequently approved the claims.
The treaties purported to define the boundaries of the annexed territories according to the borders they had on the day Russia claimed to admit them into the Russian Federation, despite Russia not controlling the entirety of those regions.
Russia previously used similar measures to formalize its control over occupied Crimea after illegally annexing the peninsula in 2014.

articles.title: Drones target Erbil as attacks fuel fears of regional spillover
articles.body:
Breadcrumb
Five drones target Erbil as attacks fuel fears of regional spillover
Five drones targeted the Iraqi Kurdish capital of Erbil at dawn on Friday, with US-led coalition air defences shooting down three of them, Kurdish security authorities said, in the latest in a series of attacks to hit the autonomous Kurdistan Region in recent weeks.
One of the drones fell near the Rotana Hotel in central Erbil after the interceptions, prompting panic among residents and scattering shrapnel across the populated area.
The Kurdistan Region’s Counter-Terrorism Service said there were no casualties in the attack.
The incident came a day after another drone struck a house in a residential neighbourhood of Erbil, underscoring mounting fears among civilians over the repeated attacks and the risks posed by falling debris after aerial interceptions.
Authorities have not publicly identified who launched Friday’s drones. However, a senior official in Erbil told The New Arab that the attacks appear to involve multiple actors operating from both inside Iraq and across the border in Iran.
The official said Iran’s Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) was targeting positions held by Iranian Kurdish opposition forces in the outskirts of Erbil, while Iraqi armed factions loyal to Tehran were launching attacks on sites in the region from the Nineveh Plain.
"The danger is not only related to the fall and explosion of the drones, but also to the fragments that are scattered with each attack over long distances, especially after the drones are intercepted by air defences," the official said.
"Residents live under constant security pressure. The sounds of planes and explosions, and their interceptions, have become part of the daily scene in the city."
Iraq’s semi-autonomous Kurdistan Region has experienced a growing number of drone, rocket and other attacks over recent weeks, affecting both Erbil and Sulaimaniyah provinces. The escalation has coincided with the US-Israel war with Iran and has continued despite no recent direct strikes between the three countries.
On 17 July, a deadly barrage of drones and rockets killed nine members of an Iranian Kurdish armed opposition group. The group blamed Tehran for the strikes, while Iran has long accused Iranian Kurdish opposition groups of acting in the interests of Western states and Israel.
The Kurdistan Region has repeatedly been exposed to attacks due to its sensitive geopolitical position. It hosts US troops, foreign oil companies and several Iranian Kurdish opposition groups, making it a focal point in the wider confrontation between Iran, its allied Iraqi factions, Washington and Israel.
Kurdish officials have previously said that some attacks were launched from Iranian territory, while others originated from within Iraqi soil.
Majid Balak, a member of the ruling Kurdistan Democratic Party, blamed the federal government in Baghdad for failing to halt the attacks.
"Protecting the airspace from internal and external attacks, and preventing the use of Iraqi territory to carry out attacks on security and facilities inside and outside the country, is the responsibility of the Iraqi government," Balak told The New Arab.
The continued strikes have raised concern that Erbil’s civilian areas could face greater danger even when air defences prevent drones from reaching their intended targets, as wreckage and explosive fragments fall into densely inhabited parts of the city.
Iran-backed militia warns Baghdad
Meanwhile, the head of the Iran-backed Badr group warned Baghdad against using force to disarm armed factions, arguing that a coercive campaign could "ignite civil war" as the government moves towards a looming 30 September deadline to bring all militias’ weapons under state control.
Mohammad Naji, head of the organisation’s political office, said in a statement posted on X that the use of force against armed groups in the country would deepen internal divisions and serve the interests of foreign powers, including the United States and Israel.
He conditioned a disarmament of weapons to three conditions: a complete withdrawal of US forces from Iraq, the removal of “strategic threats” and the full rebuilding of Iraq’s armed forces.
Naji also criticised Iraqi Prime Minister Ali al-Zaidi, accusing him of succumbing to pressure from Washington. Al-Zaidi had ordered officials to prepare a draft mechanism for the disarmament of Iraqi armed factions, arguing it undermines the authority of security institutions.

articles.title: Trump Plans to Claim Strait of Hormuz as US Territory
articles.body:
US President Donald Trump stated on Friday, Aug. 14, that he intends to declare the Strait of Hormuz a US territory following the conclusion of the war with Iran.
Accoding to Clash Report, speaking at the David S. Mack Training and Intelligence Center in Garden City, Trump said the US currently controls the waterway.
JOIN US ON TELEGRAM
Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official.
“After we finish defeating Iran, which is currently suffering a crushing defeat, I will fairly soon declare the Strait of Hormuz a territory of the United States,” Trump said. “Essentially, that is exactly what it is. We have established a blockade. No ship will pass unless we want it to.”
Reuters reported that commercial traffic through the Strait of Hormuz nearly halted on Friday following attacks on two additional vessels. The US government indicated it is prepared to maintain the maritime blockade indefinitely.
A senior Iranian source stated that negotiations to extend a June ceasefire agreement yielded no results. Following the breakdown of the ceasefire, Iran resumed attacks on vessels it claims are attempting to navigate the strait without authorization from Tehran.
Trump on Iran:
Pretty soon, I will be declaring the Hormuz Strait a territory of the United States. pic.twitter.com/ySyIIhvF5V
Iranian demands and prior negotiations
The escalation follows a list of demands issued by Iran for reopening the strait.
Mohammad Bagher Zolqadr, Secretary of Iran’s Supreme National Security Council, stated that Tehran requires the immediate lifting of the US naval blockade, the withdrawal of US military forces, an end to hostilities, financial compensation, and access to frozen assets.
Zelensky Struggles to Find Ukraine’s Next Envoy to Trump
On Aug. 2, Trump announced a temporary suspension of planned US military strikes to allow for diplomatic negotiations. He stipulated the immediate opening of the strait as a primary condition for any agreement.
Impact on US weapons stockpiles
The ongoing conflict has resulted in a depletion of US military stockpiles, affecting security commitments in other regions. The US has utilized over 1,500 Patriot interceptor missiles in the Middle East, reducing its current inventory to fewer than 1,700 units.
The shortage of Patriot systems, along with ATACMS and Precision Strike Missiles, has delayed arms shipments to partners in Europe and Asia, affecting Ukraine’s air defense capabilities against Russian attacks. In the Indo-Pacific, the Pentagon redeployed air defense units, naval destroyers, and Tomahawk missiles from allied nations to support the Middle East campaign.
In response, the US Department of Defense directed defense contractors to accelerate production. Defense Secretary Steve Feinberg issued a letter to leading defense companies requiring plans within 21 days to expand manufacturing capacity for critical weapons.

articles.title: Zelensky Confirms Flamingo Missile Strikes Deep in Russian Territory
articles.body:
President Volodymyr Zelensky confirmed on Saturday, Aug. 15, that Ukrainian forces executed long-range strikes targeting strategic facilities in Russia, including the use of “Flamingo“ missiles against an aerospace plant in the Samara region.
In a statement on Telegram, Zelensky detailed the outcomes of what he termed deep strikes into Russian territory.
JOIN US ON TELEGRAM
Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official.
He confirmed that the Progress Space Rocket Centre, a key enterprise within the Russian state corporation Roscosmos involved in electronics production, was struck in the Samara region.
Zelensky explicitly stated that “Flamingo” missiles were utilized for this attack, noting the facility is located approximately 900 kilometers from the Ukrainian border.
The president also reported that long-range weapons struck the Savasleyka airfield in the Nizhny Novgorod region. He specified that the base, situated roughly 700 kilometers from Ukraine, hosts aircraft used as carriers for Russian missiles targeting Ukrainian cities and villages.
Furthermore, Zelensky confirmed an attack on an oil facility in the port of Ust-Luga in the Leningrad region, located over 800 kilometers from the border, stating that the necessary damage to the target was recorded.
According to the General Staff of the Armed Forces of Ukraine, units of the Ukrainian Defense Forces struck the “Progress” Rocket and Space Center in Samara. A direct hit on the target was confirmed, followed by a fire on the facility’s grounds.
Romania Reports Fourth Discovery of Drone Debris in 24 Hours
The “Progress” Rocket and Space Center is one of the key enterprises in the Russian Federation’s rocket and space industry, producing launch vehicles of the “Soyuz” family. These are used to launch Russian spacecraft for military, reconnaissance, and communications purposes into orbit.
In particular, the “Soyuz-2.1b” is used to deploy the Russian “Rassvet” satellite constellation – a broadband satellite communications system that Russia positions as an analogue to Starlink.
The Progress Rocket and Space Center also manufactures Earth observation satellites, which the enemy uses for reconnaissance purposes.
The extent of the damage is being assessed.
In addition, the Savasleika airfield in the Nizhny Novgorod region of the Russian Federation was struck. A direct hit on the target was recorded, followed by a fire on the airfield grounds.
“Savasleika” is used, in particular, to base and deploy MiG-31K interceptor fighters – carriers of the Kh-47M2 “Kinzhal” aeroballistic missiles.
Prior reports of Samara aerospace plant strikes
The presidential confirmation followed reports from earlier on Saturday regarding explosions at industrial aerospace enterprises in Samara.
Following the initial blasts, Denis Shtilerman, chief designer at the Ukrainian defense company Fire Point, published footage depicting the launch of an FP-5 “Flamingo” missile.
Samara region Governor Vyacheslav Fedorishchev reported a missile strike on an unnamed industrial facility, while Mayor Ivan Noskov stated that the city’s industrial infrastructure sustained localized damage.
Open-source intelligence analysts reviewing images of the site identified the location as the shared industrial zone of the Aviakor aviation plant and the Progress Space Rocket Centre. Progress manufactures Soyuz-2 carrier rockets and space satellites, while Aviakor produces and maintains aircraft.
Concurrent drone activity in Crimea
The strikes on Russian territory coincided with reports of drone activity in occupied Crimea on Saturday morning.
Local residents reported explosions in Sevastopol and the Bakhchysarai district. Following the blasts, local Telegram channels reported power outages in Sevastopol and a fire in the Balaklava area.
Russian occupation authorities did not issue an immediate statement regarding the incidents.

articles.title: Ukraine Strikes Russian Air Base Hosting MiG-31K Kinzhal Missile Carriers
articles.body:
- Category
- War in Ukraine
Ukraine Strikes Russian Air Base Hosting MiG-31K Kinzhal Missile Carriers
Ukrainian forces struck Russia’s Savasleyka military air base in the Nizhny Novgorod region overnight on August 15, where MiG-31K aircraft capable of launching Kh-47M2 Kinzhal ballistic missiles are based, Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy confirmed.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
Footage published by the Ukrainian monitoring channel Exilenova+ on August 15 showed a fire near Savasleyka following explosions at the airfield. Local residents also reported explosions in the area during the morning attack.
Savasleyka is a Russian military aviation facility located roughly 12 kilometers northwest of Kulebaki and approximately 650–700 kilometers from Ukraine’s state border. The airfield hosts a branch of Russia’s 4th State Center for Aviation Personnel Training and Military Testing and operates several variants of the MiG-31 interceptor.
Among them are MiG-31K aircraft modified to carry Russia’s Kh-47M2 Kinzhal, an air-launched ballistic missile repeatedly used in strikes against Ukraine.
An open-source monitoring channel reported on August 15 that Russia moved four MiG-31K aircraft away from Savasleyka after the attack began. The aircraft reportedly flew toward Begishevo Airport in Tatarstan.
In a statement published on Telegram on August 15, Zelenskyy said Ukraine’s long-range strikes had reached Savasleyka, describing the airfield as a base for aircraft carrying Russian missiles used to strike Ukrainian cities and villages. He placed the facility at about 700 kilometers from Ukraine.
The latest attack came as strikes were also reported hundreds of kilometers farther east in Russia’s Samara region, where one of the missiles struck the main production building of the Progress Rocket Space Center.
Progress is part of Russia’s state-owned Roscosmos corporation and manufactures Soyuz-2 carrier rockets. The rockets are used for civilian launches as well as missions from the Plesetsk Cosmodrome that place Russian military satellites into orbit.
The facility is also involved in producing Earth-observation spacecraft, including the Bars-M military reconnaissance satellite series.
Discuss this article:

articles.title: Royal Navy drone warship fleet could triple missile capacity
articles.body:
War games examining the Royal Navy’s planned shift towards crewed and uncrewed systems are claimed to have produced roughly three times the missile capacity for a North Atlantic conflict, according to a former senior Royal Navy officer.
War games examining the Royal Navy’s planned Hybrid Navy concept are claimed to have produced a substantial increase in combat mass and roughly three times the missile capacity available for a North Atlantic conflict, the UK Defence Journal understands.
The assessment comes from Rear Admiral (retired) James Parkin CB CBE, a former Royal Navy Director Develop, writing for the Council on Geostrategy’s Britain’s World magazine. Parkin argues that the combination of high-end crewed warships with larger numbers of autonomous and remotely operated systems offers one of the few realistic routes to increasing naval mass without a corresponding rise in personnel or the cost associated with building additional major warships.
He writes that testing of the concept through hybrid war games has produced what he describes as a substantial increase in combat mass and “roughly threefold missile capacity for a North Atlantic contest”. The figure is presented as a claimed result of war gaming rather than an operationally demonstrated capability, but it provides an indication of the scale of effect being sought through the Royal Navy’s future force structure.
The Hybrid Navy concept was formalised in the 2025 Strategic Defence Review, which envisaged highly capable crewed submarines, warships and aircraft operating alongside much larger numbers of uncrewed systems. The 2026 Defence Investment Plan subsequently described a network of crewed ships and uncrewed surface and underwater vessels connected through a Maritime Fighting Web, alongside plans for at least six Common Combat Vessels and autonomous collaborative aircraft under Projects VANQUISH and PANTHEON.
Parkin argues that the concept should not be interpreted as a replacement for conventional warships. He warns against drawing direct conclusions from Ukraine’s use of uncrewed vessels in the Black Sea, distinguishing between sea denial in a relatively enclosed maritime environment and the sea control required by Britain and NATO across the North Atlantic.
He writes: “Cheap, massed, and precise systems matter, but Britain must protect oceanic trade routes, nuclear-power ballistic missile submarine (SSBN) bastions, and NATO strike groups operating far from friendly ports.” Parkin argues that the Hybrid Navy must therefore remain centred on high-end crewed platforms, with uncrewed systems providing additional sensing, weapons capacity and persistent presence.
The memorandum also identifies regulatory constraints as a potentially significant obstacle. According to Parkin, the permissions required to operate uncrewed surface vessels larger than 24 metres routinely in British waters have yet to be established. He states that no uncrewed vessel above that size has so far received either Maritime and Coastguard Agency or Defence Maritime Regulator operating clearance, while neither civilian classification societies nor the Naval Authority and Technical Group have approved such a design.
Parkin argues that addressing this will require more than changes to individual regulations, calling instead for Defence to make greater use of the freedoms already available to it to conduct experimentation. He advocates giving operators greater scope to “learn by doing” and to fail safely during development rather than allowing lengthy approval processes to slow experimentation with new systems.
A second issue identified is the speed at which lessons from trials and operations are fed back into equipment development. Parkin contrasts traditional British defence acquisition cycles, which he says can take months or years to incorporate changes, with the much faster development cycle seen in Ukraine. He cites the so-called “rule of six”: six hours for operator feedback to reach a manufacturer, six days for software updates, six weeks for hardware modifications and six months to replace a system entirely where necessary.
The memorandum argues that a similar continuous feedback model will be required if the Hybrid Navy is to deliver the intended increase in mass and weapons capacity. Parkin also warns that the programme will require specialist maritime knowledge throughout acquisition and development, rather than treating the transition primarily as a conventional programme-management exercise.
The Royal Navy’s underlying challenge is one of numbers and cost as Parkin notes that large complex European warships can now cost around £2 billion to £2.5 billion per hull, while specialised naval aircraft can approach £100 million each. Against that background, the Hybrid Navy is intended to distribute functions traditionally concentrated aboard individual ships across a much larger network of crewed and uncrewed platforms.
Parkin served in the Royal Navy for 28 years and was Director Develop in Navy Command Headquarters between 2021 and 2025. His assessment is presented as analysis rather than an official Ministry of Defence statement, but it sets out both the potential operational gains and the regulatory, cultural and acquisition challenges involved in turning the Hybrid Navy concept into a deployable force.

articles.title: Ukraine: 18 of 26 Russian oil and stolen-grain ships face no sanctions
articles.body:
On 14 August, Ukraine's Military Intelligence (HUR) published data on 26 vessels via its War&Sanctions portal, noting that 18 ships face no sanctions from any of Ukraine's partner countries.
The agency said the ships carry Russian oil, liquefied natural gas (LNG), or agricultural products from occupied Ukraine. Euromaidan Press could not independently verify HUR’s vessel records.
Russia relies on maritime trade both to fund its war through energy exports and to sell crops taken from occupied Ukraine. Kyiv began building a dedicated system against Russia’s shadow grain fleet in April, modeled on its oil-fleet campaign. A US bill introduced this week would also target vessels, owners, insurers, and ports involved in sanctions evasion. HUR’s new list shows how many ships remain outside those restrictions.
Russia’s grain shadow fleet
HUR divided the 26 vessels into three groups:
- oil tankers serving Lukoil, Rosneft, Surgutneftegas, Novatek, Tatneft, and Gazprom;
- dry-cargo ships using the occupied ports of Berdiansk, Sevastopol, Kerch, and Feodosia;
- LNG carriers moving gas from the sanctioned SAAM FSU floating storage unit, which holds LNG from the sanctioned Arctic LNG 2 project.
HUR highlighted three of the 18 vessels that are not facing partner sanctions. The bulk carrier LAMAR S repeatedly loaded wheat at the Avlita terminal in occupied Sevastopol in 2026 for delivery abroad, including to Syria, the agency said.
NAYA FALCON carried baking soda and granulated wheat bran from occupied Sevastopol to Egypt and Cyprus, HUR said. The agency linked the oil tanker GREGAL to UAE-based Cymare Navigation FZC, which it described as affiliated with Sovcomflot, Russia’s state-controlled shipping company.
Russia steals grain while striking Ukraine’s exports
Crops taken from occupied land are sold abroad as Russian produce, while Russia's attacks leave Ukraine’s legitimate harvest with fewer routes to market.
Ukraine’s Foreign Intelligence Service said Russia sold more than 2 million tons of grain from occupied Ukraine as Russian produce in 2025. The agency said ship-to-ship transfers at Kavkaz helped conceal its origin.
Meanwhile, Russian attacks have squeezed Ukraine’s legitimate grain trade. Strikes on civilian ships brought the Black Sea corridor to a near standstill during the July harvest peak. Ten people died when Russian missiles hit the grain-laden Golden Leo on 19 July.
HUR called on Ukraine and its partners to synchronize sanctions and detain vessels that violate restrictions. It said the measures could curb Russia’s maritime logistics and war funding.

articles.title: Captured Akhmat fighter says he chose Ukraine and a drone guided him away from Russia’s ranks
articles.body:
A former fighter from the Akhmat forces, armed formations loyal to Chechnya’s Kremlin-backed ruler Ramzan Kadyrov, said he wants to fight for Ukraine after nearly a year in captivity.
Identified only as Magomed, he gave his account to Dmytro Karpenko, a Ukrainian journalist and blogger known for interviewing Russian prisoners of war, in a video published on 9 August 2026. Militarnyi, a Ukrainian military news outlet, reported on the interview on 13 August.
Magomed’s reported crossing reflects a divide that has placed Chechen fighters on both sides of Russia’s war. Since 2014, Kadyrov-loyal formations have fought for Moscow, while anti-Kremlin Chechens seeking independence from Russia have supported Kyiv.
Magomed’s account traces one fighter’s claimed passage from the first camp toward the second after Russians allegedly killed his brother. His account has not been independently verified.
The Chechen fighter said he had served near Svitlodarsk, Bakhmut, and Horlivka, including evacuating soldiers’ bodies.
Magomed also claimed two Chechens had crossed before him, prompting Russian commanders to check fighters’ phones and tighten surveillance.
According to Magomed, he later followed a Ukrainian drone toward Ukrainian positions with other Chechens. Ukrainian troops dropped medicine, water, and a radio to guide them. A Russian FPV drone attacked during the crossing and killed one Chechen, he alleged.
Ukrainian forces received the survivors and handed Magomed to the police brigade "Liut". His captivity began on 29 August 2025. Magomed also alleged that Russians killed his brother and called the death an epileptic seizure. Magomed said that drove him to fight Russia.
Militarnyi reported that Magomed had joined the International Legion, which is run by Ukraine's military intelligence. However, Karpenko’s video description says he wants to join the legion. Neither source explained the discrepancy.
What is Akhmat?
Akhmat, the unit Magomed belonged to, provides Russia with frontline troops and rear-area security. UK intelligence estimated in 2024 that around 9,000 personnel served in pro-Russian Chechen units in Ukraine.
Kadyrov’s reach has also expanded during the war. A later investigation found that his armed network had grown to 20 units across Russia’s military and security structures.
The Akhmat group's influence may extend beyond military operations. In January 2026, ATESH, a Ukrainian-Crimean Tatar partisan group, said Moscow planned to hand occupied Mariupol to Akhmat as a reward for Chechen leaders’ loyalty. The resistance organization claimed that arriving Chechen forces sought control of the city’s resources and industry.
Chechens also fight for Ukraine
On the other side, Chechens seeking an independent Ichkeria (the indigenous Chechen name for Chechnya) have fought for Ukraine since 2014.
In April 2026, Ukrainian intelligence said Shamanbat, a Ukrainian special unit that includes Free Ichkeria fighters, helped conduct drone and artillery strikes on Akhmat positions. The agency claimed the operation killed dozens of Akhmat personnel and wounded about 80.

articles.title: Daily Update: Russia Loses 1,370 Troops, 3 Air Defense Systems, and 62 Artillery Systems
articles.body:
- Category
- War in Ukraine
Daily Update: Russia Loses 1,370 Troops, 3 Air Defense Systems, and 62 Artillery Systems
Russian forces suffered an estimated 1,370 personnel casualties and lost five tanks and 62 artillery systems over the past 24 hours, according to Ukraine’s latest battlefield assessment.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
Ukraine’s General Staff reported on August 15 that the latest figures bring Russia’s total estimated personnel losses since the start of its full-scale invasion on February 24, 2022, to approximately 1,465,810.
According to the General Staff, Russian forces also lost three armored combat vehicles, two multiple launch rocket systems, three air defense systems, 12 unmanned ground vehicles, and 1,835 operational-tactical UAVs during the reporting period.
Ukraine additionally reported the destruction of 522 vehicles and fuel tankers and four pieces of special equipment.
Russia’s cumulative equipment losses are now estimated at 12,269 tanks, 25,144 armored combat vehicles, 47,932 artillery systems, 2,026 multiple launch rocket systems, 1,568 air defense systems, 439 aircraft, 354 helicopters, 2,241 unmanned ground vehicles, 461,484 operational-tactical UAVs, 5,007 cruise missiles, 35 ships and boats, two submarines, 134,375 vehicles and fuel tankers, and 4,528 pieces of special equipment.
Ukraine’s General Staff recorded 233 combat engagements across the front over the past 24 hours. Russian forces carried out 71 airstrikes during the day, dropping 241 guided aerial bombs on Ukrainian positions and populated areas.
They also deployed 10,626 strike drones and conducted 3,042 attacks against Ukrainian settlements and military positions, including 36 strikes using multiple launch rocket systems.
Over the same period, Ukrainian aviation, missile forces, and artillery struck two Russian command posts, five areas where Russian personnel were concentrated, three artillery systems, and eight UAV control points.
Earlier, Ukrainian SBU drones struck several high-value Russian air defense assets, including a key 92N6 engagement radar from an S-400 system, two Pantsir-S2 systems, and Kasta-2E2 and Sopka-2 radars, with the targeted equipment valued at more than $170 million.
