articles.title: Raid Hunter: Northrop’s new gun-based air defense system
articles.body:
- Northrop Grumman unveiled Raid Hunter, a 50mm gun-based air defense system, on Aug. 11 to counter cruise missiles and drone swarms.
- The system uses a guided 50mm round derived from a Navy-funded 57mm program and can be transported by C-130 aircraft.
U.S. defense giant Northrop Grumman unveiled Raid Hunter on Aug. 11, a 50mm gun-based air defense system built to counter cruise missiles and drone swarms at short range around military bases and other critical sites.
The system pairs the company’s XM913 Bushmaster III chain gun with newly developed precision-guided 50mm ammunition and a networked system controller for battle management, Northrop Grumman said. It is designed to defeat “high-volume, mixed-threat aerial raids,” engaging multiple targets in rapid succession rather than the single-target engagements typical of most short-range air defense systems.
“Raid Hunter addresses a critical short-range defense gap by delivering rapid, high-capacity protection against complex, mass aerial threats like cruise missiles and drone swarms,” said Kenn Todorov, vice president and general manager for command and control and weapons integration at Northrop Grumman. “It provides warfighters with a cost-effective, flexible tool to decisively defeat evolving threats now and in the future, strengthening the security of vital bases and infrastructure.”
The current version is palletized for transport aboard C-130 aircraft, with vehicle-mounted and container-based configurations planned for the future. Northrop Grumman said the system is already undergoing testing, with additional trials planned through the rest of the year to validate performance and support faster fielding. The company positions Raid Hunter within its broader Raid Defense Solutions portfolio, intended to work alongside its other air defense systems in a layered architecture.
Northrop Grumman says the 50mm caliber provides “lethal, cost-considerate engagement with deep magazines and fast reloads,” aiming to address the cost mismatch between expensive interceptors and cheap drone threats. Company officials told Warsight that guided ammunition also extends the system’s effective range and reduces dispersion at longer distances compared with unguided rounds, since the round corrects its own course rather than relying purely on the accuracy of the initial shot.
Northrop Grumman’s initial announcement included little imagery of the system, an absence noted by Sam Cranny-Evans, editor of Calibre Defence, on social media. Earlier photos of a scale model exist from Eurosatory 2026 in June, where Northrop Grumman first showed the then-unnamed concept and where Warsight editor Mark Cazalet interviewed company officials about the design.
At Eurosatory, Northrop Grumman displayed the system as a palletized turret fitted with a radar for target acquisition and an optoelectronic sight for fire control, armed with the XM913 cannon chambered in 50x228mm ammunition, dubbed “Supershot,” with 400 ready rounds, according to Warsight‘s reporting. Company officials told Warsight the guided 50mm round builds on a separate, Navy-funded program to develop a guided 57mm round for the Mk 110 remote weapon station used on littoral combat ships. Northrop Grumman has not disclosed the guided round’s seeker type, saying only that testing results have been positive.
Company representatives told Warsight that two of the palletized units fit on a single C-130 and can also be moved by CH-47 Chinook helicopter, and that four to six units could provide 360-degree coverage at a large airfield. The system is designed to integrate with the Integrated Battle Command System, allowing it to work alongside longer-range interceptors such as Patriot, IRIS-T and NASAMS, engaging threats those systems let through.
Beyond the Navy-funded 57mm work, Northrop Grumman said it is in discussions with the Army and other potential customers about the 50mm system, though the company has not disclosed any procurement contracts or timelines for Raid Hunter beyond the ongoing test schedule.

articles.title: The Armed Forces of Ukraine struck an air defense missile system, UAV storage facilities, and Russian command posts in several areas at once
articles.body:
The Armed Forces of Ukraine struck an air defense missile system, UAV storage facilities, and Russian command posts in several areas at once
Kyiv • UNN
Ukraine's Defense Forces struck Russian military targets in the Luhansk, Donetsk, and Zaporizhzhia regions. A "Strela-10" air defense missile system, UAV storage facilities, and two command posts were hit.
On August 14 and during the night of August 15, 2026, the Defense Forces of Ukraine struck a number of military facilities of Russian forces in the temporarily occupied territories of the Luhansk, Donetsk, and Zaporizhzhia regions. The General Staff of the Armed Forces of Ukraine reported the destruction of a Russian air defense missile system, UAV and materiel warehouses, as well as two command posts, UNN writes.
Details
In particular, Ukrainian forces struck a Strela-10 surface-to-air missile system in Kreminna, Luhansk region.
A warehouse containing drones belonging to Russian forces in Vuhledar, Donetsk region, and a logistics warehouse in Lysychansk, Luhansk region, were also hit.
The plant in Samara was hit by Flamingo – confirmation has emerged 15.08.26, 10:43 • 2750 views
In addition, the Defense Forces struck two enemy command posts. One of them was located in Selydove, Donetsk region, and the other in Mykhailivka, Zaporizhzhia region.
The General Staff noted that the extent of the damage caused and the final results of the strikes are currently being clarified. Ukrainian forces continue to target key military facilities of Russian forces.

articles.title: Israeli strike kills 7 in Lebanon, 2 tankers attacked in Hormuz and other news from the Middle East
articles.body:
Vessel is attacked in Hormuz, Israeli strike kills 9 in Lebanon, and other news from the Middle East
The United Arab Emirates accused Iran of attacking a vessel in the Strait of Hormuz, while the Iran-backed Houthis struck a Red Sea port in Yemen.
In Southern Lebanon, nine people were killed in Israeli airstrikes, some of the deadliest since a shaky truce between Israel and Hezbollah went into effect on June 20.
Here’s a look at the latest developments in the Iran war and the wider Middle East. Full coverage can be found here.
A vessel is attacked in the Strait of Hormuz
A tanker owned by Abu Dhabi’s state-owned oil and gas company ADNOC was attacked while transiting through the Strait of Hormuz, Emirati state-run WAM news agency said Saturday.
The attack happened Friday evening, and there were no injuries, the agency reported. This is the third such attack on vessels operated by ADNOC in the critical waterway in the last week.
In a statement Saturday the United Arab Emirates blamed Iran for the attack and called on it to stop the unprovoked strikes.
The United Kingdom Maritime Trade Operations center said that a bulk carrier was struck by an unknown projectile that hit the hull on Friday. It was not immediately clear if it was the same vessel.
Shipping has been disrupted and the strait has been virtually closed since the Iran war started on Feb. 28 with U.S. and Israeli strikes on Iran. About one-fifth of the world’s traded oil and natural gas passed through the waterway at the mouth of the Persian Gulf before the war.
The attacks in the Strait have continued as Iran seeks to control the key waterway as a form of leverage. Talks between the U.S. and Iran have stalled while Iran is in discussions with Oman about how to manage the passageway.
Israeli strikes kill 9 in southern Lebanon
Israeli airstrikes on southern Lebanon killed at least nine people Saturday, in some of the deadliest attacks since a precarious truce between Israel and Hezbollah went into effect on June 20.
Lebanon’s Health Ministry and state news agency said one of the airstrikes that targeted a home on the edge of the village of Ansar killed seven people, including three children, and wounded two. The second, on the village of Deir al-Zahrani, killed two and wounded nine.
The death toll from the airstrikes makes it one of the deadliest days since the Lebanese government and Israel announced a “framework agreement” in June laying out a plan for Israeli forces to withdraw from southern Lebanon in exchange for the disarmament of the Iran-backed Hezbollah militant group.
Hezbollah refused direct talks and was not part of the agreement.
Israel said it struck Hezbollah infrastructure in southern Lebanon in response to actions taken by the group against Israeli soldiers operating in the security zone.
Houthis in Yemen attack Red Sea port, killing at least 1
Yemen’s military said Saturday the Iranian-backed Houthis attacked a crucial Red Sea port under the control of the internationally recognized government, killing at least one security guard.
Col. Majed al-Nazili, the spokesman for the military, said in a statement that the Houthis fired six ballistic missiles Friday evening on the Mokha port, in a “new terrorist aggression that targeted a vital civilian facility.” He said the attack wounded eight people and left two marines missing.
The attack was the latest by the Houthis on government-held areas and on Saudi Arabia and part of an escalation threatening to plunge Yemen into a full-fledged conflict. A 2022 ceasefire stopped heavy fighting during the country’s civil war.
Analysts say the Houthi escalation reflects how Iran is scaling up pressure on the United States and its regional allies.

articles.title: Zelenskyy held a meeting of the Staff: Russia’s plans and countermeasures, shortages, and weapons needs were discussed
articles.body:
Zelenskyy held a meeting of the Staff: Russia’s plans and countermeasures, shortages, and weapons needs were discussed
Kyiv • UNN
The President of Ukraine held a meeting of the Staff, where defense financing for the autumn-winter period and needs for the latest weapons were discussed. Intelligence provided updated information on Russia’s plans; asymmetric countermeasures are being prepared.
President of Ukraine Volodymyr Zelenskyy said that he held a meeting of the Staff of the Supreme Commander-in-Chief, where they discussed defense financing deficits and needs for weapons development, including rocket interceptors, and received a number of reports, including on the plans of the russian federation, UNN reports.
I held a Staff meeting. The key issue is the funding needed for our Defense Forces and the security of Ukraine for the autumn-winter period. We identified the main deficits and additional needs for developing the most innovative and technologically advanced types of weapons, accelerating the production of our strike capabilities and new types of defensive weapons, including rocket interceptors. The intelligence services provided updated information on Russia's plans – we are preparing a response and our asymmetric countermeasures
Deep strikes and middle strikes
"On a weekly basis, we analyze the results of long-range sanctions against Russia, as well as medium-range sanctions. The designated sanctions plan is being implemented, and we are promptly adjusting priorities so that Ukraine's capabilities 100% match the need to achieve all the objectives of our sanctions plan," the President said.
According to him, Secretary of the National Security and Defense Council Ihor Klymenko reported on the "status of implementation of the decisions of the Staff and the National Security and Defense Council, and the areas requiring additional attention."
"There was also a separate report from the special services on the status of targeted operations against collaborators in the temporarily occupied territory, in particular in Sevastopol, who are involved in Russia's strikes against Ukraine and Ukrainians. The collaborators' accountability is inevitable. Glory to Ukraine!" Zelenskyy said.

articles.title: Trump says record-setting Navy deployment to support Iran operations ‘not nearly long enough’
articles.body:
Trump says USS Lincoln’s record time at sea during Iran operations ‘not nearly long enough’
WASHINGTON (AP) — President Donald Trump on Friday downplayed the toll on American sailors enduring nearly nine months at sea on the USS Abraham Lincoln as concerns escalated about mental health and supply issues aboard the aircraft carrier supporting U.S. operations against Iran.
In a brief exchange with reporters before flying to New York for an event to highlight falling violent crime rates across the U.S., Trump refuted that family members have raised concerns about the deployment’s length and even said that the deployment — which includes a record-setting uninterrupted time at sea of more than 240 days — is “not nearly long enough.”
“That ship is moving right now, or very shortly, and it’s being replaced with another very similar ship,” Trump said when asked about the lengthy deployment. The acting navy secretary, Hung Cao, said the Lincoln “will return home soon” in a social media post on Friday.
Trump strode into office for a second term vowing to avoid lengthy and expensive military entanglements. And after launching the Iran war, alongside Israel, Trump and his advisers said the conflict would last a matter of weeks. The war is now more than five months old.
But on Friday, during his crime address in Garden City, New York, he acknowledged that he’s used the U.S. military “a little bit more than I wanted to,” while asserting anew that the U.S. operation against Iran is going well. He even said, seemingly in jest, that “pretty soon I’ll be declaring the Hormuz Strait a territory of the United States.”
“I’ll never apologize,” Trump added about the war and its impact on oil prices. “I did the right thing.”
Democrats demand Pentagon briefing on USS Lincoln
Extended deployments of carriers during the Iran conflict have raised concerns about the impact on service members who are away from home for long periods as well as the increasing strain on the ships and their equipment.
Several Democratic lawmakers, including Sens. Richard Blumenthal of Connecticut and Ruben Gallego of Arizona, are pressing for accountability from the Pentagon over conditions aboard the Lincoln, which Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth on Thursday said were “completely misrepresented.”
Rep. Jason Crow, D-Colo., who served three tours in Iraq and Afghanistan with the 82nd Airborne Division and 75th Ranger Regiment before being elected, took to social media to criticize Trump’s comments, saying on X that “President Trump does not care about our servicemembers or their families.”
Top Democrats on the House Oversight Committee have requested a classified briefing on the ship’s food inventory, sanitation issues and healthcare availability, as well as an assessment of how much longer it would be deployed before relief arrives.
Republicans have been less outspoken about the situation on the Lincoln. The GOP chairmen of the House and Senate armed services committees did not immediately respond to a request for comment.
While hostilities between the U.S. and Iran have calmed in recent weeks, the Navy has reimposed a blockade on Iranian ports in the crucial Strait of Hormuz, and the Trump administration has offered no clarity on how it intends to wind down the war. Hegseth said the U.S. military can maintain the blockage of Iranian ports “indefinitely.”
Another aircraft carrier, the USS George Washington, left port in Da Nang, Vietnam, last week, and is expected to replace the USS Lincoln, one of two aircraft carriers currently deployed in the Middle East.
After reports emerged that sailors on the Lincoln are struggling with mental health concerns, the Navy said it has “not observed an increase in suicidal ideations or attempts aboard the ship,” though officials have declined to provide data, citing operational security and patient privacy concerns.
A Navy official said a sailor aboard the Lincoln went overboard in early August but the person was quickly recovered, treated by the ship’s medical department and transferred off ship for follow-on care. The official would not say whether it was being considered a suicide attempt.
U.S. Central Command, which oversees military operations in the Middle East, has also pushed back on reports about poor conditions.
___
AP writers Collin Binkley in Garden City, New York, and Michelle L. Price and Lisa Mascaro in Washington contributed to this report.
——
This story has been corrected to show that the USS Abraham Lincoln has spent more than 240 days of uninterrupted time at sea and its overall deployment has exceeded 260 days.

articles.title: NATO jets shoot down drone over Latvia near Russia
articles.body:
An Italian Eurofighter shot down a drone over north-eastern Latvia in the early hours of Friday, in an incident the Latvian armed forces attribute to Russian electromagnetic warfare pushing the aircraft off course and into NATO airspace.
The drone came down near the village of Rugāji in the Balvi region, close to the Russian border. Latvia’s National Armed Forces said NATO fighter jets had successfully shot down a foreign unmanned aerial vehicle that entered the country “as a result of Russian electromagnetic warfare”.
A NATO spokesperson said two Italian Eurofighters based in Lithuania were scrambled and one of them destroyed the drone, with two Turkish F-16s based in Estonia also launched. “All aircraft were operating under NATO command,” the spokesperson said, adding that an investigation is ongoing.
Airspace alerts were issued across several eastern and southern regions of Latvia and lifted at 4.50am local time. Finland separately restricted airspace and a sea area in the eastern Gulf of Finland as a precaution, with the Finnish Defence Forces saying no drones entered the country and the restrictions lifted shortly after 7am.
Latvia’s defence ministry confirmed this was the second time a drone had been shot down in Latvian airspace, following a first incursion in June that was also handled by NATO fighters.
Baiba Braze, the Latvian foreign minister, thanked Italy for “maintaining (the) integrity of NATO airspace”.
The origin of the drone was not immediately established, and the Latvian statement did not identify it. Earlier on Friday more than 50 Ukrainian drones attacked targets in Russia’s western regions including Leningrad and Tver, striking the port of Ust-Luga and a warehouse belonging to the e-commerce company Wildberries.
The electromagnetic warfare claim is a recurring problem along the alliance’s eastern flank, and is more likely rather than a deliberate incursion. Jamming and spoofing of satellite navigation signals has been widespread across the Baltic region since 2022, affecting civil aviation and shipping as well as military traffic, and a drone relying on GPS to hold its track can be pushed across a border by interference intended for something else.
Whether the aircraft was Russian or Ukrainian in origin therefore remains open, and neither Latvia nor NATO has said. Drones from both sides have come down in NATO territory during the war, with Romania recovering fragments on multiple occasions and Poland scrambling aircraft repeatedly during Russian strike waves against western Ukraine.
Baltic Air Policing has run continuously since 2004, when the three Baltic states joined NATO without fighter forces of their own. Allied detachments rotate through Šiauliai in Lithuania and Ämari in Estonia on four-month tours, and the mission has shifted from routine interception of Russian aircraft transiting to Kaliningrad towards the more demanding business of intercepting small, slow targets that radar systems designed for fast jets do not handle easily.

articles.title: Abbas fought the Taliban alongside US and Australian troops. Now exiled in Iran, he feels abandoned
articles.body:
War is Abbas’s* earliest memory.
As a child, the first iteration of Taliban rule forced his family to flee – with nothing but the clothes on their backs and what food they could carry – for the relative safety of far-distant hills.
War became his profession. Joining republican Afghanistan’s fledgling army, Abbas fought alongside American, Australian and British troops, believing in the foreigners’ ultimately false promise that they could bring peace and prosperity to his homeland.
Conflict is his constant attendant now, over Afghanistan’s border in neighbouring Iran, as the US, the country he fought with, rains bombs on the land of his exile. Back home, the resurgent Taliban – unreformed, unrepentant and firmly in charge – seek him still.
The war – for all its varied complexions, it feels the same war – goes on.
In the five years since Kabul dramatically fell back into the hands of the Taliban, those who served Afghanistan’s republican government have found themselves the targets of violent retribution. Those who took up arms against the Taliban are particular targets.
Abandoned US military databases – containing Afghans’ personal and biometric data such as fingerprints, photographs, and home addresses – are being used to hunt former soldiers who served the “infidel” west.
Social media groups share information on the latest atrocities, videos of former soldiers being whipped in the street, shot in summary executions, or dragged away in night raids to be tortured in Taliban prisons.
Abbas joined the military – initially at least – for the money. For a poor boy from the provinces, the army represented a regular income and a full belly, a reliable way to support his family. That there was a war on was barely a consideration: there was always a war on.
After basic training, he passed a selection course to serve in the special forces.
“At first I joined for money but when I entered the commandos everything changed,” Abbas tells the Guardian. “There were foreign forces teaching us … they gave speeches about global terrorism.
“It was not about money any more. I became very committed; I just wanted to serve my country and fight Taliban and destroy the terrorist groups.”
He spent 12 years in the Afghan national army, most of those wearing the distinctive red badge of the special forces, “and we fought many hard battles”.
Abbas served alongside Australian troops in southern Afghanistan, night-time missions by helicopter in late 2011, in the restive and mountainous Khas Uruzgan district.
“There were many forces we served with: Germans in Kunduz, French in Kapisa, and especially we were with Americans. The Australian forces were in Uruzgan, and we went there. We took part in combat alongside them, especially in Khas Uruzgan, we … executed two missions with them by air.”
Abbas said he and his comrades “were always on the frontline”.
“We spent many days and nights with foreign forces. I performed combat duties in [approximately] 20 provinces of Afghanistan.”
He was wounded in a firefight in Laghman district, shot twice at close range. His bulletproof vest deflected the bullet that struck the left side of his chest, “but another hit my left arm, breaking the bone”. He was taken by US helicopter to Bagram hospital: “I still have a metal plate in my left arm.”
Abbas remembers the camaraderie of his days serving alongside western troops with fondness: “We risked our lives to help each other on and off the battlefield and to rescue one another. They always called us brothers.”
But he remembers too, the commitments that were made to him.
“They promised they wouldn’t abandon us. But in the end, when they withdrew, they simply left us. And they did it in such a way that we were left with our hands tied, the entire army was disarmed.
“Those who were high-ranking officials left, while the rest of us, sergeants like me, were left behind. No one even asked about us.”
When Kabul fell, Abbas was forced to burn most of his documents and destroy photographs: incriminating evidence in the eyes of the Taliban.
A bare handful remain secretly in his possession: pictures on patrol with western forces, certificates of appreciation from foreign militaries commending his “outstanding commitment, dedication and support” to their operations.
Life since the fall, with a wife and young son, has been precarious, often dangerous. His has been a shifting, uncertain existence in the shadows.
As the Taliban swept northwards across Afghanistan, expanding and consolidating its control from the major cities to smaller, more distant villages, there were fewer and fewer places to hide.
With his family, Abbas fled over Afghanistan’s arid, inhospitable border into Iran.
There, with no legal rights, he is vulnerable to exploitation and extortion: landlords demand thousands of dollars for tiny apartments that have been condemned as unfit for habitation; he has been forced to take dangerous, illegal work for far less than a living wage.
When US bombs started raining down on Tehran, Abbas and his family fled once again for the mountainous countryside.
“Our life in Iran is very difficult; refugees face a lot of problems. Especially for us former military personnel … we are still being threatened by Taliban groups even here. We also fear that we might be deported to Afghanistan.”
Abbas said his family’s future depends on being able to find a safe country, far from the reach of the Taliban, and the American war which has blighted his Iranian exile.
“I am waiting to see what will happen, but I am hopeful … I will build a better life for my family, a better future for my son.”
Many in Afghanistan feel as Abbas does – betrayed by the foreign forces in whom they placed their trust.
On the day of his second inauguration as US president, Donald Trump halted all Afghan refugee resettlement by executive order. The shutdown left more than 1,000 Afghan former interpreters and soldiers stranded in a US-run camp in Qatar, and hundreds of thousands more vetted applicants stuck in neighbouring countries like Pakistan.
In Germany, a new government sought to renege on a commitment to resettling hundreds of Afghan refugees it had identified as being at risk. The country’s highest court ruled it could not arbitrarily cancel hundreds of resettlement places it had already promised.
And in Britain, a House of Commons committee report this month reported that a massive data breach from within the UK government’s Afghan relocations and assistance policy exposed thousands of Afghans to potentially life-threatening danger. Afghans still trapped inside the country are being told by the UK government to “self-move” to safe third countries, a policy that “risks excluding people the UK has promised to help,” the committee chair, Tan Dhesi, said.
A spokesperson for Australia’s foreign affairs minister, Penny Wong, said five years on from the fall of Kabul: “We stand firm in our pursuit to do all we can to protect the people of Afghanistan from the oppressive acts of the Taliban, particularly women and girls.
“We also remain committed to assisting those who helped Australia’s mission in Afghanistan.”
Until 2023, the Australian government ran a dedicated “locally engaged employee” (LEE) program for Afghans who worked for and with Australia “and are at risk of harm as a result of their work”.
The program certified 2,059 Afghans – but only 1,208 of those have reached Australia, according to the latest government figures (along with 4,493 immediate family members).
But hundreds of Afghans still living in hiding inside the country, or stranded in perilous situations elsewhere, say they were unable to apply before the LEE program closed, or had their applications rejected despite providing evidence of support for Australia, including fighting alongside Australian troops. A government review of the program found it was riven by “delays, double handling and confusion”, and it imposed an unreasonable administrative burden on those fleeing the Taliban seeking safety.
Abbas has family in Australia, and, having fought alongside Australian troops on their missions in Afghanistan, he applied for LEE protection from Australia.
He was rejected, the government ruling he had not been “in a direct employment relationship with defence”.
“While the applicant might have worked alongside the coalition forces, including members of the Australian Defence Force in partnership on operations in Afghanistan, it does not appear that the applicant was ‘employed with’ the ADF,” the government decision states.
Wong’s spokesperson said the current government had approved more LEE applications than any before it. “Since the Albanese government took office, Dfat has certified close to 650 applications from Afghan Locally Engaged Employees, more than the total approved under all previous foreign ministers combined since the program began in 2013.”
Australia, too, has provided broader support – more than $310m in humanitarian assistance, through established partners and UN agencies – “to ensure our aid supports those most in need – not the Taliban”.
Zaki Haidari, a former Afghan refugee who is now an Australian citizen, remains in close contact with dozens of former soldiers, interpreters and others who supported western nations in their failed two-decade mission in Afghanistan.
“Almost every conversation I have with people inside Afghanistan is filled with fear, uncertainty and hopelessness. Families tell me they struggle to afford food, many have lost their livelihoods, and parents worry constantly about the future of their children,” Haidari, Amnesty International’s Australian refugee rights advocate, says.
Haidari said women live under constant surveillance, fearing arrest for speaking out or failing to comply with the Taliban’s ever-tightening restrictions. Members of the Hazara ethnic and religious minority – for decades Taliban targets – are forcibly evicted from homes and face discrimination and violence.
Haidari said Australia’s LEE program “undoubtedly saved lives”, but there were still thousands endangered by their support and assistance for Australia.
Hopes that a Taliban desperate for international legitimacy would temper their more repressive instincts have proven illusory: with global attention shifted to other conflicts, the Taliban has further entrenched their brutality across Afghanistan.
Australia’s obligation to the people of Afghanistan “did not end with the military withdrawal”, Haidari says.
“Many people who supported Australia’s mission remain at risk and continue to wait for protection.
“Many fear for their lives every day.”
*Name/s have been changed

articles.title: Zelenskyy after Staff meeting: Jet interceptor production to be accelerated
articles.body:
President of Ukraine Volodymyr Zelenskyy reported on holding a meeting of the Supreme Commander-in-Chief’s Staff, with the main issue being the financing of the Defense and Security Forces of Ukraine for the autumn-winter period.
"We identified the main deficits and additional needs for developing the most innovative and technological types of weapons, accelerating the production of our strike assets and new types of defensive weapons, including jet interceptors. Intelligence provided updated information on Russia’s plans – we are preparing countermeasures and our asymmetric counter-steps," Zelenskyy wrote on Telegram on Friday.
According to him, the plan for long-range and medium-range strikes against Russia is being executed. "We are operationally adjusting priorities so that Ukraine’s capabilities 100% meet the need to achieve all goals of our sanctions plan," the president noted.
Zelenskyy also reported a separate report by special services on the status of executing targeted operations against collaborators in the temporarily occupied territory, particularly in Sevastopol, who participate in Russian strikes against Ukraine and Ukrainians, and emphasized the inevitability of responsibility for collaborators.
Earlier on Friday, former Minister of Defense of Ukraine Mykhailo Fedorov reported the start of the testing phase for Ukrainian means of combating Russian jet drones. "The first Ukrainian jet interceptor drones for fighting jet Shaheds are undergoing combat testing. Today we see a trend: the Russians are gradually replacing conventional Shaheds with jet ones. This is a change in the strategy of warfare in the sky. Our response must be swift to continue defeating Russia in every technological cycle… Over the year, our team issued grants to manufacturers through Brave1, analyzed solutions, and helped with testing. Today, several Ukrainian manufacturers already have such solutions," he wrote on Telegram.
Acting Minister of Defense Yevheniy Khmara, during an August 10 discussion with the Ministers of Defense of Sweden and Norway regarding financial support for drone production and countering ballistics, cruise missiles, and jet Shaheds, as well as the development of the Freyja anti-ballistic project, named countering ballistics, cruise missiles, and jet Shaheds an urgent priority. "For this, Ukraine already needs interceptor missiles and means for asymmetric action," he said.

articles.title: Flamingo missiles reportedly strike an industrial site beside a factory building rockets for Russia’s Starlink rival
articles.body:
Samara Oblast Governor Vyacheslav Fedorishchev confirmed that a missile struck an unnamed industrial enterprise overnight on 15 August 2026. Andrii Kovalenko, head of Ukraine’s Center for Countering Disinformation, said the Progress Rocket Space Center was burning. He provided no damage details.
Progress would be a significant target because it builds Soyuz-2 rockets used to launch Rassvet, Russia’s planned alternative to Starlink. Its Soyuz-2.1b rockets carried Russia’s first serial-production Rassvet satellites into orbit this year. However, neither the governor’s statement nor available imagery establishes that Progress itself was hit.
Exilenova+ published early footage from Samara and reported that a Flamingo cruise missile had struck the city.
A mature Rassvet network could reduce Russia’s dependence on unauthorized Starlink terminals. For now, neither damage to Progress nor the reported use of a Flamingo missile has been independently confirmed.
Open-source analysts at Falcon Insight Map geolocated the smoke near Aviakor’s Building No. 106. Militarnyi said Aviakor and Progress sit a few hundred meters apart, and available images could not establish which enterprise was hit. The industrial area lies roughly 900 kilometers from Ukraine.
Kyiv pushes strikes deeper into Russia
Ukraine has increasingly attacked factories far behind the front to disrupt the supply chains sustaining Russian weapons production.
Speaking separately to Euromaidan Press, defense scholar Marc DeVore urged Ukraine to disrupt Russian missile production and launches. Retired US Lieutenant General Ben Hodges noted that Ukraine’s interceptor shortage means it is better to “kill the archer” than try to stop every arrow.
In June 2026, Ukrainian cruise missiles hit a Voronezh semiconductor plant supplying components for the Pantsir-S1, Iskander-K, and Kh-101.
A reported Flamingo strike in July also damaged the Avitek defense plant in Kirov, more than 1,200 kilometers from Ukraine.
The deeper strikes come as Ukraine’s military intelligence (HUR) says Russian factories are producing 110% to 120% of their monthly missile quotas.
How the Samara plant supports Russia’s Starlink alternative
The Progress factory in Samara makes the Soyuz-2.1b rockets used to launch Rassvet satellites developed by Russia’s Bureau 1440. A second batch of 16 entered orbit in July, bringing the serial constellation to 32.
Rassvet’s coverage remains intermittent. However, Moscow plans to deploy 292 satellites by the end of 2027 and 924 by 2035. A Ukrainian defense adviser estimated that continuous service would require 200–250 satellites.

articles.title: President announces new sanctions targeting Russia's defense industry and financial networks
articles.body:
President announces new sanctions targeting Russia's defense industry and financial networks
President Volodymyr Zelensky said this in his nightly video address, according to Ukrinform.
"Our sanctions against Russian oil refineries and other facilities in Russia's oil sector, our mid-range strikes against Russian military logistics, and our operation in the waters of the Black Sea and the Sea of Azov – all of this is working to limit Russia's war potential. It is important to continue this with more active political and legal measures as well," he said.
He recalled that Ukraine had imposed a sanctions package today targeting companies and vessels involved in exporting grain and other goods stolen in the temporarily occupied territories of Ukraine.
"We are preparing new sanctions packages against Russia's war industry, financial chains, and intermediaries. Unfortunately, a significant number of Russian enterprises working for the war are still not under international sanctions, and this must be corrected during August and September. We will raise this with leaders at all working levels," Zelensky said.
He also emphasized a direct task for Ukrainian diplomats: "In major jurisdictions around the world, sanctions are imposed on those Russian companies and individuals, as well as those who help Russia, whose influence truly matters in terms of prolonging this war and producing Russian missiles and drones."

articles.title: HUR Cyber Specialists Attack Wildberries Digital Infrastructure
articles.body:
Cyber specialists from Ukraine’s Main Intelligence Directorate (HUR) attacked the digital infrastructure of the Russian e-commerce company Wildberries on Aug. 10-11, the agency reported.
HUR stated on Facebook that the cyber operation, conducted by the Cyber Corps group, resulted in large-scale disruptions despite the facility’s security measures.
JOIN US ON TELEGRAM
Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official.
The attack affected the company’s main remote customer service channel and partially destabilized its payment infrastructure.
The intelligence agency noted that the attack led to mass complaints from users unable to complete financial transactions, creating additional strain on the company’s contact centers.
According to HUR, the cyber operation compounds the damage caused by recent kinetic attacks by Ukrainian defense forces on Wildberries warehouses.
The agency stated that targeting the company is part of an effort to disrupt an entity that helps sustain the Russian economy and its war effort against Ukraine.
Economic impact of warehouse strikes
The cyberattack follows a sustained campaign of Ukrainian drone strikes targeting Wildberries’ logistics infrastructure.
Ukraine has targeted at least 23 Wildberries facilities since mid-July, with nine company workers reportedly killed in the attacks.
The analysts estimate that the company has lost up to one-third of its warehouse space, with the destroyed or damaged facilities containing goods worth approximately 480 billion rubles ($5.7 billion).
Europeans Seek Role in Ukraine Peace Talks Amid US Uncertainty
The financial losses are roughly equivalent to the annual budgets of some wealthier Russian regions, such as Krasnoyarsk Krai, and are larger than the budgets of several poorer regions. At least 1.18 million square meters of Wildberries warehouse space had been affected.
The destruction has impacted tens of thousands of businesses that rely on the platform. While the Russian government is reportedly preparing support measures like tax breaks and loan holidays, a Kremlin-linked source told Reuters that direct compensation for destroyed goods is not currently planned, raising concerns about potential bankruptcies among sellers.
Rationale for targeting
Kyiv has stated that Wildberries is a legitimate military target because the marketplace sells goods used by the Russian armed forces.
While the company denies supplying the military and maintains that weapons are prohibited on its platform, The New York Times reported that first-person-view (FPV) drones, fiber-optic cables, and other equipment with potential military applications were available for purchase on Wildberries in early August.
The marketplace is a major component of Russia’s consumer economy, accounting for approximately 10% of the country’s retail sales. Following the attacks, SberIndex reported a sharp decline in spending on non-food goods through online marketplaces in recent weeks.
Wildberries’ co-founder Tatyana Kim has stated the strikes are intended to destabilize the company and create panic among the Russian population.

articles.title: Putin is trying to unite Russians around the idea of war against Ukraine ahead of the elections - ISW
articles.body:
Putin is trying to unite Russians around the idea of war against Ukraine ahead of the elections - ISW
Kyiv • UNN
Russia rejects all proposals for a ceasefire, insisting on the terms of Ukraine's complete capitulation. ISW notes that the Kremlin uses pro-war rhetoric to consolidate society ahead of the State Duma elections.
Kremlin officials continue to claim that Russia is unwilling to participate in any meaningful peace negotiations that allegedly do not meet the Russian Federation’s demands for Ukraine’s complete capitulation, despite Kyiv’s repeated calls for talks. This is reported in an article by the Institute for the Study of War (ISW), according to UNN.
Details
Analysts point to a statement by Russian Foreign Minister Sergei Lavrov, who said that Russia does not want to agree to a ceasefire that would freeze the current front line and that it will continue the war in Ukraine until it can secure a “long-term, reliable, and sustainable” settlement on its terms.
The Kremlin is likely doubling down on its firm rejection of the concept of negotiations in order to unite the Russian public around a pro-war platform ahead of the State Duma elections on September 18–20, 2026. The Kremlin’s routine rejection of all Ukrainian proposals for a ceasefire and peace indicates Russia’s continued unwillingness to end the war in Ukraine on any terms that do not meet Russia’s maximalist demands
They point out that Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy has repeatedly reaffirmed his commitment to peace negotiations and readiness to make compromises to end the war.
“Russia rejected Turkey’s and Ukraine’s proposals for a moratorium on strikes against maritime targets in the Black Sea, once again underscoring the fact that Moscow systematically refuses even the smallest diplomatic proposals from Ukraine and third countries,” ISW concludes.
We will remind you
According to ISW’s assessment, Russian dictator Vladimir Putin overestimates his chances in the war against Ukraine.

articles.title: DOD Leader Calls for Counter-Drone, Airborne Directed Energy Weapons
articles.body:
A top Pentagon tech official called on industry this week to help the military develop “lighter, more efficient” directed energy weapons designed to go on aircraft and conduct special operations missions or down drones—areas where the Air Force’s directed energy efforts have been quiet as of late.
Directed energy systems such as high-energy lasers and high-power microwave systems are an appealing alternative to expensive munitions for all branches of the U.S. military since they offer deep magazines and can be used near populated areas with a lower risk of collateral damage than high-explosive weapons pose.
Dodd, the assistant secretary of defense for critical technologies, said this promising technology is moving “out of the lab and toward the fight” in an Aug. 12 post on the social media platform X. But there is still critical work to be done, he added.
A key area where the Pentagon needs more from industry is the size and power of these systems: “Smaller. Lighter. More efficient,” Dodd wrote. “Size, weight, and power decide what flies. We want tech on aircraft and high-altitude platforms for counter-drone, expeditionary and special operations missions, and disrupting adversary C2.”
Dodd’s overall message to industry: “Bring us your best. Not slideware—hardware we can put on a range and stress.”
The Air Force has shown a particular interest in directed energy weapons to defend its air bases from drone attacks. Air Force Secretary Troy E. Meink told lawmakers in May 20 congressional testimony that the service is “focusing on electronic warfare to directed energy to kinetic capabilities to defend our Airmen and Guardians.”
The Air Force Research Laboratory has worked on high-power microwave technology for years, but the last publicly known test of the Tactical High-power Operational Responder, or THOR, occurred in 2023. The trailer-sized system was “exceptionally effective at disabling” a drone swarm during the demonstration. AFRL announced it was developing a follow-on system to THOR called “Mjolnir,” the name of the hammer wielded by the Norse god Thor.
No tests have been announced since. In its 2027 budget request, the Air Force has requested $91.8 million in research, development, test and evaluation for directed energy technology, with no mention of directed energy in the procurement account. The service projects another $406.6 million in funding between fiscal 2028 and fiscal 3031 to conduct further research on the technology, according to budget documents.
The potential exists for the service to acquire commercially available capabilities including directed-energy tech through the Joint Interagency Task Force 401, according to Air Force officials working on service’s point-defense effort to counter drone attacks.
Besides taking down adversary drones, one of the Air Force’s other major directed energy efforts was the Airborne High Energy Laser, which was planned for the special operations AC-130J gunship. But the AHEL weapon was canceled in 2024 after the program missed its “available integration and flight test window,” Military.com reported.
Besides size and power, Dodd was also critical of the amount of live-fire testing for these critical technologies.
“We need to shoot more, and shoot sooner,” Dodd wrote. “Live fire, in the field, with the units who will actually use these systems — air, land, sea, space. Testing can’t be a once-a-year event on a range. It has to be routine.”
This may be achievable since restrictions on testing directed energy weapons in U.S. airspace have loosened, according to David Bagnati, executive director of JIATF 401.
“We are now accepted to use high-energy lasers in the national airspace,” Bagnati told an audience Aug. 12 at the Space and Missile Defense Symposium in Huntsville, Ala.
Bagnati added that JIATF 401 is now doing “operational assessments at the border. It’s become our operational test bed. We’re also using the southern border as a springboard to bring new capabilities into the national airspace.”
Testing restrictions on directed energy technology in the U.S. eased in April after the Pentagon and the Federal Aviation Administration “completed a thorough safety assessment of a high-energy laser counter-drone system.”
Pentagon and FAA officials agreed to the March assessment after the FAA shut down all flight traffic over El Paso in February in reaction to a U.S. military laser designed for counter-drone operations being fired into the airspace over the U.S.-Mexican border.
Dodd also stressed in his post that the Pentagon needs systems that that combine “every sensor we have and fuse it into one picture.”
“Track and defeat many threats at the same time,” he wrote. “Directed energy has to work alongside kinetic and non-kinetic options, so the operator picks the right effect in seconds.”
Space Editor Courtney Albon contributed to this report.

articles.title: Battlefield sees 233 clashes, heaviest fighting on Kostiantynivka front – Ukraine's General Staff
articles.body:
Battlefield sees 233 clashes, heaviest fighting on Kostiantynivka front – Ukraine's General Staff
A total of 233 combat clashes have occurred on the battlefield over the past day between Ukraine's defence forces and Russian troops.
Source: General Staff of the Armed Forces of Ukraine on Facebook, information as of 08:00 on 15 August
Details: On the North Slobozhanshchyna front and in the operational zone in Russia's Kursk Oblast, Ukrainian defenders stopped six Russian attacks.
On the South Slobozhanshchyna front, Ukrainian units repelled 12 Russian attacks. The Russians attempted to advance near the settlements of Starytsia and Vovchansk and towards Izbytske, Vilcha, Lyman, Shyroke, Anyksyne and Khatnie.
On the Kupiansk front, 14 Russian offensive actions were recorded towards the village of Petro-Ivanivka and near Holubivka.
On the Lyman front, Ukrainian forces repelled Russian attempts to break through the defences, with the Russians launching five attacks towards the settlements of Drobysheve and Lyman.
On the Sloviansk front, the Russians conducted 23 assaults near the settlements of Riznykivka, Zakitne and Kryva Luka and towards Rai-Oleksandrivka, Ozerne and Mykolaivka.
On the Kramatorsk front, the Russian forces conducted one offensive action towards the village of Yurkivka.
On the Kostiantynivka front, 34 Russian attacks were recorded. The Russians conducted assaults near the settlements of Kostiantynivka, Ivanopillia, Illinivka, Toretske and Sofiivka and towards Stepanivka, Dolha Balka and Kucheriv Yar.
On the Pokrovsk front, the Russians conducted 29 attacks. They attempted to advance near the settlements of Dorozhnie, Kotlyne and Udachne and towards Svitle, Novyi Donbas, Muravka, Bilytske, Shevchenko, Vasylivka and Serhiivka.
On the Oleksandrivka front, the Russians conducted six attacks towards the settlements of Piddubne, Myrne, Verbove and Kalynivske.
On the Huliaipole front, the Russians attacked Ukrainian defence positions seven times. They attempted to advance towards the settlements of Rivne, Verkhnia Tersa and Novoselivka.
On the Orikhiv front, Ukrainian defenders stopped one Russian attempt to advance towards the village of Pavlivka.

articles.title: Polish Defense Ministry annoyed by Zelensky’s manner to ask for Patriot missiles — portal
articles.body:
MOSCOW, August 14. /TASS/. Poland is annoyed by the way Vladimir Zelensky is asking Warsaw for missiles for Patriot anti-aircraft missile systems, Wirtualna Polska portal quoted defense sources.
"Zelensky counted Polish missiles for Patriot systems and concluded that [Poland] can afford a large tranche [of missiles]," a Defense Ministry source told the portal. "First of all, we are confused as to how he's so sure about the number of PAC 3 MSE missiles we have in our warehouses. Secondly, it is better to start a discussion on this topic through an official request. Such issues are not resolved through interviews."
According to Defense Ministry Spokesman Janusz Sejmej, the ministry has not yet received an official request from Kiev to transfer missiles for Patriot.
According to the sources, Warsaw is ready to transfer only a small number of such missiles and only as part of a broader NATO tranche.
Besides, Wirtualna Polska said that Kiev may try to exchange the transfer of weapons for new permits to search for the victims of the Volyn massacre. A Foreign Ministry official told the portal that "the history and issues of exhumation [of victims of the Volyn massacre] will not be a subject of bargaining."
According to Wirtualna Polska sources, Zelensky's decision to rebury the remains of one of the leaders of the OUN (Organization of Ukrainian Nationalists, recognized as extremist and banned in Russia) Yevgeny Konovalets from the Netherlands in the Ukrainian capital may dampen Warsaw's desire to transfer to Kiev "expensive and complex weapons systems such as ammunition for Patriot."
Earlier, Polish Prime Minister Donald Tusk said that Warsaw would continue to provide Ukraine with military assistance, including missiles for Patriot. According to Defense Minister Wladyslaw Kosiniak-Kamysz, a final decision has not yet been made. In the spring, Poland already transferred several missiles to Patriots under the NATO coalition.

articles.title: Zelensky holds command meeting as Ukraine prepares asymmetric countermeasures to Russia’s new plans
articles.body:
Zelensky holds command meeting as Ukraine prepares asymmetric countermeasures to Russia’s new plans
According to Ukrinform, the head of state announced this on Facebook.
“I chaired the Headquarters meeting. The key issue is the funding needed for Ukraine’s defense and security forces for the fall and winter period. We identified the main shortfalls and additional needs for the development of the most innovative and technologically advanced types of weapons, as well as for accelerating the production of our strike capabilities and new types of defensive weapons, in particular missile interceptors,” Zelensky said.
He noted that intelligence agencies provided updated information on Russia’s plans and assured that Ukraine is preparing countermeasures and asymmetric responses.
Separately, the President emphasized the continuation of long-range sanctions against the aggressor country.
“We analyze the results of long-range sanctions against Russia, as well as medium-range sanctions, on a weekly basis. The established sanctions plan is being implemented, and we are promptly adjusting priorities so that Ukraine’s capabilities are 100% aligned with the need to achieve all the goals of our sanctions plan,” the head of state said.
According to him, Ihor Klymenko reported on the status of implementing decisions by the General Staff and the National Security and Defense Council, as well as areas requiring additional attention.
“There was also a separate report from the special services on the status of targeted operations against collaborators in the temporarily occupied territory—particularly in Sevastopol—who are participating in Russian attacks against Ukraine and Ukrainians. The collaborators will inevitably be held accountable,” Zelensky emphasized.
As reported by Ukrinform, the “Ukrainian Council of Arms Manufacturers,” an industry association of Ukrainian manufacturers, released a statement today in which manufacturers of weapons and military equipment call on the Ministry of Defense to ensure the continuity of contracts for the Ukrainian defense industry and the supply of necessary weapons to the Defense Forces.
Archive photo: Office of the President

articles.title: Ukraine Hits the Control Network Behind Russia’s Geran and Gerbera Drones
articles.body:
- Category
- War in Ukraine
Ukraine Hits the Control Network Behind Russia’s Geran and Gerbera Drones
Ukraine’s Defense Forces struck two ground-based relay stations used to control Russian Geran and Gerbera strike drones, as well as five UAV command posts, on August 13 and overnight into August 14, Ukraine’s General Staff reported.
The two ground-based relay stations were targeted near Zaliiznyi Port in Ukraine’s Kherson region. Such systems transmit control and communications signals between drone operators and unmanned aerial vehicles, extending their operational range and improving the stability of their connection.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
Ukrainian forces also struck five Russian UAV command posts located in areas including Chasiv Yar in Donetsk region and Zaliiznyi Port in Kherson region.
Three additional UAV command posts were targeted in Russia’s Kursk and Ukraine’s Zaporizhzhia regions, specifically near Volfinsky and Hordiyivka in Kursk region and Luhove in Zaporizhzhia region, according to the General Staff.
The strikes come as Russia continues to expand its production of attack drones. Ukraine’s Main Intelligence Directorate (HUR) estimates that Russia’s defense industry plans to manufacture 11,000 strike UAVs in August.
In an interview with RBC-Ukraine, HUR Deputy Chief Vadym Skibitskyi said the planned output includes Geran-1, Geran-2, Geran-3, Geran-4, and Geran-5 drones, as well as Harpy and several Gerbera variants, including strike and seeker versions.
According to Skibitskyi, Russia reduced both the intensity of its drone attacks and production volumes in July while restructuring its manufacturing capacity. The reconfiguration was aimed at increasing output of the turbojet-powered Geran-4 and Geran-5 drones.
Against this backdrop, Ukraine is also targeting the infrastructure that supports Russia’s drone operations. On August 13, Ukraine’s Unmanned Systems Forces struck 29 energy infrastructure facilities in Russian-occupied parts of Donetsk, Luhansk, and Zaporizhzhia regions and Crimea.
