articles.title: Ukrainian missiles attack Russian region – governor
articles.body:
Ukrainian missiles attack Russian region – governor
An industrial facility in Russia’s Samara Region was attacked by Ukrainian missiles, local governor Vyacheslav Fedorishchev said.
Emergency services have been deployed on site, Fedorishchev wrote in a Saturday morning post on Max.
The information regarding damage and casualties is currently being verified, he added.
In the Rostov Region, around 1,000 residents of seven villages were left without electricity after a Ukrainian drone damaged powerlines in the area, according to local governor Yury Slusar.
Around a dozen UAVs and three missiles were destroyed by air defenses in the region overnight, Slusar said. There have been no reports of injuries, he added.
Ukraine has several types of long-range missiles in their arsenal, including British-supplied Storm Shadow and homemade Flamingo munitions.
Moscow Mayor Sergey Sobyanin wrote on Max that at least 16 incoming drones were shot down on the approach to the Russian capital during the night.
In the town of Shatura in Moscow Region, a UAV hit a private home, injuring a 9-year-old boy and a 55-year-old woman, local governor Vyacheslav Vorobyeb wrote on Telegram. The child was hospitalized in serious condition, he added.
The Russian Defense Ministry said that a total of 598 Ukrainian UAVs were shot down or intercepted by electronic warfare means above 20 of the country's regions overnight.
Moscow has condemned Ukrainian drone strikes on Russia’s civilian infrastructure and residential areas as terrorist attacks aimed at compensating for Kiev’s setbacks on the battlefield, where Russian forces continue their steady advance.
Russia has responded by intensifying long-range missile and drone strikes against Ukraine’s military-industrial facilities and logistics infrastructure. Moscow maintains that it does not target civilians and that its strikes are directed solely at military targets and infrastructure supporting Kiev’s forces.
The Defense Ministry in Moscow said on Friday that a total of 14 such strikes had been launched over the previous week, hitting drone production plants, weapons, and logistics centers, as well as fuel, energy, and transport infrastructure. Military airfields and ports where cargo used by Kiev’s troops are unloaded and stored have also been targeted.
The Russian military also struck 15 oceangoing vessels operating in the interests of the Ukrainian military, including a tanker, seven dry cargo ships, two tugboats, and five patrol boats, it added.

articles.title: US military loses 25% of its MQ-9 drones as stocks dwindle in Iran war
articles.body:
US military loses 25% of its MQ-9 drones as stocks dwindle in Iran war
TEHRAN — The US military has suffered a 25% reduction in its MQ-9 Reaper drone fleet during the conflict with Iran, losing at least 45 aircraft valued at over $1.3 billion combined.
The Reaper can cost between $30 million and $50 million depending on the type of sensors and weapons it carries, according to the Air Force.
Heavy operations over the vital Strait of Hormuz—coupled with enemy strikes and persistent communications failures—have severely depleted these high-value surveillance and strike platforms alongside critical missile stockpiles, leaving US inventory stretched thin and forcing major strategic adjustments across the region.
The mounting drone losses reflect a broader, systemic strain on American military readiness as the campaign drags on. Before the outbreak of hostilities on February 28, the US military maintained a fleet of approximately 185 Reapers across the Air Force and Marine Corps, excluding classified intelligence assets. By May, senior Air Force leadership confirmed to Congress that active inventory had dropped to around 135 units. While the Marine Corps’ Pacific-based Reapers have avoided losses, the Air Force fleet patrolling Middle Eastern airspace has taken the brunt of the attrition. Flying at slow speeds and relatively low altitudes, the non-stealthy aircraft have proven to be vulnerable targets for Iranian forces and resistance groups operating in Yemen and Iraq.
Beyond uncrewed aircraft, the sheer intensity of the air campaign has rapidly drained America’s most advanced munitions. In the first month of hostilities alone, US forces expended over 850 Tomahawk cruise missiles and more than 1,000 Patriot and Terminal High Altitude Area Defense (THAAD) interceptors. This unprecedented burn rate—compounded by years of prior military assistance to Ukraine—has severely degraded stockpiles of key long-range strike capabilities and high-demand air defenses. Consequently, frontline commanders have been forced to change defensive tactics, rationing interceptors and holding back missiles in reserve unless an incoming strike poses a direct threat to personnel or key installations.
Restocking these depleted arsenals presents a daunting long-term industrial challenge. While the White House is pressing Congress for a $67 billion emergency supplemental war budget, financial infusions alone cannot overcome manufacturing bottlenecks. Analysis from defense think tanks highlights that critical systems face multi-year production backlogs. For instance, manufacturing a single THAAD interceptor takes nearly three years, with maximum national production capacity capped at just 96 units annually. Meeting the Pentagon’s multi-year requirement for thousands of interceptors could take decades at current factory output levels.

articles.title: Trump says record Navy deployment in Iran operations 'not nearly long enough'
articles.body:
Trump says record Navy deployment in Iran operations 'not nearly long enough'
US President Donald Trump on Friday dismissed concerns about the toll on sailors aboard the aircraft carrier USS Abraham Lincoln, who have endured a record deployment of almost nine months, saying that the deployment had been “not nearly long enough”. The Lincoln has been supporting the US war against Iran, and reports have emerged of sailors struggling with mental health issues.
US President Donald Trump on Friday downplayed the toll on American sailors enduring a record-setting deployment of nearly nine months on the USS Abraham Lincoln as concerns escalated about mental health and supply issues aboard the aircraft carrier supporting US operations against Iran.
In a brief exchange with reporters before flying to New York for an event to highlight falling violent crime rates across the US, Trump refuted that family members have raised concerns about the deployment's length and even said that the more than 260-day deployment is “not nearly long enough.”
"That ship is moving right now, or very shortly, and it’s being replaced with another very similar ship,” Trump said when asked about the lengthy deployment.
The Lincoln has been supporting the US war against Iran, and several Democratic lawmakers, including Sens. Richard Blumenthal of Connecticut and Ruben Gallego of Arizona, are pressing for accountability from the Pentagon over conditions aboard the carrier, which Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth on Thursday said were “completely misrepresented”.
To display this content from YouTube, you must enable advertisement tracking and audience measurement.
One of your browser extensions seems to be blocking the video player from loading. To watch this content, you may need to disable it on this site.
Rep. Jason Crow, D-Colo., who served three tours in Iraq and Afghanistan with the 82nd Airborne Division and 75th Ranger Regiment before being elected, took to social media to criticize Trump’s comments, saying on X that “President Trump does not care about our servicemembers or their families".
Extended deployments of carriers during the Iran conflict have raised concerns about the impact on service members who are away from home for long periods as well as the increasing strain on the ship and its equipment.
While hostilities between the US and Iran have calmed in recent weeks, the Navy has reimposed a blockade on Iranian ports in the crucial Strait of Hormuz, and the Trump administration has offered no clarity on how it intends to wind down the war. Hegseth said that the US military can maintain the blockage of Iranian ports “indefinitely”.
Another aircraft carrier, the USS George Washington, left port in Da Nang, Vietnam, last week, and is expected to replace the USS Lincoln, one of two aircraft carriers currently deployed in the Middle East.
Read moreIran vows to keep Strait of Hormuz closed until US meets demands
After reports emerged that sailors on the Lincoln are struggling with mental health concerns, the Navy said it has “not observed an increase in suicidal ideations or attempts aboard the ship”, though officials have declined to provide data, citing operational security and patient privacy concerns.
A Navy official said that a sailor aboard the Lincoln went overboard in early August but that the person was quickly recovered, treated by the ship’s medical department and transferred off ship for follow-on care. The official would not say whether it was being considered a suicide attempt.
US Central Command, which oversees military operations in the Middle East, has also pushed back on reports about poor conditions.
(FRANCE 24 with AP)

articles.title: Russia’s MoD threatens to “freeze” Ukrainians this winter, Kyiv responds by saying it will “get warm by the flames of Russian refineries”
articles.body:
On Aug. 14, Russia’s Ministry of Defense published a post on its Telegram channel showing drones with a caption reading: “You’re in for a deep freeze this winter.” The post followed a ministry statement about strikes “on Ukraine’s port infrastructure and seagoing vessels used in the interests of the Armed Forces of Ukraine.”
Several hours later, the AFU’s Center for Strategic Communications responded on its own channel with an image of a burning Russian oil refinery bearing the following caption: “We’ll warm ourselves with the flames of Russian refineries.”
Earlier today, Russian Foreign Minister Sergey Lavrov said it was unacceptable to halt the fighting along the current line of contact:
“This is not just about how comfortably someone lives today. Our people are suffering, people are dying from these terrorist acts. It is about our responsibility for the thousand-year history of the Russian state.”
Lavrov said Russia would intensify its actions against Ukraine.
“We are already doing this,” he said. “They are already starting to groan.”
The previous day, Aug. 13, Reuters reported that Ukraine had sent Russia a proposal through a third party to mutually halt attacks on civilian sites in the Black Sea, saying the fighting in the region had threatened global food supply chains. Several days earlier, Turkish Foreign Minister Hakan Fidan said Ankara had sent Kyiv and Moscow proposals to create a moratorium mechanism on strikes against commercial vessels in the Black Sea.
“Russia has not received a formal Turkish appeal through official channels specifying the terms of this initiative,” Russian Foreign Ministry spokeswoman Maria Zakharova responded on Aug. 14.
In June, Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky published an open letter to Vladimir Putin proposing a direct meeting between the two and a ceasefire along the entire front line for the duration of the talks. But no such developments ever materialized.
Since 2022, Russia has been intensifying its strikes on Ukraine’s energy infrastructure every fall in an effort to leave the country without electricity and heating during the winter months. In fall 2024, Russia managed to disable about 80% of Ukraine’s power generating capacity, damaging nearly all the country’s major thermal power plants. Ahead of the upcoming winter, Russian forces have focused on destroying the infrastructure of Ukraine’s electricity grid, targeting substations and power lines in the Sumy, Chernihiv, and Kharkiv regions.

articles.title: ‘The fear keeps building’: Residents of Russia’s Nizhnekamsk on life after a deadly Ukrainian drone attack
articles.body:
‘The fear keeps building’: Residents of Russia’s Nizhnekamsk on life after a deadly Ukrainian drone attack
A Ukrainian drone attack on Nizhnekamsk, a city in Russia’s Republic of Tatarstan, on August 10 killed 13 people, including citizens of Uzbekistan and Tajikistan. Residents quickly erected a makeshift memorial with flowers and candles, authorities canceled the city’s anniversary celebrations, and Tatarstan declared a period of mourning. The independent journalist cooperative Bereg reports on what residents of Nizhnekamsk saw and heard that day. Meduza is publishing the text in full.
Nizhnekamsk, a city on the Kama River 220 kilometers (137 miles) from Kazan, grew up around the Nizhnekamsk petrochemical plant, once one of the largest in the Soviet Union. Two oil refineries now operate there, Taneko and TAIF, and both have become regular targets for Ukrainian drones, with strikes recorded both in June and in July. But the attack on August 10 stood out.
The oil refineries were the intended targets, according to the General Staff of Ukraine’s Armed Forces, but the drones also struck residential buildings in the city and a hostel in the industrial zone. Russian officials said 13 people were killed, including citizens of Uzbekistan and Tajikistan and a 5-year-old girl who was sleeping on the balcony of a building on Shkolny Boulevard when a drone hit a tree and exploded, shattering a window. Another 78 people were injured.
The apartment building on Shkolny Boulevard, where the girl had lived, took the worst damage of any building in the strike: windows were blown out in 60 of its 132 apartments. Ninety-three residents applied to the Nizhnekamsk city administration for temporary housing, and 25 of the injured were hospitalized.
Here is how local residents reacted to the attack.
‘I’m an adult man, I’ve seen a lot, but I couldn’t hold back here’
Ruslan (name changed), a 53-year-old lawyer, was at home during the attack. He heard the sirens, since the balcony and windows in his apartment were open. He said he was among the first to reach the apartment building on Shkolny Boulevard.
“I stood near that building with tears in my eyes. I’m ashamed to admit it. I’m an adult man, I’ve seen a lot, but I couldn’t hold back here,” Ruslan said in a conversation with Bereg.
He didn’t know anyone among the dead or injured and learned about the victims from official reports, though what he saw on Shkolny Boulevard hit him harder than any report could. “It’s one thing to read about it in the news, and quite another to see the aftermath with your own eyes,” he said. “My first reaction was, of course, shock. It’s still very hard psychologically.”
A makeshift memorial appeared outside the city museum on August 10. Ruslan said people brought flowers, candles, icons, and children’s toys until evening. Many came as families, and local bikers arrived to lay carnations, he added.
“I stayed there for about 40 minutes, there were a lot of people. It’s amazing how close-knit our city is, how good our people are,” he told Bereg. He added that he worries most about the children: “At moments like this, you still end up thinking about the children rather than yourself.”
Olga (name changed) works on art projects in collaboration with a large local company. She doesn’t live in Nizhnekamsk full time but regularly travels there for work. “I don’t think it’s gotten more alarming, because I’ve already gotten used to everything that’s happening. It’s unsafe everywhere, really,” she said.
Olga said the attacks and restrictions have mostly disrupted her work schedule. Airport closures and rescheduled flights often force her to change plans and cancel meetings, which she said “affects her productivity overall.”
“There were times when we couldn’t get food [during business trips] because many cafes closed due to the drone threat,” she said. “But people there [in Nizhnekamsk] are calm. There’s no noticeable panic among residents.”
Despite the drones striking more often, her team has no plans to scale back its work in Nizhnekamsk. “People need this [the art projects] to cope somehow,” Olga said.
Unlike her, 44-year-old Alina (name changed) has lived in Nizhnekamsk her entire life. She told Bereg that in “recent months” she has often heard the sounds of drones at night. “It usually happens around four in the morning,” Alina added. She said that, over time, she has come to find these nights “harder and harder” to bear.
Alina was home during the August 10 attack, and this time, she recalled, the sound lasted longer than usual and seemed especially close:
The sound was long and happened not once but two or three times. The window was open, and the sound was very close, but nothing could be seen in the dark. I was very scared.
She said also heard “strange sounds” on August 12, even though authorities reported no drone attacks that day; other residents also wrote about the sounds in local community groups on social media.
Alina learned about the aftermath of the August 10 attack from her husband. “My anxiety kept growing, and I had to see a doctor. I’m afraid for my children and want to leave the city. The fear keeps building up because the strikes have become more frequent and more destructive,” the Nizhnekamsk resident said.
She’s especially worried about the start of the school year. Alina said parents in Nizhnekamsk school chat groups are already debating the September 1 assemblies. “Opinions are split 50-50. Some aren’t afraid, while others worry that large gatherings of people could be a reason for another drone attack. The school administration left the decision up to the parents,” she said. She plans to keep her own children home on September 1.
The children see things differently, she said. “They still don’t fully understand the danger,” Alina said with a sigh, adding that they don’t want to leave Nizhnekamsk, where they have friends, school, and their “familiar life.”
“But my husband and I are considering moving to a rural settlement where we have a plot of land. We don’t have enough money yet to fully build a house, [so we can’t leave right away],” Olga explained to Bereg.
‘These people should have been in shelters, but they weren’t’
Seven of the 13 people killed were citizens of Uzbekistan and two were citizens of Tajikistan. Their names were never published, and Bereg was unable to locate their relatives or friends. According to media reports, they were eating breakfast in a cafeteria when the strike hit Nizhnekamsk.
“We simply failed to meet the standards that are required by regulation. These people should have been in shelters, but they weren’t,” the head of Tatarstan, Rustam Minnikhanov, said after visiting the hostel.
A few days later, authorities announced the bodies of the dead had been sent to Uzbekistan and Tajikistan.
After the attack, Nizhnekamsk residents began petitioning the city administration to cancel the celebration of the city’s 60th anniversary, scheduled for August 15, writing on social media that holding a mass celebration so soon after people were killed would be inappropriate.
“They want to spend 60-80 million [rubles] on the city’s anniversary, that’s what was reported. Who needs this bravado when this kind of thing is happening. That money would be better spent on defending the city,” one person wrote on the social media site VK.
“All the celebrations should be canceled! The money would be better spent on strengthening the city’s defenses! How can there be any festivities while innocent civilians are dying!” another Nizhnekamsk resident wrote on social media.
In the end, authorities in Tatarstan declared a period of mourning and canceled City Day along with all other entertainment events. Nizhnekamsk Mayor Radmir Belyaev said City Day had been postponed indefinitely and would likely be held “in a different format.”
Ruslan, the lawyer, wants to see a permanent memorial built on Shkolny Boulevard in Nizhnekamsk to honor those killed on August 10. He has seen many people on social media express the same view and believes most residents of the city would support the idea.
At Meduza, we are committed to transparency about our use of artificial intelligence in the newsroom. The story you’re reading was written by one of our living, breathing journalists and translated from Russian using an AI model configured to follow our strict editorial standards. This translation process is the result of extensive testing and refinements to ensure our English-language coverage is timely and accurate. A Meduza editor reviews every draft before publication.
If you find any errors in this translation, please contact us at [email protected].
To read Meduza’s exclusive content in English, please subscribe to our newsletter.

articles.title: NATO Plans Thousands of AI Drones Along Russia and Belarus Borders
articles.body:
- Category
- War in Ukraine
NATO Plans Thousands of AI Drones Along Russia and Belarus Borders
NATO is planning to strengthen its eastern flank with a network of thousands of drones, sensors, and satellites linked through artificial intelligence, according to Politico on August 14.
The system is being developed under the Eastern Flank Deterrence Initiative (EFDI) and is intended to monitor threats along NATO’s borders with Russia and Belarus, stretching from northern Finland to the Black Sea.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
NATO plans for the network to detect violations of allied airspace and borders and serve as the first line of defense.
The system would combine data from multiple sources in real time. For example, if a drone detects a hostile UAV, AI could compare that information with satellite images, sensor readings, and radar data before sending the information to NATO allies.
Commanders would then be able to choose which forces should respond. NATO refers to the concept as a “kill web,” designed to send information directly to operators instead of moving it through multiple levels of command.
“Previously, information went through many intermediaries. Today, it can come directly from a sensor to a tool of influence,” US Army Captain Ronan Sefton said.
The platform is being developed in Wiesbaden with military personnel from the US, Canada, Lithuania, Poland, Germany, and other countries, according to Bild.
It is designed to connect allied command systems and allow them to exchange data. “The network works in real time. We are moving at high speed,” Canadian Lieutenant Colonel Mike Mendika said.
According to US Army Major Brian Hobek, if Russia attacked a NATO member, information about the attack would reach Wiesbaden and a response could be launched within five minutes.
The system is also intended to automate some of the most routine parts of drone operations. US Army Major Ben Schiff said this could include keeping a drone over a battlefield for long periods while it searches for targets.
The Wiesbaden team is also using 3D printing to develop drones. Schiff said new parts can be produced and tested on the same day, whereas development and testing previously could take months.
NATO believes the system should allow the alliance to adapt to changes on the battlefield faster than an adversary. The project is planned for implementation on a short timeline, as reported by Politico.
On July 7, 2026, NATO launched a new $40 billion initiative called Drone Edge to strengthen the Alliance’s ability to counter unmanned aerial threats.
Announced by Secretary General Mark Rutte during the NATO Defense Industry Forum in Ankara, the five-year program was developed using lessons learned from recent wars, including Russia's full-scale invasion of Ukraine.
Under the initiative, NATO member states committed to investing in counter-drone technologies, expanding drone pilot training, and increasing the number of drone operators in their armed forces fivefold by the end of 2027.

articles.title: Israeli airstrike on southern Lebanon kills 7 people, Lebanese state media say
articles.body:
Israeli airstrikes on southern Lebanon kill 9 people, Health Ministry says
BEIRUT (AP) — Israeli airstrikes on southern Lebanon killed at least nine people Saturday, in some of the deadliest attacks since a precarious truce between Israel and Hezbollah went into effect on June 20.
Lebanon’s Health Ministry and state news agency said one of the airstrikes that targeted a home on the edge of the village of Ansar killed seven people, including three children, and wounded two. The second, on the village of Deir al-Zahrani, killed two and wounded nine.
Israel and the Lebanese government announced a “framework agreement” on June 26, laying out a plan for Israeli forces to withdraw from southern Lebanon, in exchange for the disarmament of the Iran-backed Hezbollah militant group. It also envisions steps toward an eventual peace agreement between the two countries — which technically remain in a state of war nearly 80 years after Israel’s establishment.
Hezbollah has refused direct talks and wasn’t party to the deal.
Lebanese Prime Minister Nawaf Salam criticized Israel’s airstrikes on southern Lebanon, saying they intimidate “residents in their homes” and undermine efforts to stabilize the situation in the south.
“The seven martyrs of the Israeli airstrike on the town of Ansar are not military infrastructure and the children and women killed were not military targets,” Salam said in comments posted on X. He added that it is the job of the Lebanese state to deal with any military infrastructure in the country.
“Israel must halt this escalation,” Salam said. He added that the security of the Lebanese people and their right to life on their land “are not subject to negotiation or bargaining.”
Intense Israeli airstrikes early Saturday also hit the strategic Ali Taher hill, which overlooks parts of the southern city of Nabatiyeh and main roads leading to it, NNA reported. Despite the truce, Israel’s military has continued its almost daily attacks on the area, which is north of the Litani River and has been a de facto boundary in Lebanon, with large areas to the south under Israeli military control.
The Israeli military said in a statement that it struck Hezbollah infrastructure in the areas of Ali Taher and Ansar in response to an action against Israeli soldiers in the area. The military added that it will not allow the Hezbollah to harm Israeli civilians or soldiers “and will continue to operate to remove threats.”
A Hezbollah official did not immediately respond when asked for comment on whether they carried out any attacks on Israeli forces in southern Lebanon.
Earlier this month, two Israeli soldiers were killed in an explosion in southern Lebanon, the first Israeli deaths since the shaky truce. Hezbollah did not comment on the blast.
Lebanon and Israel have held seven rounds of talks; the most recent took place in Rome earlier this month.
The Iran-backed Hezbollah has refused to disarm and accuses the Lebanese government of making too many concessions without guaranteeing an Israeli withdrawal.
The latest Israel-Hezbollah war erupted on March 2, when Hezbollah fired rockets across the border two days after the U.S. and Israel launched their attacks on Iran. More than 4,000 people have been killed by Israeli strikes in Lebanon since then, including hundreds of civilians. About 40 soldiers and three civilians — including a military contractor — have been killed on the Israeli side.
____
Associated Press writer Sam Mednick contributed to this report from Tel Aviv, Israel.

articles.title: Washington quizzes NATO allies on support for Trump – Bloomberg
articles.body:
US issues NATO members ‘loyalty test’ – Bloomberg
The US is making military support for NATO members contingent on how closely they align with President Donald Trump’s foreign policy, Bloomberg has reported.
Washington has recently sent NATO members a document containing a series of questions aimed at gauging their alignment with the Trump administration, the agency said.
Governments were asked whether they had “been publicly supportive” of US foreign-policy initiatives, including those in the Middle East and Western Hemisphere, the outlet reported, citing a copy it had reviewed. Washington also wanted to know what “restrictions” individual countries have imposed on US forces operating from military bases on their territory.
The answers could factor into decisions about how US military capabilities are distributed among NATO members, according to Bloomberg.
The apparent loyalty test comes amid widening tensions between Washington and its traditional European allies, with Trump repeatedly accusing NATO members of relying on US protection while failing to contribute enough to their own defense.
Trump has long been a fierce critic of NATO countries’ defense spending, repeatedly accusing European members of underfunding their militaries and effectively relying on Washington to bankroll their defense.
Earlier this summer, he renewed his criticism ahead of the NATO summit in Ankara, arguing that the US “spends more money on NATO than any other country, by far, to protect them, without getting any benefit.” He contrasted nearly $1 trillion in annual US defense spending with significantly smaller expenditures by individual European allies.
NATO members agreed at last year’s summit in The Hague to raise defense and security-related spending to 5% of GDP by 2035. Trump hailed the pledge as a victory for Washington but has since questioned whether all members are on track to meet the target.
Defense spending is not the only source of friction, however. Tensions have intensified further over the US war with Iran, with Trump criticizing European allies for refusing to become more directly involved and complaining that “they were not there for us.”
Several NATO members also refused to allow Washington to use jointly operated military bases for offensive operations against Iran. US Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth branded the restrictions “shameful,” arguing that they had put American troops “at risk.”
The US, however, still maintains an extensive military presence across Europe, including tens of thousands of personnel in Germany. Ramstein Air Base is one of Washington’s most important military hubs outside the US and a key logistical center for operations in Europe, Africa, and the Middle East.
The growing disagreements have, in turn, fueled debate in Europe about reducing its reliance on Washington for security. European officials have increasingly discussed “strategic autonomy” and the need to develop greater capacity to defend the continent should US priorities diverge from the rest of NATO.

articles.title: Schools serving US military families put new emphasis on Western civilization and Christianity
articles.body:
AP Exclusive: US military base schools put new emphasis on Western civilization and Christianity
WASHINGTON (AP) — The Department of Defense is introducing a course centered on Western civilization and Christianity this fall in the schools it operates for military families, part of an effort by Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth to redirect the education system toward patriotic values and classical learning.
The Department of Defense Education Activity operates about 160 schools across 11 countries and educates roughly 70,000 students who are children of active-duty military or civilian service members. Conservatives have eyed the schools — which, unlike most public schools, are run by the federal government — as a testing ground for reshaping education.
The Western civilization course planned for this fall will use a textbook published by Encounter Books, a conservative publishing house. Titled “The Golden Thread: A History of the Western Tradition, Volume I: The Ancient World and Christendom,” it includes suggested lesson plans created in partnership with Hillsdale College, a conservative Christian school in Michigan that has also developed influential materials for K-12 schools.
Historians and educators who reviewed excerpts of the text told The Associated Press it depicts points throughout history in misleading ways, representing Western civilization and Christianity as one and the same and casting Islam as a threat to both.
“You’ve got to wonder a bit whether Western civilization is a Trojan horse for classical Christian education,” said Phil Gorski, a historical sociology professor at Yale University.
The course is part of a wider reshaping of the Defense Department’s schools. They have begun hiring classical learning teachers, and the department has brought in new academic chiefs with ties to classical learning charter schools and to Republican-led efforts to promote more patriotic education.
In a written statement, the Pentagon said it “remains committed to providing all of its military-connected students with the best possible education and opportunities.” It did not respond directly to a series of questions about the textbook and the broader push for classical learning.
Classical education broadly refers to a teaching style built on the liberal arts, with an emphasis on critical thinking and citizenship. Students are taught to imitate the rhetoric and style of great thinkers and writers. While some classical educators have pushed to incorporate diverse scholars, critics have argued the movement focuses too heavily on foundational texts from Greek, Roman and other Western writers and gives short shrift to achievements in Asia, Africa and the Middle East.
Conservatives see classical learning as an antidote to unflattering depictions of US history
Conservative politicians have embraced classical learning, especially as the Trump administration and Republican-led states have pushed schools to emphasize patriotism and put boundaries around how they teach unflattering parts of American history.
In his writing and public remarks since before becoming defense secretary, Hegseth has advocated for parents to embrace classical Christian education.
In his 2022 book “Battle for the American Mind,” Hegseth, a former Fox News host, describes a history of progressives working to remove God and religion from public and private schools. For parents, he writes, not sending their children to classical Christian schools would be to admit defeat.
“It is certainly not sustainable, merely passing the same losing hand to the next generation,” Hegseth writes. “With this approach, we lose. We lose America — and Western Civilization.”
Many classical Christian schools focus on reclaiming Western civilization from external threats. But across the broader field of classical education — including secular private schools — the field is increasingly split on this point, said Susan Wise Bauer, the author of a popular classical homeschooling program. She said there is a range of approaches on which texts are worth studying.
“Whenever you have a system of education where that is the impulse, ... ‘This is us, and they are them over there,’” she said, “then the idea of a shared literary heritage becomes a weapon.”
Textbook casts Western civilization as under threat
In the Pentagon’s system, high school students can take the new course, Western Civilization to 1500, to fulfill a world history graduation requirement, according to a news release. The course is offered through the department’s virtual school.
In the textbook’s introduction, the authors write: “The dangers presented by the neglect of Western history are not trivial.”
“When citizens of Western countries are utterly ignorant of history, as most now are, they are left unarmed against the general hostility to their own tradition that has become so destructive a force in contemporary culture,” they write.
The idea that external forces will displace the dominant culture is a common right-wing political narrative, said Curtis Dozier, a professor of Greek and Roman studies at Vassar College.
“It’s this right-wing idea that when immigrants come to a country, they care more about their own traditions and history and seek to replace the tradition of the place,” he said.
The textbook’s authors credit early Christianity with promoting the idea that all people must be treated humanely. It argues that “Christian faith also supported a humane cosmopolitanism.”
The book describes Islam as inherently more violent than Christianity. In a chapter on the Middle Ages, the text describes Arabs as resentful or bitter toward Christians and Jews.
In a section titled “Holy War and Martyrdom in Battle,” the book describes wars fought by Christians, such as the Crusades, as intended to defend and protect other Christians. Islam, in contrast, glorifies violence and war, the book says, invoking the Oct. 7 Hamas attacks and 9/11.
“In recent decades, Islam as a religion has, understandably, aroused acute hostility from a great many non-Muslims around the world thanks to the behavior of radical Muslim terrorists. Sometimes referred to as Islamists, their atrocities have been applauded by depressingly large numbers of ordinary Muslims,” the book says.
Matthew Gabriele, a history and religion professor at Virginia Tech, said the book’s description of the Crusades and the conflicts with the Islamic world strips out important details and context to depict Islam as an aggressive religious tradition and downplays the religious motivations and violence of the Christian church.
“It’s trying to make a contemporary political point by continuously referencing things that happened in the 21st century,” Gabriele said. “The fact that (the book) does this very selectively and only when it suits a particular political project suggests to me that this is not a scholarly history in any kind of real sense.”
The book’s publisher, Roger Kimball, said it was peer-reviewed by 15 experts. “As the proud publisher of this incomparable work, I stand behind it in every detail,” he said.
One of the book’s co-authors, Harvard emeritus professor James Hankins, said the text does not attempt to characterize Christianity and Western civilization as one. Segments of the book acknowledge the West’s cultural debts to the Islamic world, said Hankins, who now teaches at the University of Florida’s Hamilton School for Classical and Civic Education, a conservative-backed project to teach Western civilization.
An emphasis on the study of Western civilization was standard until the 1970s, Hankins said. He criticized the move away from teaching it, noting that other countries such as China study their own civilization.
“Abandoning it has been foolish in my view, and is one cause of the growing cultural disorientation of the last couple of generations,” he said in an email. “People no longer know where they come from or where they belong in the story of our civilization.”
The Trump administration aligned the military’s education system with its political vision
In speeches and interviews, Hegseth has drawn a line from the country’s founding to Western civilization and early Christianity, a religion he describes as under attack by outside forces. He often argues the U.S. was founded as a Christian nation and troops should embrace God.
At an event last September recognizing a civics education initiative, Hegseth emphasized the need to teach these values to children early on.
“That type of brilliance didn’t come out of thin air,” he said of the Founding Fathers. “It was first inspired by God (and) inspired by an understanding of human history, an understanding of biblical history (and) an understanding of Western civilization philosophy and theology and civics poured into a generation of men and poured into an American experiment — it wasn’t an accident.”
President Donald Trump’s administration also has moved to align the military’s education apparatus with its broader vision for American schools. Admissions offices at U.S. military academies now accept the Classical Learning Test, a college entrance exam that positions itself as a classical alternative to the SAT. And last year, the ACLU sued the defense school system over its decision to ban hundreds of books that covered topics like race, gender and democracy.
In March, the department abruptly changed the leadership of Department of Defense Education Activity schools, replacing Beth Schiavino-Narvaez with Paul Craft as director. In a news release at the time, Hegseth described Craft as the right leader to reorient the school system “toward patriotic values and classical learning.”
The Pentagon also replaced the education activity’s chief academic officer, hiring Tiffany Hoben, who previously worked in the Florida Department of Education under Republican Gov. Ron DeSantis. In Florida, she oversaw the rollout of a civics curriculum that was criticized for claiming America’s founders did not intend for a full separation of church and state.
This summer, the department announced the hiring of Matthew Kirby as the system’s Americas regional director. Kirby is the CEO of Liberty Classical Schools, an Atlanta-based network of charter schools.
In an all-hands meeting after his appointment, Craft described classical learning as a priority that came directly from Hegseth.
“He has tasked us with taking the best that we can from the lessons learned from classical learning in a private school setting to say, ‘How do we expose our kids to that in a public school setting like us?’” Craft said.

articles.title: A Russian soldier kept a Ukrainian woman in a basement and raped her for two months – Ukrainian court sentences him to 12 years
articles.body:
A Ukrainian court has sentenced a Russian soldier to 12 years in prison for repeatedly raping a 57-year-old civilian woman for about two months in an occupied village in Donetsk Oblast, Ukraine’s Prosecutor General’s Office said on 14 August.
Ukrainian authorities and international monitors have documented hundreds of cases of conflict-related sexual violence by Russian forces in Ukraine, while warning that the true number is likely higher because many cases go unreported, particularly in occupied territories.
Woman was trapped with Russian soldiers
The 50-year-old Russian serviceman entered a village in the Pokrovsk district in September 2025 as part of a small infantry group, according to prosecutors. He and two other Russian soldiers occupied the basement of a private home where two local civilians were sheltering from Russian attacks.
During one of the attacks, the civilian man was killed. The woman was then left in the basement with the three armed Russian soldiers.
In early October, one of the soldiers began sexually assaulting her. The court found that the abuse became systematic and continued for about two months.
The soldier threatened to kill the woman if she refused. Two other Russian servicemen were present during this period, while the woman was effectively unable to leave the basement or protect herself.
The abuse ended in December, when Ukrainian forces captured the Russian soldier during fighting. The woman was freed.
Convicted Russian soldier had spent 32 years in prison
The convicted man is a resident of Russia’s Sverdlovsk Oblast who had spent a total of 32 years in prison for robbery and armed robbery before joining the Russian military.
He signed a contract with the Russian army while serving his sentence and was later deployed as a rifleman with the 114th Separate Motor Rifle Brigade of Russia’s 51st Combined Arms Army.
The defendant denied committing the crime in court. Prosecutors presented evidence that the court found sufficient to establish his guilt in the cruel treatment of a civilian.
He was sentenced to 12 years in prison, the maximum punishment under the provision of Ukraine’s Criminal Code used in the case.
Sexual violence as a weapon of Russia’s war
Ukraine’s Prosecutor General’s Office had recorded 401 cases of sexual violence against civilians allegedly committed by Russian military personnel since the start of the full-scale invasion as of June 2026.
The victims included 250 women and 151 men, including 23 girls and one boy.
Donetsk Oblast had the second-highest number of documented cases, with 92, behind Kherson Oblast’s 124. Ukrainian prosecutors had sent 64 indictments involving 81 people to court, while Ukrainian courts had issued 19 verdicts against 26 individuals. All those convicted received prison sentences.
The documented figures do not capture the full scale of the abuse. The Prosecutor General’s Office has noted that the actual number may be higher because these are cases victims have been able to report.

articles.title: Zelensky on Air Defense: ‘It Is Not Easy, but It Will All Happen’
articles.body:
“It is not easy, but all of this will happen,” President Volodymyr Zelensky said Friday, as Ukraine ramped up efforts to secure air-defense missiles and domestic weapons production agreements.
“We continue working to secure air defense for Ukraine... and agreements for production in Ukraine,” Zelensky said in his evening address.
JOIN US ON TELEGRAM
Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official.
The president pointed to technologies once considered unattainable for Kyiv – including F-16 fighter jets, advanced missiles and the annual production of millions of drones – as proof that Ukraine can deliver on ambitious defense goals.
He expressed similar confidence in securing anti-ballistic capabilities and additional Patriot systems.
But Zelensky warned that political delays carry a human cost.
“Every delay, which unfortunately exists at the political level, simply takes lives,” he said, urging international partners to move faster.
Strengthening defenses against Russian ballistic missiles remains one of Kyiv’s top priorities.
Ukraine is seeking additional Patriot systems and interceptors, production licenses for anti-ballistic capabilities and expanded contributions to the PURL weapons-purchasing program.
Kyiv’s longer-term goal is not only to obtain Western air-defense systems, but to expand production of critical defensive weapons inside Ukraine.

articles.title: Russia admits new petrol shortages amid ongoing long-range Ukrainian strikes
articles.body:
Ukraine has been targeting Russia's energy sites with drones and missiles for months, hoping to hit a vital source of revenue for the Russian army.
Russian authorities acknowledged on Friday that some regions face new petrol shortages, as Ukraine steps up attacks on the country's oil refineries.
Ukraine has been targeting Russia's energy sites with drones and missiles for months, hoping to hit a vital source of revenue for the Russian army.
Russia has shut down one major refinery at Orsk, around 1,300 kilometres from the front line, for six months after it was attacked this week.
"The situation remains tense in several regions of the country regarding fuel supplies to service stations," the government said in a social media post.
Oil companies are "taking the necessary measures to increase deliveries to the most vulnerable regions," according to the statement.
It said a government meeting had been held on the shortages and the Deputy Prime Minister responsible for energy, Alexander Novak, has ordered that fuel prices be monitored.
Companies and car drivers have suffered repeat shortages in recent months because of the conflict.
Nearly every Russian region has at some point had to limit fuel sales or impose other kinds of rationing, such as banning the filling of jerry cans.
The Krasnodar region on the Black Sea, known for its tourist beaches, has been one of the worst hit.
"The situation regarding petrol supplies at service stations has become complicated," regional governor Venyamin Kondratyev said.
Oil companies "have again started imposing restrictions on the amount of fuel supplied and reduced service station opening hours," he added.
"This is causing concern among the region's residents and visitors," the governor added, stating that he had asked the authorities to send more fuel.
The governor of the Orenburg region, where the Orsk refinery is located, said on Thursday it had been shut down and repairs would take months.
Rare admission
Russian President Vladimir Putin acknowledged for the first time in June that his country was facing a “certain deficit” of fuel.
Speaking at a meeting with officials that focused on the fuel situation, Putin admitted that the country was “going through a difficult period,” but insisted that Moscow would “honour all its social obligations.”
Shortly after, he told state TV that the country's arms industries will quickly ramp up production of air defence systems to fend off Ukrainian attacks.
Claiming the issues that arise are not critical, Putin also said that Russia will import more fuel and speed up repair works at oil facilities to end the “temporary deficit.”
Ukraine’s President Volodymyr Zelenskyy has referred to strikes on Russian energy sites deep inside Russia as “long-range sanctions.”

articles.title: Hsiao says stronger Taiwan defenses required to deter China
articles.body:
TAIPEI (Taiwan News) — Taiwan must strengthen its defenses and make military action more costly for China, Vice President Hsiao Bi-khim (蕭美琴) said Friday.
Speaking in an interview with Al Jazeera, Hsiao said China's intention to take control of Taiwan is well known, while its willingness to use military force remains a serious concern. She said Beijing has been steadily building its military capabilities and some assessments suggest it could be ready for a possible attack by 2027.
Taiwan must therefore improve its ability to defend itself and raise the cost of any Chinese military action, Hsiao said. Preventing conflict is important not only for Taiwan's security but also for regional stability and the global economy.
Hsiao said China is using pressure below the level of open warfare, including cyberattacks, interference in domestic affairs, disinformation, legal measures, and psychological operations. She said Taiwan needs stronger social resilience and democratic institutions to respond to these threats.
China has also increased activities that could be used to pressure Taiwan through a maritime blockade. Hsiao said Beijing has used its coast guard and other nonmilitary forces to carry out maritime actions that Taiwan says have no basis in international law.
She added Taiwan must work with other countries to protect freedom of navigation, the rule of law, and peace in the Indo-Pacific. She said similar maritime tensions involving China have emerged in the South China Sea and waters near Japan, making the issue a wider regional concern.
Asked about possible US military involvement if Taiwan were attacked, Hsiao said the question was hypothetical and that the focus was instead on preventing such a situation. She said Taiwan and the US continue to cooperate to strengthen defenses and maintain peace and cross-strait stability.

articles.title: IN BRIEF: Russian citizen sentenced to 23 years in jail for spying for Polish intel
articles.body:
MOSCOW, August 14. /TASS/. The Moscow City Court sentenced Russian national Georgy Pirogov, who collected data about advanced Russian weapons used during the special military operation, to 23 years behind bars on charges of spying for Poland, the press service of Russia’s Federal Security Service (FSB) said.
TASS has summed up key facts about the situation.
Spying for Polish intelligence
According to investigators, Pirogov, who left Russia in April 2022, initiated contacts with the Polish National Defense Ministry’ Military Intelligence Service.
He was tasked with collecting and sharing classified data about advanced weapons used by the Russian army in the course of the special military operation.
According to FSB, drawing on his contacts among the Russian defense sector’s workers, Pirogov obtained classified information for foreign intelligence services regarding the production and deployment of missile systems
Apart from that, the man shared personal data of individuals who have access to state secrets to involve them in activities against Russia’s security.
It was also discovered that he transferred cryptocurrency to the Ukrainian army, purchased equipment for armed groups, and organized its deliveries from Poland to Ukraine.
Confession
Pirogov has confessed to working for Polish intelligence, according to FSB.
He said he knew he was collaborating with a Polish organization.
He admitted to doing it of his own volition.
Pirogov also said he had been paid "for the very fact of collaboration and some future perspectives."
According to Pirogov, the Polish side is evidently interested "in some sort of comprehensible technical documentation, orders, executive documents, technical projects."
The communication took place via the Telegram messenger, he added.
Criminal case and verdict
A criminal case was opened under article 275 of the Russian Criminal Code (high treason in the format of espionage and financial assistance to a foreign state in its activities against Russia’s security).
The Moscow City Court sentenced the man to 23 years in a maximum security penal colony, an 800,000-ruble (roughly $9,500) fine, and 2-year custodial restraint.
The verdict has taken effect.

articles.title: First warehouses burned, now payment system is down: Ukraine launches dual campaign against Russia’s largest marketplace that reportedly moves drone parts
articles.body:
Ukraine has hit Russia's biggest marketplace in cyberspace as well as with drones. Cyber specialists disrupted Wildberries' operations across Russia, Ukraine's Defense Ministry's Main Intelligence Directorate (HUR) reports.
Ukraine says that Wildberries is not ordinary commerce but a piece of Russia's war logistics. According to the military command, the network moves military-related goods, and President Zelenskyy has said Russia uses the platform to bring in sanctioned drone components, which is why Ukraine has spent weeks burning its warehouses and now strikes its servers.
HUR reports that on 10 and 11 August, specialists from the Cyber Corps community attacked Wildberries' digital infrastructure, causing failures in its payment and customer service systems.
The attack hit payments and support
The disruption struck where customers feel it. Because of the problems with the payment infrastructure, users complained they could not complete certain transactions.
For a platform whose whole value is the frictionless movement of goods and money, a payment system that will not process transactions is a direct hit to the business.
The strain spread to customer service. At the same time, the load on the support service rose, causing failures in the contact centers, so the attack degraded both the ability to pay and the ability to get help across Russia.
It pairs with the warehouse strikes
In July, Ukrainian drones destroyed eight Wildberries warehouses, about 15.4% of the marketplace's storage.
Pairing strikes on physical infrastructure with Ukrainian cyber operations strengthens the pressure on the company, HUR assessed.
The logic is to squeeze the same target from two directions at once: burn the warehouses that store the goods, then disable the systems that move them to customers, so damage in one domain amplifies damage in the other.
Earlier, Ukraine hit the Progress Rocket Space Center in Samara, which builds Soyuz-2 rockets used to launch Rassvet, Russia’s planned alternative to Starlink.

articles.body:
Evening news wrap: Delhi HC gets bomb threat; US loses 45 Reaper drones in Iran war, & more
TOI News Desk / TIMESOFINDIA.COM / Updated: Aug 14, 2026, 18:11 IST
Comments

Delhi HC receives bomb threat ahead of Independence Day; US has reportedly lost nearly 45 Reaper drones in Iran war (Photo: Agencies)
The Delhi High Court received a bomb threat email a day before Independence Day, with the message mentioning the Red Fort and khaki-clad attackers.
The US military has reportedly lost at least 45 MQ-9 Reaper drones during its war with Iran, representing about 25% of its fleet.
Chief Justice Surya Kant strongly disapproved of the Bar Council of India's now-revoked action against NALSAR students following their protest against the CJI's invitation as chief guest.
The Congress has questioned the Centre's approach to the caste census, saying the absence of a pre-prepared list of castes raises “serious doubts on intent”.
Former Manchester United and Aston Villa goalkeeper Jimmy Rimmer has died at the age of 78.
Here are the top 5 stories of the day
‘Lal Qila ta nishana hove ga’: Delhi HC bomb threat ahead of Independence Day mentions khaki-clad attackers
A bomb threat was received at the Delhi High Court through an email at around 11.43 am, prompting authorities to activate the standard operating procedure and carry out extensive security checks on the premises. The threatening email reportedly mentioned August 15 and contained the warning, “Lal Qila ta nishana hove ga” (the Red Fort will be targeted). The email also made a reference to those carrying out the bombing being dressed in khaki. Read full story
US loses 45 Reaper drones in Iran war, representing 25% of fleet worth $1.3 billion: Report
The US military has reportedly lost at least 45 MQ-9 Reaper drones during its war with Iran, representing about 25 per cent of its fleet. The Reaper is used for surveillance and targeted strikes and can cost between $30 million and $50 million, depending on its sensors and weapons, according to the US Air Force. The losses could therefore represent more than $1.3 billion in equipment costs, according to three US officials familiar with Pentagon data, quoted by the Washington Post. Read full story
BCI action, U-turn and SC rebuke: How NALSAR students' protest against CJI kicked up a row
Chief Justice of India Surya Kant strongly disapproved of the Bar Council of India's now-revoked decision to stop enrolment of 2026 graduates of Hyderabad's NALSAR University of Law as advocates after students opposed his invitation as chief guest for the university's convocation.
The Supreme Court said students had a right to protest peacefully and stayed any coercive action against NALSAR students or faculty by the BCI or state Bar Council. Read full story
'Serious doubts on intent': Congress attacks Centre over caste census format; cites Telangana model
The Congress questioned the Centre's approach to caste enumeration in the upcoming Census, saying the decision not to provide a pre-prepared list of castes for respondents to choose from raised “serious doubts on intent”. The party also alleged that political parties had not been consulted on the questionnaire.
Congress general secretary in-charge of communications, Jairam Ramesh, said it was widely expected that the caste question would include a state-wise list, similar to the caste surveys conducted in Bihar and Telangana. Read full story
Jimmy Rimmer dies at 78: Tributes pour in for the Manchester United and Aston Villa star, exploring the European Cup winner career’s best highlights
Former Manchester United and Aston Villa goalkeeper Jimmy Rimmer has passed away at the age of 78. The veteran goalkeeper enjoyed a career spanning more than two decades. He won the European Cup with both clubs. Rimmer was part of United's 1968 European Cup-winning squad. He later became a key player for Aston Villa, started their European Cup campaign in 1982 and helped them reach the final against Bayern Munich. Read full story

articles.title: Putin Orders Military Leadership to Destroy NATO and the EU from Within — NYT
articles.body:
In late 2025, Russian dictator Vladimir Putin convened a briefing with military leaders and set a goal for 2026: “to dismantle NATO and the EU from within.”
This was reported by The New York Times, citing officials from both countries familiar with the details of the meeting.
According to the newspaper’s sources, Moldova plays a key role in these plans. According to representatives of Western intelligence agencies, subjugating Ukraine ranks first on Russia’s list of priorities, while establishing control over Moldova ranks second.
According to the newspaper’s sources, Moldova could serve as an ideal springboard for Russia to launch further aggression against both Ukraine and the West. They added that Putin still intends to seize territories in southern Ukraine to create a land corridor connecting Russia with Moldova.
To achieve these goals, Russia, in particular, attempted to interfere in the parliamentary elections held in Moldova on September 28, 2025—through cyberattacks, disinformation, as well as vote-buying and campaigning.
Moldovan priests were also recruited for the Kremlin’s campaign; in exchange for a thousand dollars, they were tasked with persuading parishioners to reject the referendum on Moldova’s accession to the European Union and to oppose pro-Western policies.
In addition, in the summer of 2025, the Russians organized a “training camp” in Serbia, where participants—mostly Moldovan citizens—were taught how to handle rifles, break through police cordons, and set buildings on fire.
Participants were paid $400 each to take part in the three- to four-day course. The camp’s instructors were personnel linked to Russian military intelligence (GRU). The goal of the camp was to train a group of fighters capable of interfering in elections, according to representatives of Western intelligence services.
Similar camps were organized in Bosnia and near Moscow. More than 100 young Moldovan citizens went through these camps. During their training, they were taught to manufacture and use incendiary devices and homemade explosive devices, as well as to operate drones “equipped with special devices for explosives or arson.”
After completing their training, some of the recruits were sent to the city of Banja Luka in Bosnia to carry out practical tasks—specifically, mapping the locations of administrative and government buildings and scouting potential sites for launching drones.
However, a few weeks before the vote, Moldovan police raided hundreds of homes and detained those who had undergone training at the camps, while Moldovan cybersecurity experts, with the support of Western allies, repelled the cyberattacks.
According to the investigation, the Moldovan prosecutor’s office is investigating the activities of more than 80 individuals suspected of inciting mass unrest. Twelve of them have already been formally charged. According to court records, participants were told that if she won, “war would break out in the country, just like in Ukraine.”
At least two individuals linked to these training camps are also suspected of involvement in other destabilization operations in France and Germany.

articles.title: Yemen government vows response after Houthi missiles hit Mokha
articles.body:
Breadcrumb
Yemen government vows response after Houthi missiles hit Mokha port
Yemen’s internationally recognised government has vowed a "harsh" response intended to deter further attacks after Houthi forces fired ballistic missiles at the Red Sea port of Mokha, in the latest escalation around the strategically important west-coast city near the Bab al-Mandab Strait.
One member of port security was killed, while two sailors were reported missing. Eight civilians, including two security personnel, were wounded, according to an initial toll issued by the government.
Colonel Majed al-Nuzaili, spokesman for the Yemeni armed forces, said six ballistic missiles struck Mokha port on Friday evening in what he called an attack on a civilian, economic and maritime facility.
"The armed forces will not allow civilian facilities to be turned into military targets," al-Nuzaili said, pledging a "deterrent and harsh" response to attacks on Yemeni infrastructure and interests.
The Houthi shelling also struck residential areas in Mokha, with Yemeni authorities reporting that four civilians were killed and several fishing boats set on fire. A military source told the state-run Saba News Agency that air defences shot down a Houthi drone during the attack.
Port officials said four ballistic missiles hit a quay where an excavator was deepening the navigation channel. Abdulmalik al-Sharabi, Mokha port’s director, said the strike appeared intended to disable the excavation work and damage its equipment, potentially disrupting shipping activity.
Mokha is a key government-held port on Yemen’s Red Sea coast, located close to the Bab al-Mandab Strait, a maritime chokepoint linking the Red Sea with the Gulf of Aden and a major route for global commerce.
Houthi military spokesman Yahya Saree said the group had carried out a large-scale operation using ballistic missiles, claiming it targeted gunboats, weapons stores and military gatherings in Mokha.
Saree said the attack had caused destruction to military equipment and killed and injured "Saudi military mobilisations", without providing evidence, a casualty figure or precise locations. The Houthis have framed the operation as a response to what they describe as Saudi-backed military deployments along Yemen’s western coast.
The government-aligned forces and port authorities, however, said civilian neighbourhoods and critical commercial infrastructure had been struck.
Government and diplomatic warnings
A source in Yemen’s Presidential Leadership Council said continued Houthi attacks on ports, civilian facilities, economic sites and international shipping lanes "will not go unpunished".
The council said Mokha was one of the supply arteries relied on by millions of Yemenis for food, medicine, fuel and other essentials, warning that continued attacks could deepen an already severe humanitarian crisis.
Foreign Minister Afrah al-Zouba also said the targeting of Mokha threatened a Yemeni "lifeline" and jeopardised efforts to safeguard shipping in the Red Sea and Bab al-Mandab. In a post on X, she accused the Houthis of seeking to undermine government forces’ efforts to curb arms-smuggling routes and secure maritime navigation.
"Bab al-Mandab will not become a tool for pressure in the hands of an armed terrorist group," she said, calling for greater support for government forces, navies and coast guards to protect commercial ports, cargo vessels and freedom of navigation.
Government artillery meanwhile targeted Houthi gatherings and movements west of Jabal Han, west of Taiz city, according to the Yemeni Armed Forces Media Centre, without providing information on casualties or damage.

articles.title: Russia Delays New Mobilization Wave Despite Rising Troop Losses
articles.body:
The Kremlin currently has no plans to initiate a new mobilization wave despite growing frontline losses and troop shortages, The Guardian reported, citing sources familiar with internal Russian discussions.
There are no indications that Russian President Vladimir Putin has authorized a new large-scale draft. An unnamed Western official confirmed the absence of preparations for a mobilization.
JOIN US ON TELEGRAM
Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official.
The Kremlin is reportedly relying on volunteer recruitment through Ministry of Defense contracts to avoid the political risks associated with forced conscription.
However, human rights advocate Alexei Tabalov stated that finding individuals willing to fight is becoming increasingly difficult, despite significant financial incentives.
An employee of a Russian recruiting agency confirmed this trend, stating that the organization is required to recruit 20 to 30 men per month to avoid financial penalties. The recruiter, speaking anonymously, noted that meeting these quotas has become harder compared to the previous year.
While internal discussions about a potential mobilization occur, the recruiter said there are no official orders or signs of an imminent draft.
Risks of a second mobilization
International analysts suggest that a large-scale mobilization carries significant risks for the Russian government.
Commentary published by the German business daily Handelsblatt indicated that a new draft could negatively impact the Russian economy by removing more workers from the labor force and could lead to public dissatisfaction, similar to the reaction following the initial mobilization in September 2022.
Russia Admits New Petrol Shortages as Ukrainian Strikes Hit Refineries
Reports suggest Moscow is seeking alternative methods to bolster its forces without resorting to a domestic draft.
According to the Polish daily Rzeczpospolita, North Korea has deployed between 30,000 and 50,000 troops to Russia.
Analysts indicate this deployment is intended to provide the Kremlin with additional personnel and delay the necessity of a second mobilization wave.

Ukraine imposes sanctions on those involved in the illegal export of grain — Zelenskyy signs decree

President of Ukraine Volodymyr Zelenskyy signed a decree imposing sanctions against individuals and companies involved in the illegal export of Ukrainian grain. This is reported on the Official Internet Representation of the President, UNN reports.

articles.title: NATO scrambles warplanes to shoot down drone over Latvia
articles.body:
NATO scrambles warplanes to shoot down drone over Latvia
A NATO fighter jet has destroyed a drone that entered Latvian airspace, the US-led bloc has said.
The announcement came as Ukraine carried out a major UAV attack against Russia’s northwestern Leningrad Region on Friday. A total of 54 drones were shot down or intercepted above the region overnight, local governor Aleksandr Drozdenko said. A fire broke out at the key Baltic Sea port of Ust-Luga during the raid, but it was swiftly extinguished, according to the governor.
There have been multiple reports in recent months of Ukrainian drones violating the airspace of Latvia, Estonia, Lithuania, and Finland, or crashing inside those countries, while on their way to Russia.
NATO spokesperson Allison Hart said on Friday that “this morning, we saw Italian Eurofighters based in Lithuania and Turkish F-16s out of Estonia scramble, with one Eurofighter downing a drone over Latvian airspace.”
The Latvian Defense Ministry also confirmed the incident, saying in a statement that “fighter jets participating in the NATO Baltic Air Policing mission successfully shot down a foreign unmanned aerial vehicle.”
The ministry claimed that the UAV “entered Latvia as a result of Russian electronic warfare activities.”
“Similar incidents involving foreign unmanned aerial vehicles entering or approaching Latvian airspace may occur” as long as the conflict between Russia and Ukraine continues, the statement added.
Last week, Latvia, Estonia, and Lithuania issued a joint demarche after Russian Deputy Foreign Minister Mikhail Galuzin said Moscow had “verified data,” showing that Baltic states had provided air corridors for Ukrainian drones attacking Russian civilian infrastructure. The governments in Riga, Tallinn, and Vilnius denied Galuzin’s accusations as “completely unfounded.”
On Thursday, Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov said the Russian military and intelligence services “see where things fly from and how they fly,” referring to incoming UAVs.
“This is well-known to everyone, and we are not going to prove anything to anyone here,” Peskov stressed.
Moscow previously warned that if Latvia, Estonia, and Lithuania knowingly help to facilitate Ukrainian drone strikes, Russia could consider them complicit in the attacks and would have the right to self-defense under the UN Charter.

articles.title: Russia’s state statisticians report the growth Putin demanded—economists doubt it will hold
articles.body:
Russia's economy grew 1.3% in the second quarter of 2026, the state news agency TASS reported on 12 August, citing preliminary estimates from the state statistics agency Rosstat — a figure that, if accurate, would end a slump that had opened the year with the country's first quarterly contraction since 2023.
And it comes from a state agency months after Putin dressed down his economic team in April and demanded "concrete measures" to restore growth — the print then beat the government's own economists in exactly the direction he wanted.
The quarter may have brought a real if shallow rebound, or the state's statisticians may have produced the figure the president wanted. Either way it matters, because Russia's economy is what pays for its war, and its strength sets the ceiling on how long the Kremlin can keep fighting.
Barely growing all year
Even taken straight, the rebound is thinner than it looks. The first quarter had closed 0.2% down, and across the whole first half of the year output rose just 0.6%, half of last year's pace and close to seven times slower than the wartime boom of 2023 and 2024. The quarterly figure jumped. The underlying trend barely moved.
The weakness had been building for over a year. War spending drove the 2023–24 boom and overheated the economy; to curb the resulting inflation, the central bank raised its key rate to 21%, choking lending and investment. It has cut rates since, to 14% in July, but money is still tight and inflation is rising again as Ukrainian strikes push up fuel prices.
Growth the war paid for
As The Moscow Times set out, reviewing the data and the economists reading it, most of the quarter's growth rested on one-off factors: more working days than a year earlier, a temporary oil-revenue spike during the Iran war, and a budget that lifted spending 16%, a third of it on the army and weapons. The split underneath is the tell.
Military plants kept raising output; civilian industry kept shrinking, down 3.2% from a year earlier by the Center for Macroeconomic Analysis and Short-Term Forecasting (CMASF), a Russian forecasting institute, according to its estimate.
Rosstat also billed the quarter as its strongest in six, and said it had beaten the forecasts of both the economy ministry, which had projected 0.9%, and the central bank, which saw 0.8%.
Few expect it to last
Russia will "remain in a state of stagnation" for the foreseeable future, said Liam Peach of Capital Economics, citing high interest rates and the fuel crisis.
Ukraine's long-range drones are adding to the strain. Their strikes have cut Russian oil refining to its lowest level in more than two decades, draining fuel supply and pushing prices up at home, and forcing Moscow, an oil giant, to import gasoline from as far as Morocco.

articles.title: Zelenskyy on air defence: It is not easy, but it will all happen
articles.body:
Zelenskyy on air defence: It is not easy, but it will all happen
President Volodymyr Zelenskyy has said that Ukraine is continuing efforts to strengthen its air defence and is negotiating agreements to produce the necessary weapons domestically.
Source: Zelenskyy in an evening address
Quote: "We continue working to secure air defence for Ukraine – the missiles needed to protect lives and agreements for production in Ukraine. All of this will happen. It is not easy, but all of this will happen.
Throughout the war, we have already spoken many times about weapons, capabilities, and equipment that we were initially told were supposedly impossible for us to obtain. Then we heard that Ukrainians supposedly would not be able to do it because it would take decades to become capable of it. F-16s, the production of millions of drones a year, specialised missile technologies – we did it."
Details: Zelenskyy said the same will happen with anti-ballistic capabilities and Patriot systems.
Quote: "But every delay that, unfortunately, is happening at the political level simply costs lives. It is important to act quickly, to focus all our efforts on protecting lives and limiting Russia's resources for war.
The aggressor must feel that the world is there – truly there – and is acting to end the war, rather than simply watching the war continue."
Background: Zelenskyy reported on 12 August that Ukraine had struck the Russian naval base in Novorossiysk with domestically-made Palianytsia drones and Neptun missiles.

articles.title: Blogger Kyivstoner May Have Been Targeted by Russian Agent in Poland Due to Preparations for New Operation Spiderweb
articles.body:
Ukrainian rapper and blogger Albert Vasilyev, known as Kyivstoner, may have been the target of an assassination plot orchestrated by Russian intelligence services in Poland.
This was reported by the Polish media outlet RMF FM, citing its own sources.
Earlier, it was reported that a Russian national recruited by Russian intelligence services was detained on August 7, thwarting an assassination attempt on a U.S. and Ukrainian citizen in Warsaw.
The identity of the potential victim was not disclosed, but Tusk clarified that this person was targeted because they posed a threat to Putin’s regime.
And today, August 14, RMF FM reported that the individual in question may be Albert Vasilyev.
The FSB accused Vasilyev of allegedly organizing the logistics for delivering drones to the Moscow region.
According to the FSB, the drones were transported through Slovakia, Poland, and Belarus for subsequent attacks on strategic facilities near Moscow. Thirty-five FPV drones for these operations were delivered to Russia disguised as a shipment of Spanish ceramic tiles via a route through Slovakia, Poland, and Belarus. The FSB also claimed that the drones were to be launched from a rented hangar near the facility.
Following this, Russian authorities added the musician to a list of individuals they consider to be involved in terrorist and extremist activities.
This may have been one of the reasons why Russian intelligence agencies viewed him as a target, particularly in light of preparations for a new operation based on the scenario of Operation Spiderweb.
Vasilyev himself denied all these allegations.
The suspect was detained in Warsaw by police officers in cooperation with the Polish Internal Security Agency (ABW).
According to RMF FM, the suspect was born in Ukraine, although Poland’s Minister-Coordinator of Special Services, Tomasz Semoniak, stated that the detainee was of Russian origin.
Albert Vasilyev rose to fame as a blogger and later became one of the founders of the Ukrainian band Hryby. After leaving the band, he continued his musical career under the pseudonym Kyivstoner.
At the same time, Polish law enforcement agencies have not officially named the person who may have been the target of the planned assassination. Therefore, the information that it was Kyivstoner is currently based on reports from Polish media outlets citing their own sources.
