articles.title: Trump threatens to declare strait of Hormuz ‘territory of the United States’
articles.body:
Donald Trump has threatened to declare the strait of Hormuz as “a territory of the United States” as his administration struggles to conclude the war with Iran.
During a speech at a police academy on Long Island, New York, on Friday, the US president said he would “pretty soon” designate the waterway – a crucial chokepoint for global trade, through which about a fifth of the world’s seaborne oil supplies typically pass – a US territory.
The comment came as peace talks with Iran remain at an impasse following failed negotiations, with Tehran refusing to reopen the strait, which has been all but closed since the US and Israel launched their war on Iran in February.
Almost six months into the war, there is little indication that negotiations will soon yield peace, as Iranian officials continue to defy Trump’s demands. The US has been blockading Iranian shipping and ports in recent months in an effort to pile economic pressure on Tehran.
“After we finish defeating Iran, which is being very badly defeated, pretty soon I’ll be declaring the Hormuz strait a territory of the United States,” Trump said on Friday. “Essentially, that’s what it is. We have the blockade. No ships get through unless we want them to.”
The seriousness of Trump’s remark, and whether it signaled a new policy position for his administration, was not immediately clear.
Responding on X, formerly Twitter, Kazem Gharibabadi, Iran’s deputy foreign minister, said Tehran would not be intimidated by threats, or a show of force, by the US – and added that the strait of Hormuz would only be opened, or closed, under Iran’s authority.
In an interview published on Saturday, Iranian foreign minister Abbas Araqchi said that Iran had not decided to resume talks with the US, and messages being exchanged via Qatar and Pakistan did not amount to negotiations, Reuters reported.
Araqchi told Iranian news outlet Shahrara News that separate talks with Oman were focused on defining a sea route through the strait of Hormuz, while the US would have to meet conditions for shipping to resume through the waterway.
Earlier this week, Trump claimed that the US had “total control” over the strait and said “I think we will keep it” on Truth Social, despite the waterway being an internationally navigable strait bordered by Iran and Oman.
Fuel prices have risen sharply since the start of the war, forcing working Americans to pay significantly more at the pump.
Nevertheless, on Friday, Trump said that Americans who have had to “pay a tiny little bit more for your gasoline” should remember that they are “doing it so that a very evil country cannot have a – really, it’s the No 1 state sponsor of terror in the world – we don’t want them to have a nuclear weapon.
“When you have to pay a little bit more, you’re at $4, it’s OK, I mean, it’s not. I’ll never apologize. I did the right thing,” he added.
Over the past six months, the Trump administration has repeatedly claimed victory in the war, saying Iran’s regime has been pleading for a deal.
Tehran has remained steadfast in its demands, saying as recently as last Saturday that it will not reopen the strait of Hormuz unless the US “corrects its behavior”, “completely compensate[s]” Iran for war damage, lifts sanctions and “unconditionally” releases frozen assets.

articles.title: Seoul called for dialogue with North Korea on formally ending Korean War
articles.body:
Seoul called for dialogue with North Korea on formally ending Korean War
Kyiv • UNN
Lee Jae-myung called for talks with North Korea, proposing to replace the armistice with a peace regime. He also emphasized the need to prevent conflict and limit Pyongyang’s nuclear capabilities.
South Korean President Lee Jae-myung called for the resumption of dialogue with North Korea to ensure peaceful coexistence and prevent a new conflict on the Korean Peninsula. The Guardian writes, UNN reports.
Details
"South Korean President Lee Jae-myung called for talks with North Korea aimed at achieving peaceful coexistence, stating that Seoul would seek guarantees to prevent conflict and emphasizing the need to replace the armistice on the peninsula with a 'peace regime,'" the publication writes.
In a speech marking the anniversary of Korea's liberation from Japanese colonial rule, Lee said that the two Koreas should hold talks aimed at coexistence.
He called for dialogue between North Korea and interested parties with the aim of ending the 1950–1953 Korean War, which was halted not by a peace treaty but by an armistice, and noted that measures to limit Pyongyang's nuclear capabilities could also be considered during the discussions.
Lee also said that Seoul would take preventive and consistent measures to ease tensions and create multilayered safeguards to prevent an escalation of the conflict.
As the publication notes, Lee's call is largely based on his pledge last year to respect North Korea's system and seek peaceful coexistence with Pyongyang.
DPRK removes references to unification with South Korea from constitution06.05.26, 11:17 • 4751 view
As the publication points out, relations between North and South Korea remain frozen. North Korean leader Kim Jong Un abandoned Pyongyang's policy of reunification, called South Korea the most hostile state, and ordered the strengthening of defenses along the front line.
North Korea rejected Lee's proposals to establish dialogue, criticized Seoul's plan for nuclear-powered submarines, and condemned joint U.S.–South Korean military exercises as provocations.
Regarding relations with Japan, Lee called for confronting the past while leaving the future open, and expressed hope of beginning a new 60 years of peace and prosperity with Japan as a "close neighbor."
To remind you
On the morning of August 12, North Korea launched a ballistic missile toward the sea, conducting its second missile test in less than a week.

articles.title: Araghchi accuses EU of ‘double standards’ on human rights
articles.body:
Araghchi accuses EU of ‘double standards’ on human rights
TEHRAN — Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi has accused the European Union and several of its member states of applying double standards to human rights and international law, arguing that their support for Israel amid the war in Gaza and their backing of military action against Iran have undermined their credibility to criticize Tehran.
Araghchi made the remarks in separate telephone conversations with his Greek and Austrian counterparts, Georgios Gerapetritis and Beate Meinl-Reisinger, as Iran faces renewed criticism from European governments over its human rights record and the use of the death penalty.
In his conversation with Gerapetritis, Araghchi rejected the EU’s “interventionist” statements on Iran, saying the bloc lacked the moral standing to lecture other countries on human rights because of its own record.
“The European Union, due to its performance in the field of human rights, lacks any moral standing to lecture others,” Araghchi said, according to the Iranian Foreign Ministry.
The dispute followed a joint statement by France and 25 other countries, together with EU foreign policy chief Kaja Kallas, condemning what the signatories described as Iran’s continued executions of protesters and use of the death penalty. They called on Tehran to halt executions and release people they claimed had been arbitrarily detained.
Araghchi separately singled out France, accusing Paris of “blatant” hypocrisy over its claims to defend human rights and international law.
“Countries like France should stop lecturing the world about ‘human rights’ and international law. The hypocrisy is blatant and embarrassing,” Araghchi wrote.
He argued that France’s support for Israel’s military campaign in Gaza and its backing of aggression against Iran had eroded any claim to moral authority.
“Your backing of Israel’s genocide in Gaza—and aggression against Iran—has destroyed whatever moral high ground you imagined you had,” Araghchi said.
Iran has repeatedly accused Western governments of applying inconsistent standards to international law, particularly in relation to Israel’s military operations in Gaza and the wider region.
Araghchi’s separate conversation with Austrian Foreign Minister Beate Meinl-Reisinger focused on bilateral relations as well as regional and international developments, according to the Iranian Foreign Ministry.
The calls with the Greek and Austrian foreign ministers form part of Tehran’s broader diplomatic engagement with European governments amid heightened regional tensions and continuing disputes over Iran’s nuclear program, sanctions, maritime security and human rights.
For Tehran, the exchanges also provide an opportunity to challenge a coordinated European effort to exert political pressure on Iran.
The conversations also touched on the continuing tensions surrounding the Strait of Hormuz, one of the world’s most strategically important energy corridors.
Araghchi told his Greek counterpart that Iran remained determined to protect its national interests and security in the face of continued US military pressure, including a naval blockade and alleged violations of a June 18 understanding.
He also briefed Gerapetritis on the latest discussions between Iran and Oman over arrangements for the safe transit of commercial vessels through the Strait of Hormuz.
Araghchi attributed the current insecurity in the waterway to US and Israeli military action against Iran and said those responsible for violations of international law should be held accountable.
The comments come as tensions between Tehran and Washington over the status and control of the Strait of Hormuz has intensified. Iran has maintained that maritime movements through the strategic waterway remain subject to the monitoring and authorization of its armed forces,
while Washington has claimed that US forces have established control over the strait.
Gerapetritis, according to the Iranian Foreign Ministry, expressed support for diplomatic efforts to reduce tensions and said Greece was prepared to provide technical and expert assistance.
The two ministers also agreed to continue consultations and preserve the longstanding bilateral relationship between Iran and Greece.

articles.title: Why Israel has done so little to rein in spiraling settler violence against Palestinians
articles.body:
There’s a reason why Israel has done little to rein in settler violence. It’s not just Netanyahu
Palestinians in the occupied West Bank village of Qusra have huddled inside their homes for days on end, unable to leave because of the threat posed by Israeli settlers.
The Israeli military, which over the past three years has displayed staggering military and intelligence capabilities from Beirut to Tehran, has yet to fully remove the settlers from the area of the village, about an hour’s drive from Tel Aviv.
The United States, which provides billions of dollars in military aid to Israel, has issued a scathing rebuke, perhaps because one of the homeowners is a Palestinian American living in Ohio.
U.S. Ambassador Mike Huckabee referred to the settlers as “terrorists.” Israel’s defense minister dismissed them as radical misfits — “boys on the hills.”
In reality, they are the tip of the spear for a much larger movement, supported by successive Israeli governments and supercharged under Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu, that is aimed at cementing Israeli rule over the territory and preventing the establishment of a Palestinian state.
Settlements built over decades now house over 500,000
Israel captured the West Bank, along with Gaza and east Jerusalem, in the 1967 Mideast war, territories the Palestinians want for a future state.
Since then, the Israeli government has built nearly 150 settlements that are home to well over 500,000 Jewish settlers. Many of the settlements resemble fully developed suburbs, with apartment blocks, shopping malls, parks and industrial zones.
Radical settlers have established hundreds of additional outposts without government authorization, while still enjoying protection from the Israeli military and often other public services.
Netanyahu’s government, the most nationalist and religious in Israel’s history, has boasted of establishing over 100 new settlements. On Thursday, as the army deployed in Qusra, members of his Cabinet celebrated the rebuilding of a settlement that had been dismantled in 2005 as part of the Gaza withdrawal.
Israel’s current government and much of its political class view the West Bank as the biblical and historical homeland of the Jewish people and see the settlements as key to maintaining security.
Most of the international community views all settlements as illegal and an obstacle to peace.
Separate laws for settlers and Palestinians
The roughly 3 million Palestinians in the West Bank live under Israeli military rule, with the Palestinian Authority exercising limited autonomy in population centers. Israel’s military operates in all parts of the territory, and Palestinians suspected of militancy can be held without charge for months or years under what’s known as administrative detention.
The settlers are Israeli citizens, with law enforcement typically handled by Israeli police and civilian courts.
Israel’s Defense Minister Israel Katz said in 2024 that Israelis would no longer be subject to administrative detention, which has also been used against settlers accused of violence. On Friday, he announced plans to fully transfer law enforcement among settlers to the Israeli police.
The military’s role “is to fight Palestinian terrorism” and “focus on protecting the borders and settlements against threats,” he said in a statement. “Not chase after boys on the hills.”
That would cement the status quo of what are already largely separate legal systems for Jews and Palestinians in the West Bank, which major human rights groups say amounts to apartheid, something Israel denies.
Israel’s police and military have been reluctant to confront the settlers
The Israeli police are overseen by National Security Minister Itamar Ben Gvir, himself a hard-line settler who has been convicted eight times for offenses that include supporting a terrorist organization. He was a defense attorney for Jewish extremists before entering politics.
The Israeli military says the settlers’ actions in Qusra are “illegal, reprehensible and unacceptable,” and that it tries to maintain law and order in the West Bank. It says it dismantled two outposts in the area of Qusra and detained one Israeli.
But rights groups say the military frequently turns a blind eye to settler violence, and that when it intervenes it often focuses on protecting the settlers. Yesh Din, an Israeli rights group, says around 94% of investigations into settler violence since 2005 have ended without an indictment, with just 3% leading to full or partial convictions.
US pressure has had little impact, and has eased under Trump
Settler violence intensified after the Hamas attack on Oct. 7, 2023, triggered the war in Gaza. The following year, the Biden administration imposed sanctions on settlers and Israeli organizations accused of violence.
Other Western nations have announced sanctions against Ben Gvir and another hard-line Israeli Cabinet minister, Bezalel Smotrich, accusing them of “inciting extremist violence” toward Palestinians.
The sanctions had little impact, as the settler community rallied around those targeted.
President Donald Trump rescinded the U.S. sanctions at the start of his second term and appointed Huckabee, a staunch supporter of Israeli settlements, as his ambassador.
During his first term, Trump had upended decades of U.S. policy by moving the American Embassy to Jerusalem and supporting Israel’s claims to other territories seized in war.
Netanyahu’s opponents criticize the violence but support settlement growth
Netanyahu will need the backing of Ben Gvir, Smotrich and other settler supporters if he hopes to keep his job after October elections. He will also need to maintain good relations with the Trump administration.
His opponents have criticized what they characterize as the growing chaos in the West Bank. But most of Israel’s political leaders — even critics of Netanyahu — support the growth of existing settlements and are opposed to Palestinian statehood.
Gadi Eisenkot, a former top general seen as Netanyahu’s main opponent, criticized the government’s handling of the events in Qusra, accusing it of undermining military commanders “in the face of anarchy and violent lawbreaking by an extremist minority.” He has also come out against plans to annex the West Bank.
But he has also told Israeli media that he has “never spoken about a Palestinian state,” and that he supports settlements that are “in line with Israel’s interests.”
Naftali Bennett, a staunch settlement supporter and another leading rival of Netanyahu, has condemned the violence, saying it amounts to “terrorism” by a minority.
“Precisely as someone who believes in our right to the land and in the settlement enterprise, we need to denounce this and eradicate the violence from within our own ranks — not wait for the Americans to tell us to do it,” he said in a recent interview with Israeli media.
When Bennett was prime minister, during the only brief period in the last 17 years that Netanyahu was out of office, his national unity government approved thousands of additional settler homes.
___
Associated Press writers Erin Cunningham in Jerusalem and Koral Saeed in Abu Snan, Israel, contributed.

articles.title: NATO condemns Russian airspace violations
articles.body:
NATO Allies have condemned recent airspace violations involving Poland and Romania, blaming Russia for the incidents and pledging further measures to strengthen air and missile defences across the eastern flank.
NATO Allies have condemned recent airspace violations involving Poland and Romania and a series of drone incidents, saying Russia bears responsibility for what the Alliance described as dangerous and unacceptable activity, the UK Defence Journal understands.
The North Atlantic Council met on 12 August to discuss the incidents and the security implications for Allied territory. According to a NATO news update, representatives of the Alliance’s member states expressed their full solidarity with Poland and Romania and reiterated their support for Allies affected by the recent activity. NATO said the violations demonstrated what it described as Russia’s increasing tolerance for risk and made clear that responsibility for the incidents rested with Moscow.
In its statement, the Alliance said: “Allies reiterated that Russia bears full responsibility for the airspace violations, which are dangerous and unacceptable, and demonstrate Russia’s increasing tolerance for risk.” The wording places the incidents within NATO’s broader assessment of Russian military activity around Allied territory, while stopping short of setting out additional details about the individual violations considered by the Council.
The statement added: “NATO Allies made clear that they stand united and resolute in the defence of Allied territory.” It added that the Alliance “continues to strengthen its integrated air and missile defences across the Alliance” and said Allies had underlined measures already taken to bolster defensive arrangements along the eastern flank.
The Council’s discussion also linked the recent incidents with the Alliance’s continuing support for Ukraine. NATO said Allies reaffirmed their backing for Ukraine’s sovereignty and territorial integrity and maintained that the incidents would not weaken their commitment to Kyiv. The statement described Ukraine’s security as contributing to the security of the Alliance as a whole.
NATO said: “Allies underscored that they will not be deterred by these and other irresponsible acts by Russia from their enduring commitment to Ukraine, whose security contributes to ours.”

articles.title: Russia transports oil and stolen grain on 26 ships — intelligence has released the data
articles.body:
Russia transports oil and stolen grain on 26 ships — intelligence has released the data
Kyiv • UNN
The Defence Intelligence of Ukraine published a list of 26 vessels used to transport Russian oil, liquefied gas, and stolen Ukrainian grain. Eighteen of these vessels are not under sanctions imposed by Ukraine’s partner countries.
The Main Intelligence Directorate of the Ministry of Defence of Ukraine published information about vessels on which the Russians transport oil, liquefied gas and stolen Ukrainian grain. This was reported by UNN.
Details
The information was published in the “Marine Vessels” section of the War&Sanctions portal. It concerns 26 vessels that Russia uses to transport grain from the temporarily occupied territories of Ukraine, Russian oil and petroleum products, as well as liquefied natural gas from the sanctioned “Arctic LNG 2” project.
The list includes:
-  oil tankers transporting Russian oil and petroleum products from ports in the Black Sea and Baltic regions in the interests of “Lukoil,” “Rosneft,” “Surgutneftegas,” “Novatek,” “Tatneft” and “Gazprom”; 
-  bulk carriers exporting agricultural products from the temporarily occupied territories of Ukraine via the ports of Berdiansk, Sevastopol, Kerch and Feodosia; 
-  LNG tankers transporting liquefied gas from the sanctioned floating storage unit SAAM FSU (IMO 9915090), where LNG from the sanctioned “Arctic LNG 2” project is accumulated. 
At the same time, 18 of the 26 published vessels are not under sanctions imposed by any of Ukraine’s partner countries.
Recall
According to the Foreign Intelligence Service of Ukraine, Russia is accelerating the creation of a “shadow fleet” to transport liquefied natural gas, preparing for the European Union’s complete ban on imports of Russian LNG, which will enter into force on January 1, 2027.

articles.title: Exclusive: Russia strikes Odesa port terminal recently acquired by Swiss investor
articles.body:
Russia strikes Ukraine's largest private port operator as Moscow rejects grain truce
Editor's note: An earlier version of this article incorrectly reported that the attack targeted a container terminal that was recently purchased by the by the Swiss-headquartered Mediterranean Shipping Company in March.
A Russian missile strike damaged a key Ukrainian port terminal on Aug. 14, as Russia continues to terrorize Ukraine's seaports.
The attack damaged at least one warehouse at the TIS terminal in Ukraine's Pivdennyi (Southern) Port complex, an agriculture-sector executive with knowledge of the matter told the Kyiv Independent under the condition of anonymity. 
TIS's press service declined to comment on the attack. 
The strike comes the same day as Russia rejected the idea of reinstating the 2022-2023 Black Sea grain initiative. Kyiv and Moscow have exchanged strikes on ports and vessels recently, leading to growing concern of a global food crisis. 
Turkey has attempted to mediate negotiations, having helped broker the original grain initiative, although Moscow has said Ankara has yet to send an official ceasefire proposal. 
Reviving the framework of the grain initiative would be "ill-advised," Russian Foreign Ministry spokesperson Maria Zakaharova told reporters on Aug. 14, accusing "the West" of using the deal to attack Russia.
She also claimed that Ukraine was currently conducting maritime terrorism and "escalating" the situation. Meanwhile, Moscow relentlessly attacks Odesa Oblast, particularly port infrastructure.
TIS is co-owned by Andriy Stavnitser, a Ukrainian businessman who also owns the Superhumans Center, a specialist clinic for war veterans.
In March, the world's largest container shipping company, the Swiss-headquartered Mediterranean Shipping Company, took a majority stake in a TIS container terminal in Ukraine's Pivdennyi (Southern) Port, marking a rare high-profile foreign investment into the country. The container terminal was not hit in the Aug. 14 attack.
Over the last two months, Russia has stepped up its attacks on Odesa's seaports and civilian vessels in a bid to choke Ukraine's key trade route. Some 90% of the country's agricultural goods are exported via the Black Sea, accounting for 20% of the country's gross domestic product (GDP) before the full-scale invasion.
With Russia striking vessels 35 times in port waters and 22 times in the Black Sea during last month alone, ships are avoiding docking at Ukraine's ports, preventing agriculture and metallurgy businesses from exporting and importing goods.
The fallout of the attacks is already dire. Ukraine's exports fell to just 30% of its target in the first two weeks of August, Agriculture Minister Taras Vysotsky said at a briefing on Aug. 14. By November, the country could lose 10.8 billion euros ($12.5 billion) in blocked agricultural exports, according to the Agriculture Ministry.

articles.title: ‘They’re Starting to Moan’: Lavrov Threatens ‘Harsher’ Strikes
articles.body:
Russian Foreign Minister Sergey Lavrov has rejected a ceasefire along the current front line and threatened to make Moscow’s strikes against Ukraine “harsher,” saying Russia would target what it claims is supporting Kyiv’s military machine.
Lavrov made the remarks in an interview with the Russian state-run propaganda outlet Vesti on Friday, Aug. 14.
JOIN US ON TELEGRAM
Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official.
“We are already doing this, and they are already starting to moan,” Lavrov said, referring to Russia’s attacks. He added that calls for Moscow to stop would not change its approach.
Lavrov rejects ceasefire along front line
Lavrov said Russia would not accept a halt to fighting along the current line of contact, arguing that such an arrangement would undermine what he described as the legacy of the Soviet victory over Nazi Germany.
“For Russia, stopping along the line of contact is unacceptable,” Lavrov said, according to Vesti.
He argued that Moscow would only consider an end to the fighting as part of what he called a “long-term, reliable and sustainable settlement.”
The remarks amount to a rejection of a simple ceasefire that would freeze the current battlefield situation.
Russia threatens ‘harsher’ strikes
Lavrov also threatened to intensify Russian attacks, claiming Moscow would not use what he called “terrorist methods” but would take tougher measures against Ukraine.
“Russia will not stoop to Zelensky’s terrorist methods, but will make its approaches harsher to destroy everything that feeds Kyiv’s military machine from the West,” Lavrov said.
‘Only a Madman’ Would Say Sending Patriots to Ukraine Weakens Poland, Polish Minister Says
He then claimed that Russia was already pursuing this approach and that its effects were being felt in Ukraine and among its Western supporters.
“We are already doing this, and they are already starting to moan,” Lavrov said.
The Russian minister did not provide specific details on what additional targets Moscow could strike.
His comments come as Ukraine continues to face Russian missile and drone attacks against its cities and critical infrastructure, while Kyiv and its Western partners discuss possible diplomatic efforts to end the war.

articles.title: Lebanon: Israel strike on south kills seven in latest escalation
articles.body:
Breadcrumb
Lebanon: Israeli strike on country's south kills nine in worst death toll since June
An Israeli strike on southern Lebanon on Saturday killed nine people including three children, state media said, the worst toll since deals in June saw a lull in hostilities between Israel and Hezbollah.
Lebanon's health ministry said seven people were killed "including three children and two women," in Ansar, with another two people killed and nine others wounded in Deir Zahrani, adding that the toll there was provisional.
The National News Agency (NNA) said "Israeli warplanes carried out a series of airstrikes targeting the Ali al-Taher ridge", a strategic hill overlooking the Nabatieh area, also reporting Israeli shelling there.
An AFP correspondent in Ansar saw a destroyed building as rescuers working to remove human remains from the rubble, and a swimming pool clouded and grey from dust and debris.
Abbas Khalil, 60, said he was doing his early morning Islamic prayers when the strike hit.
"We were shocked... There's no justification for this," he told AFP.
An Israeli army statement said that it struck "Hezbollah terror infrastructure in the areas of Nabatieh and Ansar", adding that the move came "in response to an action by the Hezbollah terrorist organisation" against Israeli soldiers in the Ali al-Taher Ridge area.
Lebanon was drawn into the Middle East war in March after Hezbollah responded to the US-Israeli military assault on Iran in early March.
Israel responded with heavy airstrikes and a ground invasion which have killed more than 4,300 people.
Violence has significantly decreased since the signing of a US-Iran memorandum of understanding in June on the broader Middle East war, followed by a US-sponsored framework deal between Lebanon and Israel later that month.
But Lebanon still reports intermittent Israeli strikes, which have caused casualties, and broad demolitions of civilian buildings in southern villages and towns.
'Humiliation'
The NNA also said Israeli forces detonated homes in the town of Bint Jbeil near the border early on Saturday.
The Israel-Lebanon framework deal includes the disarmament of Hezbollah, a gradual withdrawal of Israeli forces from south Lebanon and the deployment of the Lebanese army to the region, starting in "pilot zones".
Israel and Lebanon are to hold an eighth round of US-sponsored negotiations in Rome early next month.
On Friday, Hezbollah chief Naim Qassem accused Lebanese authorities of subjecting the country's armed forces to undue pressure by implementing the deal.
"How can you accept this ongoing humiliation of the Lebanese army, exposing it to bombardment and Israeli pressures, instead of acting as its protectors?" Qassem said.
Earlier this week, Israel's Defence Minister Israel Katz visited southern Lebanon, vowing to keep troops in a so-called "security zone" there and saying the Israeli military was "destroying the underground infrastructure" and "destroying all the houses" in the area.
When asked about Katz's remarks, a US State Department official told AFP that "a permanent military presence in south Lebanon is not consistent with the commitments made in the framework".
Also this week, Lebanon said President Joseph Aoun and army chief Rodolphe Haykal met visiting US General Joseph Clearfield, who heads a coordination group involved with the Israel-Lebanon agreement, to discuss arrangements regarding the deal.
Human Rights Watch meanwhile urged the United Nations to keep an international force in Lebanon after its peacekeepers' mandate ends this year, calling the troops "a crucial deterrent against attacks on civilians and human rights abuses".

articles.title: Lebanon: Israel strike on south kills nine in latest escalation
articles.body:
Breadcrumb
Lebanon: Israeli strike on country's south kills nine in worst death toll since June
An Israeli strike on southern Lebanon on Saturday killed nine people including three children, state media said, the worst toll since deals in June saw a lull in hostilities between Israel and Hezbollah.
Lebanon's health ministry said seven people were killed "including three children and two women," in Ansar, with another two people killed and nine others wounded in Deir Zahrani, adding that the toll there was provisional.
The National News Agency (NNA) said "Israeli warplanes carried out a series of airstrikes targeting the Ali al-Taher ridge", a strategic hill overlooking the Nabatieh area, also reporting Israeli shelling there.
An AFP correspondent in Ansar saw a destroyed building as rescuers working to remove human remains from the rubble, and a swimming pool clouded and grey from dust and debris.
Abbas Khalil, 60, said he was doing his early morning Islamic prayers when the strike hit.
"We were shocked... There's no justification for this," he told AFP.
An Israeli army statement said that it struck "Hezbollah terror infrastructure in the areas of Nabatieh and Ansar", adding that the move came "in response to an action by the Hezbollah terrorist organisation" against Israeli soldiers in the Ali al-Taher Ridge area.
Lebanon was drawn into the Middle East war in March after Hezbollah responded to the US-Israeli military assault on Iran in early March.
Israel responded with heavy airstrikes and a ground invasion which have killed more than 4,300 people.
Violence has significantly decreased since the signing of a US-Iran memorandum of understanding in June on the broader Middle East war, followed by a US-sponsored framework deal between Lebanon and Israel later that month.
But Lebanon still reports intermittent Israeli strikes, which have caused casualties, and broad demolitions of civilian buildings in southern villages and towns.
'Humiliation'
The NNA also said Israeli forces detonated homes in the town of Bint Jbeil near the border early on Saturday.
The Israel-Lebanon framework deal includes the disarmament of Hezbollah, a gradual withdrawal of Israeli forces from south Lebanon and the deployment of the Lebanese army to the region, starting in "pilot zones".
Israel and Lebanon are to hold an eighth round of US-sponsored negotiations in Rome early next month.
On Friday, Hezbollah chief Naim Qassem accused Lebanese authorities of subjecting the country's armed forces to undue pressure by implementing the deal.
"How can you accept this ongoing humiliation of the Lebanese army, exposing it to bombardment and Israeli pressures, instead of acting as its protectors?" Qassem said.
Earlier this week, Israel's Defence Minister Israel Katz visited southern Lebanon, vowing to keep troops in a so-called "security zone" there and saying the Israeli military was "destroying the underground infrastructure" and "destroying all the houses" in the area.
When asked about Katz's remarks, a US State Department official told AFP that "a permanent military presence in south Lebanon is not consistent with the commitments made in the framework".
Also this week, Lebanon said President Joseph Aoun and army chief Rodolphe Haykal met visiting US General Joseph Clearfield, who heads a coordination group involved with the Israel-Lebanon agreement, to discuss arrangements regarding the deal.
Human Rights Watch meanwhile urged the United Nations to keep an international force in Lebanon after its peacekeepers' mandate ends this year, calling the troops "a crucial deterrent against attacks on civilians and human rights abuses".

articles.title: Inside Russia’s new gulag: what The New Yorker found in a Rostov cell of Ukrainian women
articles.body:
Inside Russia’s new gulag: what The New Yorker found in a Rostov cell of Ukrainian women
Since 2014 — and especially since 2022 — Russia has seized and still holds at least 1,878 Ukrainian civilians. These are only the confirmed cases; the real number is likely far higher. At least 223 of them are women. Like Ukrainian prisoners of war, many civilian hostages from Ukraine have been tortured and are held in inhumane conditions. But unlike military prisoners, they have little hope of going free in an exchange. Ukraine, citing the Geneva Conventions, insists they should never have been detained at all. Russia points to rulings from its own courts and says they are serving sentences for terrorism, treason, and other serious crimes. The two sides do not trade military prisoners for civilians, which leaves the return of these detainees unresolved.
The New Yorker has published a long piece about Ukrainian women who ended up sharing a cell at Rostov pretrial detention center No. 1. For the story, the magazine’s Joshua Yaffa spoke with former inmates and exchanged letters with several of the women still held there. Some had served in Ukraine’s armed forces; others had no ties to the military. The first group has been exchanged; the second is still in custody. Meduza retells the stories of two of them.
Warning: This article contains descriptions of torture.
Valentina Zayarnaya, 66
Zayarnaya taught English in Amvrosiivka, a small city near Donetsk. Two months into the full-scale war, she got a call from an old acquaintance, a former Ukrainian border guard whom she knew only as Dima. They had met in 2018 at the Hnutove crossing, on the de facto border between the self-proclaimed Donetsk People’s Republic (“DNR”) and the Ukrainian-controlled parts of the Donetsk region. They struck up a conversation, exchanged phone numbers, and stayed in regular touch over the following years. Zayarnaya had once lost a child she had wanted to name Dima, and she came to think of this second Dima not simply as an acquaintance but as family.
Dima was not his real name. The man who introduced himself to Zayarnaya that way is Denys Storozhuk. At the start of the full-scale war, his border-guard unit was sent to defend Mariupol. Storozhuk spent three weeks hidden in a utility shaft deep inside the Azovstal plant, then made it out of the city and called Zayarnaya. When she told him she had gotten her son Kostya out of the embattled city, Storozhuk asked her to get him out, too. He lied, telling her he had taken no part in the war. She drove down the very next day and brought him from Mariupol to Amvrosiivka. They got lucky at the checkpoints: no one searched the car or asked for their documents.
Storozhuk lived with Zayarnaya for nearly a year. One day, he asked her to pick up a package for him at an address in Donetsk. Inside was a forged passport that would have let him leave occupied territory. When she arrived, FSB officers were waiting and quickly arrested her. Under questioning, Zayarnaya learned the truth about him: He was a lieutenant colonel in the Ukrainian military and had fought at Azovstal, escaping before Ukrainian forces surrendered. He had also stayed in touch with fellow servicemen, and investigators said he had hidden weapons and explosives at her house. Zayarnaya was accused of helping Storozhuk plan an assassination attempt on a “DNR” lawmaker and was sentenced to 12 years. Storozhuk was detained as well, but he was exchanged in the fall of 2024, before the trial; he was later sentenced in absentia to 22 years.
Zayarnaya’s cellmates were frustrated that Storozhuk had concealed his identity. But by their account, she always defended him — even though, during the investigation, FSB officers had beaten her son and threatened to send him to a mental hospital unless she gave them the testimony they wanted. She signed a confession, then tried to kill herself.
In a letter to The New Yorker, Zayarnaya called Storozhuk a second son and wrote: “The most important thing is that my boys are alive and free.” She said she considers prison “a school of survival, a test of the humanity and decency in each of us.” In custody, she has gone on teaching English — now to her cellmates.
Natalia Vlasova, 44
Vlasova has been in detention for more than seven years. In court, she said it all began in 2018, when an acquaintance who worked for the SBU, Ukraine’s security service, asked her to go to Donetsk and fill in for Serhii Hruzinov, an agent working at a chandelier shop who needed to travel to Kyiv. Vlasova agreed because, in return, she was promised help with a criminal drug-possession case against her. Soon after that trip came another: this time, she was asked to check whether Hruzinov had switched sides. She was detained trying to enter the “DNR” on a forged passport.
Vlasova was taken to Izolyatsia, a former insulation-materials plant in Donetsk that was turned into a secret prison in 2014. There, she was tortured for months. Her captors stripped her, bound her with tape, and shocked her with electricity. A doctor was present at many of these sessions; when she lost consciousness, he revived her by shoving a cotton ball doused in ammonia up her nose, and the torture started again. She said that one of her torturers was Vasily Yevdokimov, an official in the “DNR” state security ministry who is believed to have created Izolyatsia. “He personally filed my teeth with a metal file, twisted my nipples, and tried to force a bottle into my vagina,” Vlasova said in court.
A person who heard her testimony told The New Yorker that when Vlasova finished describing the torture, a judge asked whether she wanted to enter her written notes into the court record. “We were in shock,” that person said. The judge’s reaction seemed to be a quiet signal: “It was a gesture on the scale he was allowed.” But despite the gesture — and despite the fact that Vlasova recanted her earlier statements in court, saying they had been extracted under torture — she was sentenced to 18 years. Her conviction included the attempted assassination of Yevdokimov, the man she said had tortured her.
Over her seven years in custody, Vlasova has watched countless times as other women were freed and she was left behind. At the Rostov detention center, she kept a bag of clean clothes at the ready, in case she, too, was one day told, “Pack your things — you’re leaving.” So far, that has not happened.
Her daughter, Yulia, who lives with her father in Kyiv, is now 11. Her father and other relatives tried to keep Yulia from seeing news of her mother’s torture, but within days of the testimony she had read the coverage. She had only one question, The New Yorker reported: “What are nipples?” Last year, Yulia took part in a rally in Kyiv’s Independence Square to call attention to Ukrainian women held prisoner in Russia. She brought a sign that referred to one of her last memories of her mother: “Mom, remember you promised me a kitten?”

articles.title: Poland says it foiled Russian plot to kill Ukrainian rapper Kyivstoner
articles.body:
Poland has detained a suspect in a plot to assassinate Ukrainian rapper Albert Vasyliev, known as Kyivstoner, the Polish radio station RMF FM reported, citing sources.
The suspect is a native of the Donbas, the station said. Polish security services believe Russian intelligence ordered him to kill the musician.
Prime Minister Donald Tusk announced on August 13 that Polish authorities had detained a Russian citizen, recruited by Russian intelligence, on suspicion of plotting a killing. Tusk said the intended target held passports from two countries: Ukraine and the United States.
Kyivstoner holds citizenship in both countries.
After Tusk’s statement, RMF FM reported that the plot had targeted a “defense industry entrepreneur” who supplied his plant’s products to Ukraine.
Russia’s Federal Security Service (FSB) announced in mid-July that it had thwarted a massive drone attack on a strategically important plant in a residential area of the Moscow region. According to the FSB, Ukraine’s Security Service planned the attack. The FSB claimed that 35 drones were to be launched remotely from a hangar near the facility. The FSB also alleged that Vasyliev was involved in organizing the attack. Vasyliev himself responded: “Are you out of your minds? Run your mouth all you want, but not about this. This is unacceptable to me!”
Vasyliev is best known as a member of the group Griby (“Mushrooms”), which he left in 2017. After the war in Ukraine began, Vasyliev left Kyiv for the United States, and years later moved to Bratislava. His wife said he has been providing financial support to the Ukrainian military.

articles.title: Military analyst: USA has cleaned out Patriot missile stockpiles of its European allies
articles.body:
News of the story 
        
                "On Point"
        
    
                                                                          
            
                                                                              
            
                        MINSK, 14 August (BelTA) – The United States of America has stripped European arsenals of Patriot missiles to replenish its own stock. Aleksandr Alesin, an independent military analyst, made the statement in a recent episode of BelTA’s project On Point.
 
The military analyst noted that according to some sources, the United States has about 800 missiles for Patriot air defense systems. The stock of these munitions has been depleted due to the war in the Middle East where these systems are used to intercept Iranian strikes. Aleksandr Alesin pointed out that because of that the USA has to remove Patriot missiles from the arsenals of its European allies.
 
“The USA has stripped the arsenals of Patriot missiles from its European allies. It left missiles with questionable shelf life and expired service life. Nobody can guarantee that they will even be able to take off and intercept anything,” he stated. “Apart from that, their total number makes up several dozens.”
 
The military analyst believes that the circumstances make Kiev’s chances of receiving missiles for Patriot air defense systems virtually zero, especially when it comes to the most advanced PAC-3 munitions. “Kiev can receive missiles of another class that can hit aeroballistic targets. Such missiles are produced in France, the UK, and Germany. But they can handle only ordinary ballistics. Even then about three missiles per warhead are required in such cases,” Aleksandr Alesin concluded.

articles.title: Russia won’t accept a new Black Sea truce, saying the West already broke its word once
articles.body:
Russia won’t accept a new Black Sea truce, saying the West already broke its word once
Moscow has not received a formal proposal for a moratorium on Black Sea strikes, Russian Foreign Ministry spokesperson Maria Zakharova said on Friday. A day earlier, Reuters reported that Kyiv had used an intermediary to deliver a proposal to Moscow for a mutual halt to strikes on civilian targets in the Black Sea. Reuters did not name the intermediary directly, but it was likely Turkey — Turkish Foreign Minister Hakan Fidan had already said on August 8 that Ankara had sent a moratorium proposal to both sides in the conflict.
“The Russian side has not received, through official channels, any formal communication from Turkey setting out the terms of this initiative,” Zakharova said.
Moscow does not see “grounds for half-measures that only give the Kyiv regime a temporary reprieve,” she said. Russia agreed to a moratorium in 2022–2023 in exchange for access to global markets for its agricultural products, she said, but “the West acted in bad faith” and did not lift sanctions.
Talk of a Black Sea truce has resumed as both sides sharply escalate attacks on merchant vessels and ports. Russia has been striking ports in the Odesa region in recent weeks, and no grain vessel has entered those ports since late July.
On August 12, Ukraine carried out a large-scale strike on Novorossiysk — Russia’s largest Black Sea port and one of its most important grain export hubs. Work stopped at all of Novorossiysk’s terminals as a result: the Novorossiysk Grain Terminal, the Novorossiysk Grain Products Plant, and the KSK Grain Terminal. They have a combined capacity of 26.1 million metric tons.
Ukraine is one of the world’s largest grain producers, and 90% of its grain exports move by sea. Shipments fell in August to about a third of the usual volume, or 463,000 metric tons, Ukrainian Agriculture Minister Taras Vysotskyi said.
If the situation does not change, he said, Ukraine could run out of storage space for its new harvest by November, and global food prices could rise by at least 25–30%. Kyiv is negotiating overland routes with Romania, Poland, Hungary, Slovakia, and Moldova, but overland shipping costs more than sea transport and is barely profitable.
Russia, in turn, is the world’s largest wheat exporter, so disruptions at the Novorossiysk terminals could ripple through the entire global market.
Even before the strikes, the Russian Union of Grain Exporters and Producers had warned that the shortfall in Russian wheat deliveries this season could reach 30–35 million metric tons, or about 15% of global wheat trade. Making up the lost volumes with supplies from other exporters would be virtually impossible, the union said. Wheat futures in Chicago rose about 3% on August 12 after the attack on the Novorossiysk terminals.

articles.title: The True Story Behind The Brink of War
articles.body:
The Reykjavik Summit—when U.S. President Ronald Reagan and Soviet Union President Mikhail Gorbachev talked in person in 1986—is not known as an iconic bit of American history. But the face-to-face conversation between the leaders, held over Oct. 11 and 12 in the Icelandic capital, proved to be an important step toward the end of the Cold War.
The summit (or meeting, depending on who you ask) came after “an unexpected invitation from Gorbachev,” says Pete Souza, the former Presidential photographer for Reagan. At the time the Reagan administration refused to call it a summit.
“Before two leaders like that have a summit meeting, there's lots of prep work that goes into it,” recalls Souza. “But this was very last minute. The Reagan administration went to great effort leading up to Reykjavik, to not call it a summit. They’d say, ‘It’s just a meeting, and we’re not characterizing it as a summit.’”
The summit’s purpose was to discuss the arms controls between the two nations, in hopes of bringing an end to the long-lasting threat of nuclear war hanging over both countries, and the world as a whole. Over 30 hours, Reagan and Gorbachev fiercely debated in an effort to bring peace and the end of the Cold War. Now, a new film from writer-director Michael Russell Gunn, The Brink of War, gives this historical moment a worthy spotlight. The film stars Jeff Daniels as Reagan, Jared Harris as Gorbachev, and J.K. Simmons as Secretary of State George Shultz.
For Gunn, the idea for The Brink of War came from a meeting he had with the real George Shultz, to whom the film is dedicated. Shultz told him all about the Reykjavik Summit. “I had never heard of this summit before,” says Gunn, “but once I found out I couldn’t stop thinking of it.”
There was one particular detail from their conversation that made Gunn realize the Reykjavik Summit was a pivotal moment in world history. “Schultz told me he asked Gorbachev years later—and I included this in the movie—what changed to bring an end to the Cold War,” says Gunn. “Gorbachev responded with one word: ‘Reykjavik.’” From that moment, Gunn knew he had a movie.
Shultz detailed a memory to Gunn about how he’d stand outside the meeting room when Gorbachev and Reagan went in, and these two military officers would be standing there, each of them holding a nuclear football. “If things had gone badly, Reagan and Gorbachev could walk out, press the buttons, and end it all,” says Gunn. “The idea of these two military officers with all the power in the world literally in their hands, was an extraordinary memory to share, and an extraordinary thing for us to film.”
Gunn was struck by how generous Shultz was with his time, and he gave the filmmaker something that would allow for an exceptionally realistic approach: the declassified transcripts of the meeting. The transcripts allowed Gunn another first-hand account of the summit, as well as the opportunity to lift dialogue directly from the real conversations into the script. A number of conversations are nearly verbatim to what the transcripts show, though Gunn admits to finessing certain moments for cinematic purposes. “I tried to make it as close as I possibly could,” says Gunn.
The only points Gunn really departed from the transcripts were things they didn’t reveal. “I didn’t have transcripts of what was going on with the advisors, or what was happening with the first ladies,” he says. For that, he researched several books, pointing to Dutch: A Memoir of Ronald Reagan by Edmund Morris and Gorbachev by Willaim Taubman to help gather a fuller sense of the people surrounding the leaders.
Gunn calls himself a lifelong fan of Souza’s photography, and he pulled the original proofs from Souza’s summit photography at the National Security Archives. On a whim, he cold emailed Souza to see if he was available to join them on the film shoot to produce the film’s still photography. To Gunn’s delight, Souza accepted. The veteran photographer provided Gunn great assistance in faithfully recreating the summit, and the photos Souza took have a striking resemblance to the original photos from ‘86.
The summit itself was an incredibly tense showdown that occurred over a brief 30 hours. The discussions of arms controls with a view to bring an end to the Cold War came tantalizingly close to fruition. At one point during the summit, Reagan and Gorbachev were close to agreeing on a deal that would remove every single nuclear missile from the planet, a moment in the transcript that Gunn was particularly stunned by. “Gorbachev proposed eliminating all these different classes of weapons that the Americans weren’t expecting,” recalls Souza. “There was a moment when Reagan and his team thought ‘This can be historic.’ There was a real excitement about it.”
That excitement was all too brief. As a condition of eliminating these weapons, Gorbachev demanded an end to the Strategic Defense Initiative (SDI), nicknamed “Star Wars,” a missile defense system proposed to protect the United States from attack. “The whole SDI thing doomed that hope. Gorbachev wanted Reagan to not go any further with the SDI. That was the sticking point, and the mood changed to disappointment,” says Souza.
“My main takeaway of President Reagan behind the scenes was he had such an even keeled disposition,” says Souza. “It would take so much to get him angry or pissed off. One of the few times where he got pissed off was at the end of Reykjavik.”
The summit was considered a failure at the time, with no agreement struck at the end. However, it ultimately provided a breakthrough between Reagan and Gorbachev. The Intermediate-Range Nuclear Forces Treaty was signed on December 8, 1987, which was an enormous step forward to the end of the Cold War, which ultimately concluded with the fall of the Soviet Union in 1991. If it wasn’t for the Reykjavik summit, it’s likely that treaty never would have been signed.
Gunn hopes the film can show audiences that if we work with people who disagree with us, we can forge a better future.
“For one, I want the audience to walk out of the cinema with hope. That as divided as we are, it's been worse,” Gunn says. “We were literally about to blow up the world with enemies, and we found a way out of that. The second thing I want people to walk out with is courage. It takes courage to engage with people you disagree with. We've decided that listening means we agree, and that's not true.”
Adds Gunn: “They didn't agree, but they listened to one another, and they found a way to make a better, safer world.”

articles.title: On the campaign trail for United Russia, Putin kicks a soccer ball, admires giant halibut, and dons a sailor’s uniform
articles.body:
On the campaign trail for United Russia, Putin kicks a soccer ball, admires giant halibut, and dons a sailor’s uniform
Russian President Vladimir Putin has been traveling actively around Russia in recent weeks — since the start of summer, he has visited seven regions outside Moscow and St. Petersburg. Before that, he had not left the two capitals and the Novgorod region (where his residence in Valdai is located) for a record seven months. In the regions, Putin is visits major industrial plants and mass events and interacts with the public; state propaganda is covers all of this in great detail. The trips themselves fit neatly into the election campaign of United Russia, which presents itself as the president’s party (and which is experiencing a ratings catastrophe). Here’s what happens in the regions when the president comes to visit.
August 3, Krasnoyarsk. The price of a liter of gasoline in the city falls by 24 rubles just before Putin’s arrival (then returns to its previous level the next day). The president attends the final of Bolshaya Peremena (“Big Change”), where the host introduces him to the stage: “The greatest dream of all the millions of kids — a man, our dear friend, the president of the Russian Federation.” Someone passes Putin a ball. He kicks it back. Applause follows. The ball is sent to a museum.
August 10, Ulan-Ude. Buses across the city are plastered with quotes from Putin, including: “I commend the energy and initiative of the people of Buryatia, and their sincere love for the Motherland.” The president meets with a boy who had “invited” him to Ulan-Ude a week earlier, in Krasnoyarsk: “I’m addressing you as supreme commander in chief: my dream is to become a pilot, please help me get into a Suvorov military school” — “We’ll sort it out.”
August 11, Novosibirsk. Electric scooters are banned from the new asphalt hastily laid in the city center ahead of Putin’s visit. He talks with young scientists: “What threats does artificial intelligence pose to us?” — “Vladimir Vladimirovich, you have nothing to fear!” — “I’ve never been afraid of anything.” On the way to the airport, Putin “spontaneously” stops his motorcade and takes photos with children who had waited there for several hours. Right nearby, a gas station’s price board has been turned off.
August 12, Yuzhno-Sakhalinsk. Putin takes part in Pacific Fleet exercises and weighs in on the day’s news, accusing the European Union of piracy over the seizure of Russian merchant ships and threatening “retaliatory measures.” The president appears in public for the first time in the new uniform of the Navy’s commander in chief. The date marks the 26th anniversary of the sinking of the submarine Kursk. Putin does not mention it.
August 13, Iturup Island. Putin visits the Kuril Islands for the first time. He had avoided the trip previously to keep from antagonizing Japan. At a fish processing plant, the president samples caviar and marvels at the enormous halibut and tuna. He talks with local residents: “What great weather you have here! A resort!” — “We thought you had arranged that, since it happens so rarely.” The governor tells Putin that residents of the region are determined to do everything for victory. “That’s the kind of people we have,” Putin says. “The genetic code of winners.”

articles.title: Ukrainians rally again for Fedorov reinstatement as organizers 'disappointed' in Zelensky's silence
articles.body:
Ukrainians rally again for Fedorov reinstatement as organizers 'disappointed' in Zelensky's silence
Protesters gathered in central Kyiv on Aug. 14 for another rally demanding that President Volodymyr Zelensky reinstate former Defense Minister Mykhailo Fedorov, as the president's silence on the issue fuels frustration among demonstrators.
Several hundreds took to the streets of the capital, a notably lower number than when the protests first started in mid-July after Fedorov was removed from his post during a chaotic government reshuffle.
Although Zelensky later dismissed then-Commander-in-Chief Oleksandr Syrskyi, fulfilling one of the protesters' main demands, he has refused to restore Fedorov as defense minister.
"The president has maximally disappointed me with his silence, especially considering that the lack of communication has effectively become the trigger for these protests," Dmytro Koziatynskyi, a war veteran and one of the protest organizers, said on social media.
The new gathering comes as the Ukrainian parliament is set to return from its summer recess on Aug. 18, with protesters waiting to see whether Zelensky will officially nominate acting Defense Minister Yevhen Khmara to the position.
Some people close to the situation believe Zelensky could avoid putting Khmara's candidacy to a vote in an effort not to further inflame public anger.
Koziatynskyi also urges people to join a march in central Kyiv on Aug. 16.
No resolution in sight
Fedorov had become one of Ukraine's most popular government officials during his tenure, overseeing major reforms and high-profile initiatives aimed at strengthening the military. His proposals won support among many Ukrainians, making his sudden dismissal surprising for the public.
Zelensky has never provided a detailed explanation for removing Fedorov. Instead, he has pointed to an alleged conflict between Fedorov and Syrskyi.
The president eventually dismissed Syrskyi and appointed General Mykhailo Drapatyi, a respected commander, as his successor. The decision was welcomed by many Ukrainians, and some subsequent protests appeared to draw smaller crowds.
Still, it did not resolve the dispute.
Protesters continued to demand Fedorov's reinstatement. Thousands gathered in a Kyiv park on July 31 before marching through the city center as part of what organizers called a "march for dialogue and reforms in defense."
The size of that demonstration showed that opposition to Fedorov's dismissal had not completely disappeared after Syrskyi's removal.
However, the protests subsequently lost some momentum, with smaller groups of around 100 or more people continuing to gather in the square each day.
Zelensky has largely avoided engaging directly with the demonstrations while continuing to address Fedorov's future.
The president said on July 21 he had offered Fedorov "a prominent position in the government" focused on strengthening Ukraine's technological sector.
According to a person close to Zelensky, the proposal envisioned either making Fedorov a deputy prime minister for military innovations or appointing him to lead Ukroboronprom, Ukraine's state-owned defense conglomerate.
Fedorov has rejected those options, making clear that he wants to return only as defense minister.

articles.title: Europe’s race for dual-use technology has a new contender: Vilnius
articles.body:
Europe’s rapid expansion of dual-use technologies is creating a new generation of innovation centers, and Vilnius is quickly becoming one of them. With strengths spanning lasers, AI, autonomous systems, and secure communications, Lithuania’s capital is building an ecosystem where research moves quickly into real-world civilian and defense applications.
From aerial drones to cybersecurity tools, technologies designed for both civilian and military use have seen increased investment and rapid development in Europe lately. Investment in these “dual-use” technologies increased 25 percent between 2024 and 2025, reaching nearly $1.2 trillion, while over 2,300 new dual-use startups launched across NATO allies in the same period. Supporting a wide range of sectors, from transport and energy to defense and communications, dual-use tech is increasingly important to Europe’s security, infrastructure, and economic interests.
In this climate, emerging tech hubs like Vilnius are establishing themselves as centers for developing and testing versatile technologies like autonomous vehicles and secure communications systems. Such initiatives lay promising foundations for the economic, employment, and security outlook of Lithuania and the wider region.
Turning research into practical dual-use solutions
In recent years, Lithuania has moved from a rich but fragmented innovation ecosystem to a tight-knit network of coordinated efforts, focused on scaling up dual-use tech with real-world applications. The capital’s well-established network of university research groups, technology startups, and defense-focused SMEs is working together, fueled by increased investment, to turn technical know-how and academic research into practical solutions for both civil and military challenges.
“Europe’s security increasingly depends on technologies that can move seamlessly between civilian and defense applications. Vilnius has the rare combination of engineering talent, advanced research, and a collaborative ecosystem that allows those technologies to be developed, tested, and deployed much faster than in larger markets,” says Artūras Medeišis, Dean of the Faculty of Electronics at VILNIUS TECH, one of Lithuania’s largest research universities for engineering, technology, and business. “The future of defense innovation won’t be built only inside defense companies. It will come from universities, startups, and deep-tech businesses working together. That’s exactly the ecosystem Vilnius has been building.”
“Dual-use technologies are no longer a niche sector; they’re becoming part of Europe’s industrial future,” says Mangirdas Šapranauskas, Head of Business at Go Vilnius, the city’s official tourism and business development agency. “Vilnius is already home to globally competitive companies developing technologies with both civilian and defense applications – from Brolis Semiconductors and Astrolight in photonics to Granta Autonomy and RSI Europe in autonomous and counter-drone systems. Combined with close collaboration between universities, startups, manufacturers and the public sector, this creates an ecosystem where innovation moves quickly from research to deployment and attracts international investment and strategic partnerships.”
Many of Lithuania’s most active dual-use areas feature technologies in high global demand. This includes lasers and photonics, cybersecurity, small satellites, wireless communications, electro-optical systems, drones, counter-drone solutions, and advanced data processing for AI and machine learning.
These tools have essential civilian functions, in everything from environmental monitoring and infrastructure inspections to supporting energy grids and government networks. But these same technologies also have important defense functions, especially for countries that face the threat of disruption to electronic systems and key infrastructure. “For countries like Lithuania, systems must remain functional under constant risk of electronic warfare, GNSS disruption, cyberattack, or infrastructure degradation,” says Medeišis. “This means that future systems must be modular, repairable, locally adaptable, and suitable for fast improvement cycles.”
Building autonomous systems at Vilnius Tech
One major step forward for Vilnius in this area is the creation of the Competence Center for Autonomous, Remotely Operated and Connected Systems (ComARC), led by VILNIUS TECH, with Kaunas University of Technology as the Lithuanian partner and Fraunhofer FKIE in Germany as the international partner. Supported by an 8 million-euro investment, the center will focus on developing technologies such as drones, ground vehicles, maritime systems, and secure communications. Core areas of development will include AI-powered sensing, autonomous navigation, drone swarm management, and specialized microelectronics for tasks such as aerial surveillance, ground logistics, and infrastructure monitoring.
“ComARC is needed now because the security environment has changed. Autonomy, drones, AI, resilient communications, and critical-infrastructure protection are no longer future topics; they are immediate strategic requirements. Lithuania cannot rely only on buying foreign technologies. It must be able to understand, test, adapt, improve, and create such systems locally,” says Artūras Medeišis.
The center is designed to grow alongside new technology and talent needs. Its plans include expanding its team to about 50 researchers, engineers, and technologists across electronics, AI, telecommunications, robotics, and materials. The center will support hands-on field testing of systems such as drones and unmanned vehicles across several Lithuanian cities, using a shared testing platform. By bringing research, industrial prototyping, and field implementation together in one location, the center will build the capacity to quickly turn experimental ideas into working prototypes and products ready to address real-world challenges.
The next generation of European innovation won’t be defined only by the biggest economies. It will be shaped by places that can quickly turn research into real-world solutions. Vilnius has built exactly that kind of ecosystem, bringing together talent, industry, and public partners to develop technologies that strengthen both economic competitiveness and resilience.
Source: govilnius.lt

articles.body:
Ukrainian FP-5 “Flamingo“ missiles struck industrial aerospace enterprises in Samara, Russia, on Saturday, Aug. 15, amid concurrent drone attacks in occupied Crimea.
Following the explosions in Samara, Denis Shtilerman, chief designer at the Ukrainian defense company Fire Point, published footage of an FP-5 “Flamingo” missile launch.

Samara region Governor Vyacheslav Fedorishchev reported a missile strike on an unnamed industrial facility in the city. Mayor Ivan Noskov stated that the city’s industrial infrastructure sustained localized damage.
Open-source intelligence analysts from the Astra and Exilenova+ Telegram channels reviewed images of the site and identified the location as the shared industrial zone of the Aviakor aviation plant and the Progress Space Rocket Centre.
Progress, a subsidiary of the Russian state corporation Roscosmos, manufactures Soyuz-2 carrier rockets and space satellites. Aviakor produces, repairs, and maintains aircraft and aviation components.
In a separate development on Saturday morning, local residents reported explosions and drone activity in occupied Crimea, specifically in Sevastopol and the Bakhchysarai district.
The “Crimean Wind” Telegram channel reported power outages in Sevastopol and a fire in the Balaklava area following the explosions. Russian occupation authorities have not issued a statement regarding the incident.
Russia Admits New Petrol Shortages as Ukrainian Strikes Hit Refineries
Drone strikes halt operations at Russian oil refinery
The Aug.15 attack follow a confirmed drone strike on the Orsknefteorgsintez refinery in Russia’s Orenburg region on Tuesday, Aug. 13.
Orenburg Governor Yevgeny Solntsev stated Thursday that the strike damaged key infrastructure, resulting in a complete shutdown of the facility, which is located 1,300 kilometers from Ukraine and processes approximately six million metric tons of crude oil annually.
Solntsev noted that repairs could require up to six months due to international sanctions restricting the import of necessary replacement equipment. Regional authorities are preparing for potential fuel shortages and reconfiguring logistics to rely on imported fuel.
Ukraine’s General Staff confirmed the strike on the Orsk facility. On Thursday night, an additional strike targeted the Gazprom Neftekhim Salavat refinery complex in Bashkortostan.

articles.title: Air defense neutralizes 124 drones, three Banderol munitions used by Russia to attack Ukraine overnight
articles.body:
Air defense neutralizes 124 drones, three Banderol munitions used by Russia to attack Ukraine overnight
The Ukrainian Air Force reported this on Telegram, according to Ukrinform.
Starting at 18:00 on August 14, Russian forces attacked Ukraine with 152 strike UAVs, among them Shahed-type drones, including jet-powered variants, Gerbera drones, Banderol loitering munitions and Parodiya-type decoy drones. The drones were launched from Kursk, Oryol, Millerovo and Primorsko-Akhtarsk in Russia, as well as temporarily occupied Donetsk.
The attack was repelled by Ukrainian combat aircraft, surface-to-air missile units, electronic warfare and unmanned systems units, and mobile fire groups of the Ukrainian Defense Forces.
According to preliminary data, as of 09:00 on August 15, air defenses had shot down or suppressed 124 drones and three Banderol munitions over northern, southern and eastern Ukraine.
Hits were recorded at 16 locations, while debris from downed targets fell at one location.
The attack is ongoing, with several enemy drones still in Ukrainian airspace.

articles.title: As Wildberries Burns, Russia Launches Military Marketplace “Roy.Market” for Drones and Defense Equipment
articles.body:
- Category
- World
As Wildberries Burns, Russia Launches Military Marketplace “Roy.Market” for Drones and Defense Equipment
Russia has taken its military-focused marketplace “Roy.Market” out of pilot operation, allowing suppliers to independently list and manage products for drones and other military equipment, RBC-Ukraine reported on August 14, citing Russian outlet Kommersant.
“Roy.Market” was initially launched in early 2025, but remained in a pilot phase as Russia’s Center for Unmanned Systems and Technologies (CBST) developed its logistics infrastructure and tested the specialized procurement model.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
Under the updated system, suppliers can now independently add products, manage inventories and prices, and process orders through personal accounts. Previously, much of this work was handled by the marketplace’s own staff, according to CBST Chairman Andrei Bezrukov.
The platform’s catalog extends beyond drone components. It includes 3D printers, fiber-optic spools, antennas, chargers, and other equipment intended for field laboratories and unmanned systems operations, according to RBC-Ukraine.
CBST plans to further expand the marketplace by adding suppliers of field uniforms, personal protective equipment, and body armor. The organization also intends to attract vendors that previously operated on civilian e-commerce platforms such as Wildberries and Ozon.
The marketplace is designed around a lower commission than major civilian platforms, according to CBST representatives, although sellers will remain responsible for logistics costs, the outlet reported.
To handle deliveries, “Roy.Market” is shifting to a distributed 4PL logistics model. Under the system, products can remain with suppliers or within existing logistics networks until an order is placed, after which several logistics operators can be involved in completing the delivery. CBST expects the model to expand the platform’s delivery coverage without requiring it to build its own warehouse network.
Access for buyers remains restricted. The marketplace operates as a closed platform requiring authentication and different levels of user access.
CBST also plans to connect other Russian security agencies to the system beyond the Russian Defense Ministry and develop its business-to-business operations.
The organization aims to expand the catalog to more than 10,000 products by 2027.
The push to expand Russia’s military-oriented e-commerce infrastructure comes as Ukrainian strikes have increasingly affected the country’s civilian logistics networks. Ukrainian drone attacks on Wildberries, Russia’s largest online retailer, have destroyed around one-third of the company’s total warehouse capacity.
The retailer generates roughly 6 trillion rubles ($74 billion) in annual sales through nearly 100,000 pickup locations.

articles.title: Vladislav Balgrabsky surrendered to save five soldiers under his command. Now Russia is putting him on trial for treason.
articles.body:
Vladislav Balgrabsky surrendered to save five soldiers under his command. Now Russia is putting him on trial for treason.
The criminal case against Vladislav Balgrabsky, a 30-year-old who fought in the war, has reached the 2nd Western District Military Court, the independent Russian outlet Mediazona reported. He is charged with voluntarily surrendering to the enemy, desertion, and treason.
In April 2025, Ukrainian journalist Yuriy Butusov published a video of Balgrabsky in which the Russian officer said he had signed a contract with Russia’s Defense Ministry in the summer of 2024 and had served as a company commander in the 7th Motorized Rifle Regiment.
Balgrabsky said he surrendered to Ukrainian forces along with five soldiers after receiving an order that was clearly impossible to carry out. “I decided to surrender in order to survive, to be able to see my family, my child. I’ll just stay alive and keep the guys alive. […] These people trusted me, and they survived,” he said in the video. At the end of the video, he called on other Russian servicemen to surrender as well.
The video drew more than 990,000 views. Eight months after it appeared, in December 2025, a case card showing that Balgrabsky’s detention had been extended was posted on the website of the Moscow Garrison Military Court. His detention was extended twice more after that. According to Mediazona, this usually means that a person is in custody and that their case is being heard in person rather than in absentia.
Balgrabsky appears to have been returned to Russia in a prisoner exchange sometime between April and December 2025 — a period in which Russia and Ukraine carried out at least seven such exchanges.
The article criminalizing voluntary surrender was added to Russia’s Criminal Code in 2022, after the start of Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine and the mobilization campaign. Russia’s Supreme Court has said that a surrender counts as voluntary when a person surrenders knowingly and has the ability to put up “decisive resistance.”
The first conviction under the statute came in April 2025, when Junior Sergeant Roman Ivanishin received a 15-year sentence in a penal colony. He had surrendered to Ukrainian forces in 2023 and appeared in a video urging other Russian servicemen to flee their units. He was later returned to Russia in a prisoner exchange.

articles.title: Military training from age 15: Belarus splits 10th-graders into drone pilots and battlefield medics
articles.body:
Starting in September, Belarusian 10th-graders will be split by gender for new practical training: boys will take a 10-hour drone-piloting course, girls an expanded tactical medicine block, Deputy Education Minister Alyaksandr Kadlubai said, according to BelTA. The changes fall under the "pre-conscription and medical training" classes already taught in Belarusian schools.
The update fits a broader pattern of militarizing education in Belarus since the 2020 protests and Alyaksandr Lukashenka's subsequent crackdown. Military-patriotic clubs, formalized under a 2022 presidential decree, have spread through Belarusian schools, sending children as young as elementary school age through weapons training and field exercises. This year, Radio Svoboda says that 10-day military field camps have become mandatory for 10th-graders, and kindergartens have opened groups with a military-patriotic focus.
Kadlubai singled out cooperation with a Minsk-based military unit, No. 5448, home to a police brigade of the interior troops, saying the ministry aims to "scale this experience across the whole of Belarus."
"We've strengthened the practical component," Kadlubai said. "We've shifted the balance toward practical classes and increased their volume."
While Belarus drills its own children, Russia indoctrinates Ukraine's
Belarus is not a neutral bystander to Russia's war. Alyaksandr Lukashenka's government let Russian forces stage the February 2022 invasion from Belarusian soil, and Kyiv says it keeps expanding the logistics routes, training grounds, and artillery positions Russia could use for future operations.
And what its ally teaches at home, Russia imposes by force on Ukrainian children under occupation. From 1 September 2026, occupation authorities roll out a curriculum built around loyalty to the Russian state — a compulsory Russian "identity" subject, a split-off military-training course, and behavior graded from the second grade as "exemplary," "acceptable," or "unacceptable." It already reaches more than 582,000 children in nearly 2,000 schools.
