articles.title: Polish PM Donald Tusk says a suspect recruited by Moscow planned the killing of a Ukrainian-American in Warsaw
articles.body:
On Aug. 7, Polish security services detained a Russian citizen who had been recruited by Russian intelligence services to organize the killing in Warsaw of a person with U.S. and Ukrainian citizenship, Polish Prime Minister Donald Tusk announced at a news conference on Aug. 14, according to Reuters.
Tusk said the target was a dual national who was inconvenient for Vladimir Putin’s regime. He said Poland’s Internal Security Agency (ABW) and police had prevented “this execution, this attack," adding that he was not authorized to disclose the name of the detainee or of the intended victim.
Local radio station RMF FM, citing unofficial sources, reported that the intended target was a defense industry entrepreneur who supplied products to Ukraine. The alleged perpetrator was said to be a 29-year-old resident of Donbas, the eastern Ukrainian region partly occupied by Russia since 2014. He was detained in Warsaw’s Mokotów District by officers from the Warsaw police department who are responsible for combating terrorism, killings, and criminal violence, with support from the country’s counterterrorism service.
Tusk stressed that this was the first case in which someone acting on Russia’s behalf had attempted to assassinate a U.S. citizen in another NATO country.
“We must assume that the Putin regime will try to eliminate people who are inconvenient for various reasons, in various places around the world,” Tusk said. “Which is why our actions in this matter will be extremely intensive, so as to prevent any further attempts against citizens of Poland or other countries, in our country.”
Tusk said he had held a lengthy discussion on the case with the minister coordinating Poland’s security services, adding that Poland would likely continue to face similar pressure in the future. “We will have to work hard to avoid such scenarios,” Tusk summed up.
In June, Semyon Skrepetsky (real name Robert Kuzovkov), a 44-year-old Russian opposition artist, was shot dead in a planned attack in the Polish city of Biała Podlaska.

articles.title: Family was asleep: mother and 9-year-old son killed in Russian strike on Sumy Oblast, father and grandmother suffer severe burns
articles.body:
Family was asleep: mother and 9-year-old son killed in Russian strike on Sumy Oblast, father and grandmother suffer severe burns
In the village of Stepanivka in Sumy Oblast, nine-year-old Hlib Kovtunenko and his mother, 29-year-old Olha, were killed on the morning of 14 August when Russia struck their home with two jet-powered drones.
Details: The boy attended Buryn City Lyceum No. 1, a specialised secondary school, and his mother had graduated from the same institution, according to a post on the school's page.
"War takes the most precious thing – the lives of our children and of those who shape our community's future. This terrible tragedy has been a heavy blow for the entire teaching staff, the student body and the parent community," the post said.
According to Oleh Hryhorov, Head of Odesa Oblast Military Administration, the child and the woman were killed at the scene. The house has been left in ruins by extensive destruction and fire.
Ukraine's national public broadcaster Suspilne reported that Russian forces began attacking the village after 05:00. The family was asleep at the time.
Olha's father-in-law said his son and wife sustained severe burns and are being taken to Kyiv for surgery. The boy who was killed had celebrated his birthday in July.
Besides the Kovtunenko family, two more people were injured.
Background:
- On the night of 13-14 August, the Russians launched more than a hundred drones at Ukraine. Air defence destroyed most of them.
- However, hits were recorded at 11 locations. Russian forces struck a residential building in the town of Smila, Cherkasy Oblast, with a drone, injuring five people.

articles.title: OSINT analysts show damage to plant in Russia's Samara where rockets for military satellite launches are equipped
articles.body:
OSINT analysts show damage to plant in Russia's Samara where rockets for military satellite launches are equipped
The OSINT community CyberBoroshno, based on an analysis of satellite imagery, identified the location where FP-5 Flamingo cruise missiles struck the Progress Rocket and Space Centre in Samara, Russia.
Source: CyberBoroshno
Details: According to CyberBoroshno, the strike most likely hit Building 106A, where onboard equipment is installed on Soyuz-2 launch vehicles. Building 106B, where their final assembly takes place, is located nearby.
"Building 106A operates under a high cleanroom standard: this is where onboard electrical systems, instruments and printed circuit boards are installed – essentially the launch vehicle's 'nervous system': the control system, cable network and instrumentation compartment. Without this stage, the rocket cannot be assembled, even when the body and tanks are ready," the analysts said.
CyberBoroshno emphasises that, given the specifics of the manufacturing process, restoring such a facility could take a considerable amount of time.
"Fire, soot and firefighting water inside a high-grade cleanroom mean this is not a matter of repairing the roof but of requalifying clean zones, recertifying the manufacturing process and carrying out repeated dust-control checks – months, not weeks," the statement reads.
The analysts also noted that, due to sanctions, the onboard electronics of Soyuz rockets depend on imported components that are subject to supply restrictions and cannot currently be purchased in sufficient quantities.
According to the OSINT community, the Progress Rocket and Space Centre is the only facility in Russia responsible for serial assembly of Soyuz-2 launch vehicles.
"The strategic importance of Progress lies in its uniqueness. It is the only assembly point for the entire Soyuz-2 range, which Russia uses to deploy and replenish its military orbital constellation – including the Liana electronic intelligence and targeting system and the Persona/Razdan optical reconnaissance systems — as well as its own 'Starlink': the Rassvet satellite internet network developed by Bureau 1440, which is deployed exclusively using Soyuz-2.1b launch vehicles. There is no duplicate facility for this production," KiberBoroshno said.
The analysts added that the extent of the damage is being clarified using satellite imagery.
Background:, In the Russian city of Samara, the Progress Rocket and Space Centre, which manufactures Soyuz rockets and spacecraft, came under attack by Flamingo missiles on the night of 14-15 August. These are used to launch satellites for the Rassvet low-Earth-orbit communications system, which is described as Russia's equivalent of Starlink.

articles.title: Explosions reported in Russia's Samara, rocket and space centre may have been targeted – photos, video
articles.body:
Explosions reported in Russia's Samara, rocket and space centre may have been targeted – photos, video
Explosions and strikes have been reported in the Russian city of Samara during an attack, with the Rocket and Space Centre Progress potentially among the targets.
Source: Exilenova+ Telegram channel; a Russian media outlet Astra; Denys Shtilerman, co-founder and chief designer of the Ukrainian defence company Fire Point; Samara Oblast Governor Vyacheslav Fedorishchev
Details: Exilenova+ posted photos and videos showing strikes in Samara.
The Rocket and Space Centre Progress, a major facility in Russia's aerospace industry, may have been targeted. The facility produces medium-class launch vehicles and automated spacecraft. The Aviakor aircraft plant, which repairs and modernises Russian aircraft, is located nearby.
An air-raid warning was issued in Samara Oblast on the night of 14-15 August due to a missile threat.
Update: Fedorishchev later confirmed that Samara had come under attack, saying that an "industrial facility" was targeted. The Russian official did not provide further details about the strike.
Update: An Open Source Intelligence (OSINT) analysis by Astra later confirmed that a workshop belonging either to the Rocket and Space Centre Progress or the aircraft plant is on fire.

articles.title: Ukraine’s Zaporizhstal may idle half its capacity to fit new EU steel quotas
articles.body:
Ukraine’s Zaporizhstal plant plans to shift much of its output to lower-value pig iron to keep exporting under the European Union’s new steel quotas. The move would idle up to half the plant’s capacity, its parent company, Metinvest, says.
The EU says the quotas shield its own producers from a global steel surplus. For Ukraine, whose steel entered duty-free after Brussels lifted tariffs after the 2022 invasion, they land on an industry already hit repeatedly by Russian strikes and cut off from the sea. The tariff-free quota fell by half on 1 July, with a 50% duty on anything above it.
Ukraine’s new allowance runs to roughly 1 million metric tons, about 60% below its 2025 shipments to the bloc, the Kyiv consultancy GMK Center calculates.
Steel makes up about 15% of Ukraine’s exports, and the EU buys close to four-fifths of it. The country’s Federation of Employers estimates the curbs could cost $1.2 billion in foreign earnings and cut GDP by 0.6%.
Falling back on pig iron
Pig iron, a semi-finished product, falls outside the quota, so lifting its share keeps the furnaces earning. But the switch would force the plant to reassign the workers behind those idled lines, Oleksandr Myronenko told Reuters. “Instead of support from the European Union, we face restrictions,” said the Metinvest chief operating officer.
Ukrainian mills cannot easily sell elsewhere: they are less efficient than cheaper Turkish and Chinese suppliers and are undercut in Europe’s own market, Myronenko said.
With the Black Sea route closed, importing coking coal through other European ports now runs $30 to $40 more a metric ton. Rail freight rose 30% this month, and an EU carbon charge has been applied to steel imports since 1 January.
A strike, and a plan in doubt
A Russian ballistic missile killed seven Zaporizhstal workers and shut the plant on 11 August.
Trending Now
North Korean ballistic missile kills 7 steelworkers on their way to shelter, shuts down Zaporizhstal plant
The fate of Metinvest’s $8 billion, 15-year plan to convert to cleaner “green steel” is unclear; Myronenko called the modernization unrealistic in wartime. Zaporizhstal is the largest employer in the Zaporizhzhia region and, with the rest of Metinvest, is majority-owned by Rinat Akhmetov, Ukraine’s richest man.
On the plant floor, senior foreman Artem Kalinevych said: “As of today it’s not clear what comes next.”

articles.title: The mobilisation that brought Putin’s war home: an excerpt from Alexandra Prokopenko’s new book
articles.body:
The mobilisation that brought Putin’s war home: an excerpt from Alexandra Prokopenko’s new book
Vladimir Putin’s invasion of Ukraine ran counter to the interests of Russia’s elite, which had spent decades looking to the West, holding assets there and tying its future to it. Yet Russia’s technocrats remained loyal to the Kremlin and helped the economy withstand the impact of sanctions. How did that happen?
In September, Hurst Publishers will release the long-awaited English edition of From Sovereigns to Servants, a book by our regular contributor Alexandra Prokopenko about how Russia’s liberal-minded officials became complicit in the war. articles.title: Palestinians besieged in West Bank village fear Israeli settlers will seize their homes
articles.body:
Palestinians besieged in West Bank village fear Israeli settlers will seize their homes
QUSRA, West Bank (AP) — From inside his home in the West Bank town of Qusra, Qusai Abu Rida watched on Friday as Israeli settlers moved from where they had erected a tent in front of his house to the valley below, rather than returning to the nearby outpost where they live.
Even as the Israeli army took positions around him and the homes of two other Palestinian families that settlers had blockaded for most of this week, the settlers remained close enough that Abu Rida feared they would again return after the army left and try to take over the home owned by his Palestinian American brother in Ohio.
“I just don’t know when this will end,” he said.
The standoff in Qusra between Palestinian families and Israeli settlers who apparently want to push them out entered a new stage Friday as activists supporting the Palestinians marched toward the besieged homes to replenish their dwindling food and water supply. But Abu Rida said he was growing tired of the pattern, with Israeli forces removing the settlers, only for them to return and reestablish their positions after the troops withdrew.
“It’s like a kids’ game, like cat and mouse,” Ziv Stahl, the executive director of the Israeli rights group Yesh Din, said. “It’s clearly not a matter of capability but a matter of will.”
The siege of the homes is the latest episode in a wave of settler violence convulsing the occupied West Bank, which Israel seized in the 1967 Mideast war and which would make up the main part of a future Palestinian state. Israel’s military said the village — roughly 10 miles (16 kilometers) from the Palestinian city of Nablus — was a closed military zone.
More than 700,000 Israeli settlers live in the occupied West Bank and east Jerusalem. The international community overwhelmingly considers Israeli settlements to be illegal and obstacles to peace.
Both Israel’s military and Israel’s police referred questions about the situation in Qusra to the other.
The West Bank has become more dangerous for Palestinians as Israel, under Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu, has approved more than 100 new settlements. Extremist settlers routinely enter Palestinian towns, clashing with villagers, burning homes, mosques and cars.
Netanyahu is courting blocs of ultranationalist voters ahead of what’s expected to be a difficult reelection campaign in October. He and members of his cabinet have largely dismissed concerns about settler violence as overblown and attributed it to fringe groups of a few hundred youths. Yet rights groups and Palestinians say the government’s policies have made it more difficult to restrain settlers, who are rarely punished for attacks.
Qusra siege reflects broader violence
The standoff in Qusra began on Sunday when dozens of settlers arrived and blocked the doors to the three houses, preventing occupants from leaving, according to the families inside.
Israeli troops intervened multiple times and arrived in large numbers Thursday.
Abu Rida and his teenage son were temporarily moved by the army on Thursday but allowed to return hours later. He told his brother in Toledo, Ohio, that he planned on staying to defend the home.
Loui Ridi, the home’s owner who spells the family name differently, has been in constant contact with his brother and watching the siege unfold on security cameras until they went offline Thursday.
He plans to travel to the West Bank next week in hopes of delivering more food and “to do whatever I can to protect my brother and my house,” Ridi told The Associated Press on Friday.
“We want it to be resolved and permanent, not just for a couple of days,” he said.
For many, the scene unfolding in Qusra — now in its sixth day — reflected broader failures by Israeli authorities to curb the violence in the West Bank.
Itamar Weil, an Israeli human rights activist from the group Bnei Avraham, said the army had threatened to use tear gas against the activists and forced them to leave, even as settlers remained in the valley below Qusra.
“The army used to prevent settlers from carrying out this kind of violence,” he said. “Now, with a government that fully supports them, they’re not doing their job. They should be protecting both sides from violence, but instead they’re removing activists while barely doing anything about the settlers.”
Palestinian officials have reported 1,476 attacks by Israeli settlers in 2026, including several earlier instances in which settlers staged takeovers of Palestinian homes on the outskirts of other West Bank towns.
A total of 87 Palestinians have been killed by Israeli settlers and soldiers in the West Bank this year, according to the Palestinian Authority’s Health Ministry. Israel says some were involved in terrorism, which it defines broadly to include militancy and rock-throwing. Three Israelis were killed by Palestinians, including two in a July clash during which four Palestinians were also killed.
Katz strips army of enforcement power against settlers
Before calm was restored in Qusra, Israeli Defense Minister Israel Katz announced on Friday that he would transfer all enforcement powers against Israeli civilians in the West Bank from the army to Israel’s police.
“The (Israeli military’s) role is to fight Palestinian terrorism, focus on protecting the borders and settlements against threats, deal with the borders and the territory itself and security threats to the settlements and the State of Israel, and not chase after boys on the hills,” Katz said in a statement.
Historically, the army has been able to arrest Palestinians and bring those accused of crimes before military courts. But when it comes to Israeli civilians, in most circumstances it can only use temporary detention for those suspected of crimes, leaving arrests, investigations and prosecutions to police and civilian courts.
Katz’s move comes after he ended the use of administrative detention against Israeli civilians in November 2024. The military had used the policy as a tool to contain settler violence, allowing it to detain suspects without charge and remove them from the West Bank.
Much like with that move, rights groups said transferring all powers to the police was unlikely to restore order or ensure Palestinian safety.
Some 2.8 million Palestinians live under Israeli military rule in the West Bank alongside more than 560,000 Israeli civilians who live in settlements that the international community largely considers illegal and an obstacle to peace.
Though the Palestinian Authority exercises limited autonomy and policing power in the territory’s largest cities, agreements that date back to the 1990s give Israel security control over large swaths of the territory, including agricultural areas and communities such as Qusra.
Stahl, Yesh Din’s executive director, said Katz’s announcement wouldn’t change or help stem the violence because police will still require army escorts to operate in Palestinian areas.
“Unless (Katz) means he’s going to apply Israeli law and have the police control the West Bank, the military is still the main body in charge,” she said.
___
Associated Press reporter John Seewer in Toledo, Ohio, contributed.

articles.title: Politico: Zelensky can’t find a Ukrainian ambassador to the US — every candidate says no
articles.body:
Politico: Zelensky can’t find a Ukrainian ambassador to the US — every candidate says no
Zelensky is struggling to find a new ambassador to the United States after several candidates turned down the post, senior Ukrainian officials and lawmakers told Politico.
Lawmaker Ivanna Klympush-Tsintsadze, who served as deputy prime minister from 2016 to 2019, said candidates with the standing and experience for the job fear they “would not enjoy the conditions they would need to do the job properly.” She said the nominee should come from Zelensky’s inner circle of trusted advisers, but that no one there meets the requirements.
A former Ukrainian diplomat said, “Framing it as if nobody wants the job would be a kind of oversimplification. Of course, there are people who want the job, but there’s no one who really measures up to it.” He said Zelensky will have “a hard time filling the position.”
Zelensky had offered the ambassador post to Yulia Svyrydenko as early as July, shortly after she resigned as prime minister, but she categorically refused, sources told the Ukrainian news outlet Ukrainska Pravda. Politico’s own sources confirmed the same. Other candidates have since been “equally reluctant,” according to the outlet, which said the appointment will be no easy task given the need to work with the “Trump’s unpredictable White House.”
Oksana Markarova had served as Ukraine’s ambassador to the United States since before Russia’s full-scale invasion in 2022, remaining in the post through nearly all of Joe Biden’s presidency. Volodymyr Zelensky appointed Olha Stefanishyna, who had previously served as deputy prime minister, to replace her in August 2025.
Stefanishyna was relieved of her post in early August 2026. She said she had resigned of her own accord, “prompted by personal circumstances.” Two days later, Ukraine’s anticorruption agencies notified her that she was suspected of involvement in illegal enrichment and submitting false information in her asset declaration. Her case is now before the courts.

articles.body:
Russia’s role in Middle East politics endures, shifts to being ‘secondary power’
Two Russian military bases will remain in Syria as the region continues to recalibrate its relations with major powers amid the Iran war
At the time, Moscow operated about 100 military facilities in the war-torn country, following its intervention in the Syrian civil conflict from 2015 to prop up then president Bashar al-Assad in alliance with Iran and its regional proxies.
According to a deal announced by the Syrian foreign ministry on Sunday, Russia’s only two official military bases outside the former Soviet Union would be turned into “joint training and capacity-building centres, within new arrangements that preserve mutual interests”.
No further details were given, but Russian military contingents would reportedly remain at both facilities under the new arrangement.

articles.title: Kiev fighting NATO’s war ‘until the last Ukrainian’ – US journalist (VIDEO)
articles.body:
Kiev fighting NATO’s war ‘until the last Ukrainian’ – US journalist (VIDEO)
The Kiev regime is fighting a NATO proxy war against Russia at the expense of its own people, while its leadership pockets Western funding, US journalist and geopolitical analyst John Varoli said.
Speaking to RT on Friday, Varoli said Ukraine’s Vladimir Zelensky and “his clique” have “absolutely no interest” in the Ukrainian people, adding that they neither represent, care for, nor serve them.
“The Ukrainian regime serves the interests of the NATO countries, which are fighting a proxy war against Russia,” Varoli said. “They are literally willing to fight until the last Ukrainian,” he added.
Varoli said Zelensky’s “masters” in Brussels, Washington, DC, and London are telling Kiev to keep fighting Russia for as long as they can.
Kiev is refusing to accept the bodies of fallen Ukrainian soldiers because it would have to compensate their families, the journalist claimed, adding that the regime has “huge amounts of money” and receives billions of dollars from NATO every month.
“But the question is, where is that money going?” Varoli said, adding: “It’s going into the pockets of Zelensky and his oligarchs. That money is being stolen.”

articles.title: Moroccan women candidates face rising political violence
articles.body:
Breadcrumb
Moroccan women candidates face rising political violence ahead of upcoming elections
Warnings are growing in Morocco over rising political and digital violence targeting women candidates ahead of the 23 September legislative elections, as women's and rights groups accuse the government of lacking "a genuine will to bring about structural change that guarantees a meaningful female presence in decision-making circles".
The National Observatory for Protection from Digital Violence, a non-governmental organisation, recently said it was deeply concerned about the increase in attacks in the digital space as the elections approach.
In a statement, it stressed that these practices violate women's rights and the principle of equal opportunities in electoral competition.
The observatory said monitoring and follow-up operations during July and the beginning of August had revealed multiple forms of targeted attacks against several female candidates.
These ranged from insults, defamation and slander and violations of privacy and dignity to the use of digital media in organised campaigns aimed at damaging their reputations and presence in the public sphere.
The observatory considered this escalation a matter of serious concern, as it is occurring during the candidate selection process and amid a context in which women's participation and access to decision-making positions remain below the expectations of parity and equality.
It highlighted that political and digital violence against women poses a direct threat that limits the exercise of their constitutional rights and spreads intimidation messages that deter women from engaging in political work and public life.
According to the observatory, the 2026 elections will be the first major test of tougher penalties introduced under Organic Law No. 53.25. Article 51 bis criminalises the misuse of social media, digital platforms and artificial intelligence to spread false information or fabricate content intended to defame candidates or undermine the integrity of elections.
Women’s political participation in Morocco is underpinned by an explicit constitutional commitment dating to 2011, when the constitution enshrined the principle of gender parity.
It stated that men and women enjoy equal civil, political, economic, social, cultural and environmental rights and freedoms.
Morocco's international commitments also require it to uphold the principle of equality, while the state has established an Authority for Parity and Combating All Forms of Discrimination to support that aim.
Despite efforts made in recent years to advance women's rights, Moroccan women's political and social participation faces real challenges.
Despite progress in recent years, women remain underrepresented in parliament, with Morocco ranking 102nd globally and falling below the international average of 27.5 percent.
As Morocco prepares for the election, the Ministry of Solidarity, Social Integration and Family launched a campaign on 18 May in partnership with UN Women and the United Nations Population Fund, with support from the Canadian Embassy in Rabat.
The campaign, which ran until 5 June, was held under the slogan "Yedek fi yedya ncharco f'tanmia", meaning "Your hand in mine; let's participate in development". It covered all regions of the country, aiming to promote values of equality and parity, raise social awareness and reinforcing the importance of the presence of women in managing public affairs.
It also aims to encourage young women to actively engage in political, party and institutional work.
Just weeks before the Sept. 23, 2026, election, National Observatory for Protection from Digital Violence President Bouchra Abdou expressed her regret over the escalation of political and digital violence currently being practised against female candidates in the upcoming legislative elections.
She explained that there are social perceptions that reject women becoming candidates and leaders and occupying the top positions on electoral lists.
Abdou told The New Arab that Moroccan political parties still do not trust women due to the absence of parity.
She said they also appear unable to stand up to the digital violence practised against female candidates in the upcoming elections.
She said women are often left to face online violence, insults, abuse, bullying and attacks on their reputation and that of their families, without political parties publicly condemning such behaviour.
"Today, female candidates in the upcoming legislative elections must be strong and have the courage to file complaints with the relevant authorities to stop the advance of the violence they are facing," she added.
"Digital violence pushes female candidates to withdraw and refuse to contest the electoral battle in its broad form due to attacks on their honour, reputation and families, and on their public and private lives, which leaves them despairing of political work."
She also stressed the need for political parties to adopt the cases of female candidates and stand firmly against all violence and bullying practised against them.
"It is time for women to receive the trust of their parties and for the principle of parity and equality to be enshrined during next year's local elections, as this remains important for women to reach political decision-making positions."
The women's rights activist said a campaign of political and digital violence in July and early August had targeted 10 candidates from different parties.
Political science researcher Sharifa Lmouir said in an interview with The New Arab that the problem extended beyond election periods. "The phenomenon of political violence against women is not only linked to electoral stages but is also the result of stereotypes and deeply rooted prejudices in our society."
"This political violence is an extension of the social violence that women experience within society, given that it involves the same practices and the same image in which it manifests itself."
Lmouir said that political violence in the digital space against women primarily aims to restrict them within the political scene and attempt to force them to withdraw from exercising their constitutional rights.
She pointed out that all this violence directed against women, whether physical, psychological or sexual, is fundamentally aimed at discouraging them from political engagement and attempting to deter them from participating in political life within society.
"Although the Moroccan legislature is trying to limit this phenomenon through several mechanisms it has adopted, they remain, in my view, insufficient, particularly as the phenomenon is widespread in society.," she added.
"Therefore, an awareness-raising approach targeting Moroccan citizens of all age groups must be adopted to reduce stereotypes targeting women in general."
Article translated from Arabic by Afrah Almatwari.

articles.title: Committee chair says threat level unchanged despite warnings of Russia’s possible attacks
articles.body:
Lithuania’s security threat level remains largely unchanged despite warnings that Russia may be considering attacks on critical infrastructure in the region using Ukrainian-origin drones, the chairman of the parliamentary Committee on National Security and Defence said Friday.
“I want to reassure the public that the information presented in this manner has caused unnecessary anxiety. The threat level remains similar,” Rimantas Sinkevičius said after a closed-door committee meeting at the Second Investigation Department, Lithuania’s military intelligence service.
Sinkevičius said intelligence agencies had already warned in June of the possibility of various types of incidents, noting that the potential threats were not limited to Lithuania but also concerned other countries in the region.
He said Lithuania was strengthening its preparedness by acquiring defensive equipment and improving coordination among state institutions. However, he added that it was impossible to be fully prepared for every possible incident.
Reports emerged last week citing Lithuanian military intelligence that Russia might be considering sabotage operations against critical infrastructure in the Baltic region using drones of Ukrainian origin, so called “false flag” operations. The intelligence did not identify specific targets or provide a timeline for any potential attacks.
Since June 18, the Lithuanian military has been assisting in the protection of key infrastructure, including the liquefied natural gas terminal in Klaipėda, the LitPol Link electricity interconnection in Alytus and the Kruonis pumped-storage hydroelectric plant.

articles.title: Ukraine Attacked the Savasleika Airfield, Where MiG-31Ks—Carriers of Kinzhal Missiles—Are Stationed
articles.body:
The Ukrainian Armed Forces attacked the Savasleika military airfield in Russia’s Nizhny Novgorod region, where MiG-31Ks—carriers of Kinzhal aeroballistic missiles—are stationed.
A video of the fire at the airfield was published by the Telegram channel Exilenova+.
The attack on the airfield took place on the morning of August 15. In local chat rooms, residents reported explosions and began asking where exactly the explosion had occurred.
The Savasleika airfield is a Russian military airbase in the Nizhny Novgorod region, located approximately 12 km northwest of the city of Kulebaki. The base houses a branch of the Russian Ministry of Defense’s 4th Centre for Combat Employment and Retraining of Personnel of the Aerospace Forces. The site is located approximately 650–700 km from the Ukrainian border, at coordinates 55.44199965223542, 42.30844483849896.
The airfield is home to various modifications of the MiG-31 fighter jet, including the MiG-31K, which carries the Kh-47M2 Kinzhal missiles.
This is not the first time the airfield has been targeted. In particular, on August 14, 2024, drones attacked Savasleika. At that time, local sources reported numerous explosions on the airbase grounds.
It later emerged that the strike targeted warehouses and fueling stations on the airfield grounds, around which traces of explosions were observed.

articles.title: Starlink won’t remove Poland from Europe after all, days after Warsaw threatened to drop Ukraine’s funding
articles.body:
Starlink won’t remove Poland from Europe after all, days after Warsaw threatened to drop Ukraine’s funding
Starlink will not remove Poland from the European region of its satellite communications network. Janusz Cieszyński, a former Polish digital affairs minister, was the first to report the reversal.
Poland’s current digital affairs minister, Krzysztof Gawkowski, and Foreign Minister Radosław Sikorski later confirmed the report. In a post on X, Sikorski thanked Elon Musk, who owns Starlink, for acknowledging that Poland is part of the European Union.
Meduza reported earlier this week that Starlink planned to drop Poland from its European region on August 17. The reasons for the change were not made public. The change would have driven up service costs for Polish customers. In response, Sikorski threatened to stop Poland’s payments for Starlink’s services in Ukraine.
Ukraine uses Starlink’s network in its war with Russia. Poland’s Ministry of Digital Affairs finances satellite communications for Ukraine’s armed forces at a cost of about $50 million a year.
Russian troops also used Starlink terminals, but large numbers of the devices went offline along the front line early this year.

articles.title: Russian kids keep getting bused to the same movie (not ‘Spider-Man’), and the institutions taking them are posting eerily similar praise for it online
articles.body:
Russian kids keep getting bused to the same movie (not ‘Spider-Man’), and the institutions taking them are posting eerily similar praise for it online
School camps and municipal children’s centers across Russia are reporting in large numbers that they took children to see The Last Warrior: Kolobok. Verstka, an independent Russian news outlet, found more than 20 such posts on social media in recent days.
The posts describe how the institutions organized trips to movie theaters for the children, and they include photos from the screenings. Verstka said the posts “actively praise” the film and that the wording in some of them is similar.
Alongside these reports, claims surfaced that the Education Ministry had ordered mandatory screenings of the Kolobok film for students in grades one through nine. The ministry called the claim fake, saying the film “is successfully attracting viewers’ attention even without additional support.”
The Last Warrior: Kolobok opened in Russian theaters in early August. Because of the film, distributors reportedly asked movie theaters to postpone screenings of the blockbuster Spider-Man: Brand New Day, which was due for a gray-market release in Russia at the same time. Theaters were threatened with sanctions if they refused.
After the Spider-Man film was postponed, the creators of Kolobok faced criticism, and viewers drove down the Russian film’s rating on review aggregator sites.
The television channel Rossiya 24 complained to the prosecutor’s office and the Investigative Committee about online critics of the film, saying they had sent threats to its creators. Investigators opened a criminal case.

articles.title: Peru Plans to Purchase 12 F-16 Block 70 Fighter Jets
articles.body:
Peru is planning to purchase a second batch of 12 F-16 Block 70 fighter jets. The Peruvian Air Force’s rearmament program calls for the acquisition of a total of 24 fighter jets.
This was reported by Infodefensa, citing a statement by Defense Minister Rafael Belaunde Llosa.
According to the minister, the previous interim government did not leave any funds, so the new administration needs some time to ensure the signing of the second contract.
The minister confirmed that the Peruvian Air Force needs to acquire 24 fighter jets to ensure a minimum deterrence capability. Therefore, in his opinion, even despite financial difficulties, it makes no sense to limit the procurement to an initial batch of 12 aircraft.
“My task is to do everything possible, everything in my power, to meet the needs of the Armed Forces,” he said.
The Peruvian Air Force and Lockheed Martin signed a contract for the purchase of the first batch of F-16C/D Block 70 fighter jets in April 2026.
Prior to this, Lockheed Martin reduced the price of the fighter jets offered to Peru to stay within the budget set by the country’s government. While the initial proposal called for the sale of 12 F-16C/D Block 70s for $3.42 billion, the new proposal includes 24 aircraft of the same model for $3.5 billion.
French company Dassault Aviation, with its Rafale F4, and Swedish company Saab, with its Gripen E/F, also participated in the selection process for Peru’s new fighter jets. It is likely that this significant price reduction was the reason Peru chose the F-16 over the Swedish JAS 39 Gripen, which had won the tender.

articles.title: A Russian court disqualifies a sitting Communist deputy over the copyright to Microsoft fonts in his campaign ads
articles.body:
A Russian court disqualifies a sitting Communist deputy over the copyright to Microsoft fonts in his campaign ads
The Samara Regional Court has stripped Mikhail Matveyev, an incumbent deputy from Russia’s Communist Party (KPRF), of his registration as a candidate for the State Duma, the lower house of Russia’s parliament.
The lawsuit was filed by Anna Sarantseva, a Party of Pensioners candidate running against Matveyev in the single-mandate district. She said his campaign materials used photographs — including some of his own — without permission from the copyright holders. They also used Microsoft fonts whose licenses the company restricted in Russia after the full-scale invasion of Ukraine. The regional election commission backed the lawsuit, and Matveyev plans to appeal the ruling.
Matveyev is considered one of the KPRF’s strongest single-mandate candidates. He won the Krasnoglinsky district in 2021, and ahead of the current campaign, he and Komi deputy Oleg Mikhailov received the most votes among 230 participants in the party’s internal “People’s Candidate KPRF” project, political analyst Konstantin Kalachev said. “Though some might see letting him win the same district twice in a row as overkill,’” Kalachev told the Russian business daily Kommersant in May.
Meduza sources reported in June that the KPRF planned to avoid nominating candidates who had defeated United Russia rivals in 2021. The tactic would hand United Russia a supermajority in the Duma large enough to amend the constitution unilaterally and to push through any measure on the votes of its own faction alone.
In the end, the KPRF itself declined to nominate two strong single-mandate candidates. In Altai Krai, the party replaced Maria Prusakova with Lyudmila Klyushnikova, who has been under criminal investigation for fraud on an especially large scale since November 2025. In Yakutia, the party chose not to nominate Pyotr Ammosov at its congress.
A source told Meduza that similar copyright complaints have begun surfacing against Oleg Mikhailov.
Copyright claims have also been used during the current campaign to remove opposition candidates from other parties. On August 12, Russia’s Supreme Court revoked the registration of Yabloko’s federal list after a lawsuit from the Rodina Party. The court cited several violations, including unauthorized use of the lyrics to Pust vsegda budet solntse (“May There Always Be Sunshine”) and Lish by ne bylo voiny (“As Long As There’s No War”), survey data from the Levada Center, and an image generated by ChatGPT.

articles.title: When consumer similarity backfires: Dark Triad personalities punish brands that act like them
articles.body:
A recent paper published in the Journal of Business Research suggests that consumers who possess manipulative or self-centered personality traits are more likely to punish brands that exhibit those same characteristics. Rather than feeling a sense of loyalty toward companies that mirror their own darker tendencies, these consumers tend to act aggressively against them. This research indicates that shared negative traits between a consumer and a brand can amplify hostility instead of building a connection.
In psychology, the Dark Triad refers to three personality traits associated with manipulative and self-serving behavior. Narcissism involves a sense of grandiosity and a need for admiration. Machiavellianism is characterized by a focus on self-interest and strategic manipulation. Psychopathy involves a lack of empathy and a disregard for social norms.
In the business world, companies can also be perceived as possessing these traits. For instance, a brand might seem narcissistic by silencing critics, Machiavellian by exploiting sustainability trends solely for profit, or psychopathic by operating with poor labor conditions.
“One thing we find particularly interesting is that brands can be judged in surprisingly human terms,” explained the researchers — Silvia Blas Riesgo and Andrea Giuffredi-Kähr of the University of Zurich, along with Lucia Malär of the University of Bern. “Consumers do not simply evaluate what brands do, they also form impressions of who brands are. They can see brands as arrogant, manipulative, or lacking empathy, much like they would judge another person.”
A widely accepted idea in marketing, known as self-congruence theory, proposes that consumers prefer brands that match their own personalities. When a person and a brand share similar characteristics, the consumer typically forms a stronger emotional attachment.
“Self-congruence has long been treated as something that is good for a brand,” the researchers noted. “When consumers perceive a brand’s personality as being similar to their own self-concept, that similarity tends to have positive effects, such as stronger attachment and greater loyalty. We wondered what happens when that self-congruence is ‘dark’: when what a brand and a consumer have in common is not a positive trait like sincerity, but traits from the Dark Triad, namely narcissism, Machiavellianism, and psychopathy.”
To explore this dynamic, the authors built on their past work measuring how companies are perceived by the public. “In our previous research, we developed and validated the Dark Triad of Brand Personality, which captures the extent to which consumers perceive brands as narcissistic, Machiavellian, or psychopathic,” they stated. “That gave us the tool we needed to test an intriguing question: if consumers and brands share these darker traits, does self-congruence still produce the favorable outcomes predicted by traditional theory, or can it actually backfire?”
The researchers first recruited 284 European consumers, with an average age of 30.5 years and a sample that was 73 percent female. Participants completed a standard psychological survey measuring their Dark Triad traits. They then read a fictional blog post about a fashion brand called ACE.
Half the participants read a version describing the brand as highly narcissistic, Machiavellian, and psychopathic, giving examples such as deleting critical comments and using unfair labor. The other half read a version portraying the brand positively. The researchers controlled for participants’ age, gender, mood, and interest in fashion.
Participants rated their willingness to engage in unethical punishment against the brand, such as lying or stealing to get even, on a scale from 1 to 7. Although overall punishment intentions were low, participants exposed to the dark brand reported higher punishment intentions, scoring an average of 1.52 compared to 1.11 for the positive brand. Participants who scored high on their own Dark Triad traits reported even higher punishment intentions. On the 7-point scale, the intention to punish the brand increased by roughly 8.7 percent among those with the darkest personality traits.
“The main takeaway is that similarity is not always beneficial,” the researchers told PsyPost. “In consumer psychology, it is well-established that people tend to respond more positively to brands that resemble them. Our research shows that this principle has an important exception.”
“Consumers who score higher on Dark Triad traits are not more forgiving of brands that appear narcissistic, Machiavellian, or psychopathic,” they added. “Instead, they are often more likely to punish them, including through unethical means such as lying to get a refund. In other words, when consumers and brands align on socially aversive traits, similarity can amplify rather than reduce negative reactions.”
A second study sought to understand the emotional mechanism behind this behavior. The scientists recruited 600 participants from the United States, with an average age of 41 and a sample that was 62.3 percent female. Using a similar procedure, participants evaluated a fictional outdoor clothing brand called Annapurna, presented as having either high or low Dark Triad traits.
In addition to measuring punishment intentions, the researchers measured reactive moral outrage. Reactive moral outrage is an immediate, spontaneous feeling of anger in response to a perceived moral violation. The researchers controlled for the same variables as the first study, along with the order in which participants took the surveys.
The second study replicated the initial findings, with punishment intentions averaging 1.83 for the dark brand versus 1.26 for the positive brand on a 7-point scale. The scientists found that reactive moral outrage acted as a bridge between the brand’s dark traits and the consumer’s desire to punish.
“The mechanism behind the effect surprised us,” the research team explained. “Consumers high in Dark Triad traits actually experienced less moral outrage, meaning feelings of anger and indignation about perceived wrongdoing, toward dark brands than other consumers. However, when they did experience moral outrage, they were much more likely to act on it. In other words, they seemed less emotionally reactive, but more willing to translate those emotions into punitive behavior.”
During this phase of the research, the scientists also asked participants how similar they felt they were to the brand, finding identical results regardless of how the connection was measured.
“We were also surprised by how robust the effect was,” the authors pointed out. “We found the same pattern even when we did not measure consumers’ Dark Triad traits directly, but instead simply asked how similar they perceived the brand’s personality to be to their own. In other words, consumers seemed to recognize the similarity between themselves and the brand, but that similarity did not make them more forgiving. If anything, it strengthened negative reactions.”
To see if these patterns apply to the real world, the researchers conducted a third study using real companies. They recruited another 600 participants from the United States, with an average age of 44 and a sample that was 49.1 percent female. Participants read adapted business articles about either Ninety Percent, a brand selected to represent low dark traits, or Loro Piana, selected to represent high dark traits.
This study measured unethical punishment intentions alongside other negative reactions, such as the desire for revenge, a motivation to disengage from the brand, and negative word-of-mouth. The scientists included additional controls, such as prior familiarity with the brands and how believable the scenarios were.
The results matched the previous experiments. The real-world dark brand elicited higher punishment intentions, scoring 1.71 compared to 1.21 out of 7. Consumers with high Dark Triad traits again felt less emotional outrage but acted on it more aggressively, with the overall effect increasing by 10 percent on the measurement scale.
This pattern extended to a desire for revenge and a motivation to cut ties with the brand. It did not apply to negative word-of-mouth. This indicates that consumers with dark traits prefer direct, brand-targeted retaliation rather than simply complaining about the company to other people.
“Consumers’ reactions were driven less by a specific transgression and more by the perception that a brand possesses enduring dark personality characteristics,” the researchers noted. “More broadly, our research highlights that not all forms of consumer-brand similarity are beneficial. The consequences of self-congruence depend not only on how similar consumers and brands are, but also on the nature of the traits they share.”
The reliance on controlled, written scenarios to introduce brand personalities presents a limitation. In the real world, consumers form opinions about a brand’s narcissistic or manipulative tendencies over long periods through repeated exposure to advertisements, news events, and personal experiences.
“Two of our three studies used controlled experimental scenarios with a fictional brand, which is a simplification of real brand relationships,” the authors stated. “Our third study replicated the pattern using real, well-known brands, which increases confidence that the findings generalize beyond hypothetical scenarios. However, all three studies capture a single point in time rather than how perceptions of brands develop over months or years of real-world exposure.”
They suggested that future research could track how consumer perceptions of dark brand traits develop naturally over months or years. “For example, a brand initially perceived as bold or disruptive may later be seen as exploitative once consumers observe the long-term consequences of its actions,” they explained.
Relying on self-reported intentions to punish a brand does not guarantee that consumers will follow through with actual behavior. People might state an intention to steal or cheat in a survey setting but act differently in real life. Observing actual marketplace behaviors, such as fraudulent returns or documented online sabotage, would provide stronger evidence for how Dark Triad traits influence consumer actions. Additionally, the studies focused primarily on Western consumers. Cultural differences in how people view manipulative business tactics or express moral outrage remain unexplored.
“There are several exciting directions for future research on Dark Triad brand personalities,” the research team observed. “One area we find particularly interesting is understanding the broader consequences of relationships with dark brands. Our research focused on punishment and retaliation, but consumers may also experience other outcomes.”
Future research could examine how consuming or identifying with dark brands affects consumer well-being, triggering feelings such as embarrassment or discomfort. The authors also plan to investigate if specific traits lead to different consumer reactions.
“While narcissistic, Machiavellian, and psychopathic brands share a common dark core, they are not identical,” they pointed out. “For example, psychopathic brands, which are perceived as lacking empathy and concern for others, may be especially likely to trigger extreme responses such as brand sabotage, where consumers actively seek to harm a brand.”
Finally, this framework could apply to individuals who operate as commercial entities. “We would like to extend this work beyond traditional corporate and product brands,” the researchers noted. “Influencers, celebrities, and online personalities increasingly function as brands in their own right. Future research could examine whether dark personality perceptions operate similarly in these contexts and whether endorsing a dark brand creates negative spillover effects for the people associated with it.”
The study, “When self-congruence backfires: how Dark Triad consumers react to Dark Triad brand personalities,” was authored by Silvia Blas Riesgo, Andrea Giuffredi-Kähr, and Lucia Malär.

articles.title: Budanov Says Moscow “Will Pay” as Ukraine Calculates Full Cost of Russian War
articles.body:
- Category
- War in Ukraine
Budanov Says Moscow “Will Pay” as Ukraine Calculates Full Cost of Russian War
The Register of Damage for Ukraine (RD4U) has opened two new categories of claims, allowing the state to bill Russia for humanitarian spending and the cost of demining territory contaminated by the invasion.
Kyrylo Budanov, the head of the Office of the President of Ukraine, announced the measure on August 14.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
The new categories allow Ukrainian authorities and public institutions to document budget expenditures caused by Russia’s full-scale invasion.
B4 includes spending on evacuations, temporary accommodation, emergency medical care, rehabilitation, and compensation for damaged or destroyed housing, including payments under the eRecovery program. B5 covers expenses related to demining, explosive ordnance clearance, specialist training, and mine-risk education.
The register serves as an international mechanism for documenting the damage caused by the invasion, allowing Kyiv to assemble a case for eventual compensation. Budanov described the additions as part of a steady effort to compile a full bill for the aggressor state, itemizing every category of expenditure.
“Russia must pay for every crime it has committed and compensate every hryvnia spent on overcoming the consequences of its aggression,” Budanov wrote. “The enemy created these losses—the enemy will pay for them.”
The inclusion of demining costs reflects the scale of that task. Almost 23% of Ukraine's territory remains contaminated by mines and unexploded ordnance, and full clearance is expected to take at least ten years.
Roughly 128,000 square kilometers are considered potentially hazardous, and clearing a single hectare of farmland can cost at least $1,400.

articles.title: Several Russian regions reintroduce fuel rationing
articles.body:
Several Russian regions reintroduce fuel rationing
Several Russian regions are once again facing fuel shortages after Ukraine resumed near-daily attacks on oil refineries across the country.
Source: Bloomberg
Details: Kaluga Oblast, which borders Moscow Oblast, will introduce a fuel rationing system based on vehicle registration numbers from Saturday.
Astrakhan Oblast, on the Caspian Sea coast, plans to limit fuel sales to 40 litres per vehicle and temporarily restrict operations at a number of urban filling stations.
Earlier this week, Orenburg Oblast introduced a rationing system allowing fuel purchases based on vehicle registration numbers, imposed limits on petrol and diesel purchases per driver at filling stations, and banned the filling of fuel cans.
By early August, regions across Russia had increased fuel purchase limits or even lifted restrictions altogether, while petrol and diesel prices at filling stations had fallen.
The resumption of Ukrainian attacks is once again putting pressure on supplies. Since the beginning of August, Ukraine has attacked 11 of Russia's 34 major oil refineries, most of them linked to the country's largest oil producers.
Several regions significantly closer to Moscow or the Ukrainian border warned of reduced fuel supplies earlier this week.
Russian energy giant Rosneft reduced petrol supply limits to Kostroma Oblast following the 6 August strike on the Yaroslavl oil refinery, one of the largest in Russia.
Voronezh Oblast governor Alexander Gusev also warned this week that fuel supplies were deteriorating.
"There are no indications that it will improve in the near future," he said, adding that the situation was being exacerbated by companies diverting fuel to other parts of the country where shortages were even more severe.
Neighbouring Lipetsk Oblast on Thursday reinstated a rationing system based on vehicle registration numbers at Gazprom, Lukoil, Rosneft and Teboil filling stations.
Background:
- In early August, Russia was hit by a new wave of fuel shortages caused by Ukrainian strikes on oil refineries. A number of regions had already introduced restrictions on fuel sales.
- Orsknefteorgsintez, a medium-sized oil refinery in Orenburg Oblast, halted operations on 11 August after Ukrainian drone strikes damaged its processing units.

articles.title: Ukraine’s Strikes Wipe Out Wildberries’ Major Warehouses as Losses Near $12 Billion
articles.body:
- Category
- World
Ukraine’s Strikes Wipe Out Wildberries’ Major Warehouses as Losses Near $12 Billion
Ukraine’s campaign targeting Wildberries has destroyed all of the Russian e-commerce giant’s major warehouses and roughly one-third of its total warehouse capacity, according to estimates cited by Forbes on August 13.
Direct losses suffered by Wildberries from the destruction of its logistics infrastructure had reached 147–223 billion rubles (around $1.75–$2.66 billion) by mid-August, Data Insight lead analyst Sergey Semko estimated for Forbes. Including the costs of dismantling damaged structures, removing debris, and restoring the affected sites, the losses could rise to 278 billion rubles (approximately $3.32 billion).
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
Wildberries sellers have also suffered substantial losses. Semko estimated that merchandise destroyed in the attacks was worth between 445 billion (about $5.31 billion) and 507 billion rubles (nearly $6.1 billion), putting the combined losses for the company and its sellers at around 800 billion rubles (almost $10 billion).
Margaret Evstigneeva, head of the Association of Suppliers of Goods for E-Commerce Platforms, placed the losses incurred by sellers even higher, estimating them at 600–700 billion rubles ($7.16–$8.35 billion). Combined with Wildberries’ losses, the total damage could therefore approach 1 trillion rubles (around $11.9 billion).
“Many lost up to 95% of all their goods. At the same time, Wildberries considers itself the affected party and paid small sellers an average of 2,000–30,000 rubles, which covered less than 20% of their losses,” Evstigneeva said.
Just a week earlier, Ukrainian long-range Liutyi strike drones targeted a Wildberries logistics facility in Yekaterinburg, Russia’s Sverdlovsk region, traveling more than 1,700 kilometers before reaching the site.
Footage from the site showed multiple fires burning beneath the roof of the large warehouse complex. Wildberries later confirmed that its logistics facility had come under attack and that a fire had broken out.

articles.title: Captured Russian soldier who raped civilian woman in Donetsk Oblast for two months sentenced to 12 years in prison
articles.body:
Captured Russian soldier who raped civilian woman in Donetsk Oblast for two months sentenced to 12 years in prison
A Russian serviceman has been sentenced in Donetsk Oblast for repeatedly raping a civilian woman in a village in the Pokrovsk district over a period of two months.
Source: Office of the Prosecutor General of Ukraine
Details: The man will serve 12 years in prison.
The 50-year-old man, from Russia's Sverdlovsk Oblast, had spent 32 years in prison for robbery and armed robbery. While serving his sentence, he signed a contract with the Russian Armed Forces and became a rifleman with the 114th Guards Motor Rifle Brigade of the 51st Guards Combined Arms Army.
In September 2025, the serviceman entered a village in the Pokrovsk district of Donetsk Oblast as part of a small infantry group. He and two other Russian servicemen occupied the basement of a house.
Two locals, a woman and a man, were also there, sheltering from attacks. The man was killed during one of the strikes. The woman was then left alone with three armed Russian servicemen, unable to defend herself or leave the basement.
"In early October, one of them began sexually assaulting her," law enforcement officials said. "The court found that the abuse became systematic and went on for around two months. The serviceman threatened to kill the victim if she rejected him."
Ukrainian forces captured the Russian serviceman in December 2025, bringing his abuse of the woman to an end.
The man pleaded not guilty in court. However, based on the evidence, he was found guilty of a war crime involving ill-treatment of civilians under Article 438.1 of the Criminal Code of Ukraine and sentenced to 12 years in prison.
Previously: The so-called head of a Donetsk pre-trial detention centre was charged with ill-treatment of civilians. He held at least five people in inhumane conditions, including mould and rats, lack of adequate food or water, and people with infectious diseases being kept together with healthy prisoners.
