articles.title: Polish opposition expels 40 lawmakers who formed breakaway caucus led by ex-PM Morawiecki
articles.body:
Keep our news free from ads and paywalls by making a donation to support our work!
Notes from Poland is run by a small editorial team and is published by an independent, non-profit foundation that is funded through donations from our readers. We cannot do what we do without your support.
Poland’s largest opposition party, the national-conservative Law and Justice (PiS), has expelled 40 of its lawmakers in response to them forming a breakaway parliamentary caucus led by PiS deputy leader and former prime minister Mateusz Morawiecki.
The decision formalises a split that began last month, when Morawiecki and his supporters refused to resign from a political association they had formed and sign a pledge of loyalty to PiS. They represented a more moderate faction that had long been unhappy with the party’s move in a hard-right direction.
Koleżeński Sąd Dyscyplinarny PiS podjął decyzję o wykluczeniu z partii 38 posłów i 2 senatorów wchodzących w skład klubu Rozwój Plus, w tym byłego premiera Mateusza Morawieckiego – przekazał rzecznik dyscyplinarny PiS Karol Karski. https://t.co/Qe6KuPVUVZ
— tvp.info 🇵🇱 (@tvp_info) August 13, 2026
On Thursday, PiS’s disciplinary spokesman, Karol Karski, announced that its disciplinary court had found that 38 MPs and two senators “seriously violated the PiS statute by leaving the PiS parliamentary caucus and joining a new caucus” founded by Morawiecki, called Development Plus (Rozwój Plus).
Karski added that all 40, including Morawiecki, had been notified of the decision by email and been sent scans of the ruling. They have seven days to appeal. If no appeal is filed, they will officially cease to be PiS members, Karski said.
A statement from the party’s disciplinary court, cited by news website Onet, also noted that Morawiecki had committed a further “serious violation” of the party’s statute by announcing last week that Development Plus would become a political party.
Mateusz Morawiecki has confirmed that his Development Plus group, which is splitting from the national-conservative opposition PiS party, will soon form a party of its own.
However, he categorically ruled out ever working with Prime Minister @donaldtusk https://t.co/J6mQaer4MA
— Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) August 4, 2026
Among those to be expelled are several former government ministers, including Janusz Cieszyński, Paweł Jabłoński, Olga Semeniuk-Patkowska and Szymon Szynkowski vel Sęk.
Some of the ousted lawmakers expressed their disappointment at PiS’s decision. “Someone who has done everything for PiS is being expelled simply because he wanted to broaden the party’s voter base,” Grzegorz Puda, another former minister, told the Fakt daily.
Another, Łukasz Schreiber, told news website Onet that, in reality, the decision to expel them had been taken when party leader Jarosław Kaczyński said in July they had effectively resigned by refusing to sign the loyalty pledge. “Everything else was just a formality.”
Morawiecki served as prime minister from 2017 until 2023, when PiS lost power to the current government, a more liberal coalition led by Donald Tusk.
The party has plunged into crisis this year, with its support in polls falling to the lowest level in over 15 years. In response to a growing challenge from the far right, Kaczyński has shifted PiS itself rightwards.
That frustrated more moderate figures around Morawiecki, who founded the Development Plus association in April this year as a way of promoting their ideas. However, that prompted criticism from some other members of the party, who saw it as a step towards creating a breakaway group.
The split in PiS is a blow to the party and its leader, Jarosław Kaczyński.
But the potential emergence of a new centre-right party led by Mateusz Morawiecki could actually help the opposition win a majority at next year's elections, writes @danieltilles1 https://t.co/xMP7e4rOFf
— Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) July 31, 2026
Matters came to a head in July, when Morawiecki and his supporters refused to quit their association and sign the pledge of loyalty demanded by Kaczyński. They then formed their own caucus, which immediately became the third largest in parliament and meant that PiS’s was no longer the biggest.
Last week, Morawiecki confirmed that his group would soon form a new party of its own. He laid out a vision of a more moderate, centre-right party that would focus on economic development rather than “ideological disputes”.
Its first policy proposal was to establish a special “salary” for parents, equivalent to the minimum wage, that they would be paid for the first three years of a child’s life, with the aim of boosting Poland’s birth rate, which is one of the lowest in the world.
According to poll aggregator eWybory.eu, Development Plus already has average support of 5.6% in polls, despite not yet being a party. Support for PiS has fallen to 20.3%, down from 24.4% in July.
Notes from Poland is run by a small editorial team and published by an independent, non-profit foundation that is funded through donations from our readers. We cannot do what we do without your support.
Main image credit: Rozwój Plus/X
Alicja Ptak is deputy editor-in-chief of Notes from Poland and a multimedia journalist. She has written for Clean Energy Wire and The Times, and she hosts her own podcast, The Warsaw Wire, on Poland’s economy and energy sector. She previously worked for Reuters.

Beijing issues ecological report to solidify South China Sea claims amid US row
In new assessment, China blames Philippines for environmental harm and coral loss at disputed Sandy Cay and Second Thomas Shoal
On Friday, the Ministry of Natural Resources’ South China Sea Bureau issued its 2025 marine ecological early-warning and monitoring bulletin, alongside a separate marine ecological protection and restoration report for the region. articles.title: Iraqi daily oil exports in August highest since start of war
articles.body:
Breadcrumb
Iraqi daily oil exports in August highest since start of war
Iraq's average daily oil exports since the beginning of August are the highest since the outbreak of the Middle East war between Iran and the United States choked off the Strait of Hormuz, the oil ministry said Friday.
Iraqi Oil Minister Bassem Mohammed Khudair told a press conference that "exports since the beginning of the month have reached a rate of two million barrels" per day, for a total of around 26 million barrels.
He said the daily rate had been achieved "for the first time since the crisis began" on 28 February after US-Israeli strikes on Iran, which retaliated by blocking the waterway crucial for global oil and gas trade.
Before the war, Iraq produced around four million barrels per day, and exported an average of 105 million barrels per month, mostly from its Basra oil terminal via Hormuz.
Ali Nizar, the head of Iraq's State Organisation for Marketing of Oil (SOMO), said in a TV interview last week that Iraq exported in July "35.5 to 37 million barrels" via Hormuz.
Another seven million barrels were exported through a pipeline to the Turkish port of Ceyhan.
According to SOMO data, Iraq exported via several routes just over 32 million barrels of crude oil in May and June, including more than 20 million barrels from its southern port.
Iraq, an OPEC founding member, was forced to halt production in most of its oil fields during the war as reservoirs filled up.
Due to the waterway disruption, it began exporting crude using tanker trucks through Syria, as well as the pipeline to Turkey.

articles.title: Space Force Adds 5 New Vendors to Space Data Network Project
articles.body:
The Space Force announced five new contract awards for its Space Data Network, broadening the vendor base for the proliferated data transport constellation.
Five companies—Rocket Lab, York Space Systems, Northrop Grumman, Lockheed Martin, and Amazon LEO for Government—will receive $12 million each to demonstrate data connectivity between their satellites and those built by other vendors, the Space Force anounced Aug. 13. Each vendor must also develop and field Space Exchange Point satellites—essentially routers that can connect directly to the network’s backbone.
“By combining on-orbit testing of high-speed optical communications routing with rigorous physical, electrical, and data interface standards, the Space Force aims to build a repeatable, secure baseline which allows different commercial satellite offerings to contribute to the network,” Space Systems Command said in a press release.
The Space Force’s vision is for SDN to manage both tactical and enterprise communication needs. The contracts follow a massive $2.9 billion deal awarded to SpaceX in May to build the SDN Backbone, an integrated, high-capacity satellite network for moving data. SpaceX is slated to deliver an operational prototype by the end of next year.
The initial award sparked concern that SpaceX would dominate the program, but Space Force officials say SDN will be competitive, with many opportunities for other providers to contribute. Col. Ryan Frazier, portfolio acquisition executive for space-based sensing and tracking—including SDN—made that committment clear in the press release.
The new awards help lay the groundwork for a multi-vendor SDN by focusing on integration, standardized interfaces, digital models, and security protocols.
“We have to break away from the old way of doing business, which too often locked the government into single-source vendors for decades,” Frazier said. “By investing in standardized interfaces now, we are creating a clear runway for any capable and innovative company to come in and compete. It keeps the playing field level and ensures we can constantly bring the best commercial technology to our missions.”
Details about the SDN architecture have slowly trickled out since the Space Force first revealed its plans earlier this year. Space Force officials have not yet provided a full picture of what programs will fall under the SDN umbrella and how they’ll be woven together and orchestrated.
Air Force Secretary Troy Meink acknowledged the lack of messaging clarity, noting in an interview with Air & Space Forces Magazine that Frazier is working to provide a clearer picture of the SDN architecture.
For now, the plan is for the program to integrate the proliferated low-Earth orbit backbone with the Space Development Agency’s transport and missile tracking layers as well as the Space Force’s more traditional military satellite communications constellations, like the Protected Tactical SATCOM program.
“Think about this as more of a unified architecture,” Frazier said. “[It’s] how we get data to support the Space Force’s architecture and how we support the joint force. We just do that through lots of different, specific systems.”
Over the next year, Frazier’s focus within SDN will be making progress on SpaceX’s mesh network as well as setting the conditions to integrate new vendors and make sure all of those systems are interoperable.
“We’re going to be really working on making an integrated architecture, and several fairly modest investments with multiple vendors to work on interoperability into the Space Data Network backbone that are required to enable the rest of the Space Force and joint force architecture,” he said. “We need to be able to connect other parts of the architecture into the backbone, make sure data is getting to users at the time and place that they need it.”
Frazier also noted that the satellites the service is buying from SpaceX are “100 percent government-owned” and aren’t just copied from the company’s Starlink broadband satellites.
“There are design changes to account for government-unique requirements, and that’s for security and resiliency,” he said, declining to expand on those differences or the number of satellites SpaceX will provide.
The Space Force is crafting a plan for what comes after SDA’s transport layer, which was intended to provide critical tactical communications links for military targeting. The Space Force plans to stop funding the effort after it launches its second tranche of satellites next year, but needs an alternative solution for beyond-line-of-sight coverage.
“The Space Force is completely committed to doing that, and so we’re building a roadmap to do that in a seamless fashion,” Frazier said. “Some of those details, they’ll be shared as time goes on.”

articles.title: Sheskharis terminal in Russia's Novorossiysk suspends operations after drone attack – Reuters
articles.body:
Sheskharis terminal in Russia's Novorossiysk suspends operations after drone attack – Reuters
Russia has suspended crude oil exports from the Sheskharis terminal at the port of Novorossiysk following a drone attack.
Source: Reuters, citing sources
Details: The Sheskharis terminal, which handles around 700,000 barrels of crude oil a day, is Russia's main oil export facility on the Black Sea.
Reuters noted that the suspension adds to pressure on Russia's energy infrastructure, which has been repeatedly targeted in attacks in recent months.
One Reuters source said that a tanker due to load oil at the port had headed out to sea early on Friday 15 August after a drone attack was attempted against the terminal.
As a result of the attempted attack, the port suspended oil loading and stopped accepting crude because its storage tanks were completely full.
The disruption came after a period of high export volumes in recent months. According to one Reuters source familiar with export data, oil loadings from Novorossiysk reached nearly 1 million barrels a day in July and around 800,000 barrels a day in June.
Background:
- Units of Ukraine's defence forces struck a naval base in the city of Novorossiysk, in Russia's Krasnodar Krai, damaging four Russian warships to varying degrees on the night of 11-12 August.
- The following targets were also hit: a 30N6E radar, which is part of an S-300 surface-to-air missile system; a mobile fire team on pier No 2 at the port of Novorossiysk; the tunnel portal of the Grushovaya oil depot leading to the Sheskharis terminal; and infrastructure at piers No 3, No 6 and No 7.

articles.title: Tunisia's opposition activists languish in jail amid dire health
articles.body:
Breadcrumb
Tunisian opposition activists languish in jail amid worsening health conditions
Some of Tunisia’s most significant opposition activists and politicians are languishing in prison with injuries and health issues, while others are going on hunger strikes to protest their conditions.
Issam Chebbi, the General Secretary of the centrist-liberal Republican Party, reportedly has a broken leg whilst in prison, which his wife Faiza Rahem stated on social media.
Rahem said she visited her husband along with other family members on Thursday, and found Chebbi with a broken leg and in a cast, as well as using a pair of crutches.
“Today, Thursday, August 13, 2026, during the weekly visit, we were startled to see him behind the glass partition with a pair of crutches; his leg was broken and in a cast—I cannot even begin to describe the feeling that overcame us," she posted on her Facebook account.
Rahem said she found Chebbi with his arm in a sling during a visit on 30 July, two weeks prior, alluding to the dire conditions opposition activists and politicians are exposed to, and the lack of medical care.
"As always, the moment he saw us, he sought to put us at ease, greeting us with his trademark smile and unwavering composure and high spirits: "I'm fine; it's nothing," Reham continued.
She said that they "know that everything is God’s will and decree," but in moments like these, “one feels a profound sense of injustice, anguish, and helplessness in the face of the oppression inflicted upon Issam and other detainees”.
In her post, Raham noted that Chebbi sought to reassure his family, greeting them warmly and insisting that the injury was "minor".
"Under such circumstances, he ought to be surrounded by his family, receiving proper medical treatment and care," she added.
"Instead, a malicious conspiracy charge — based on anonymous sources — has led to nearly four years of imprisonment under an unjust, authoritarian, and one-man rule that spares neither women nor men," she continued.
In recent weeks, alarm has been raised over the conditions of imprisoned opposition members and activists in Tunisia, jailed amid President Kais Saied’s increasingly authoritarian rule and clamp down on critics and what he calls "traitors and terrorists". Among them is the opposition party Ennahda's president Rachid Ghannouchi, who had fainted in prison last month, according to reports.
Chebbi was arrested in February 2023 as part of what Tunisian authorities called a "conspiracy against state security" case.
Prosecutors accused him of "plotting to destabilise the country and overthrow or undermine President Saied's authority".
The charges brought against Chebbi include conspiracy against the internal and external security of the state.
In April last year, he was handed an 18-year-long sentence, along with politicians and activists Ghazi Chaouachi, Jawahar Ben Mbrak and Ridha Belhaj.
Chebbi was previously held at Mornaguia Prison near Tunis, where his brother, Ahmed Nejib Chebbi, and Ghannouchi are also imprisoned. However, he was reportedly transferred in May 2025 to Borj Erroumi without his family or lawyers being notified in advance.
In 2024, Chebbi was suggested as a potential presidential candidate to counter Saied in the presidential elections of that year. Saied won the election, beating out Ayachi Zammel with a reported 90% win.
Also in Tunisia, the prominent lawyer and activist Chawki Tabib has gone on a hunger strike in prison to protest his imprisonment, his wife said, according to Tunisian media reports.
Mariem Ben Azzouz said that the former head of the Tunisian bar association and ex-chief of Tunisia's National Anti-Corruption Authority was carrying out his hunger strike in protest against injustice he perceives in his case. Ben Azzouz also expressed concern about the impact of this latest protest action on his health, asking: "How much of one's health, dignity, and life must be sacrificed for one's voice to be heard?"
Tabib was jailed in March this year for 10 years on charges including "forging documents" and "possessing and using forged documents".
Tabib's anti-graft body was dissolved in 2021 after a sweeping power grab by Saied, described by rights groups as a trigger in a major rollback of press freedom and freedom of expression.

articles.title: Operation Bambi: Ukrainian forces rescue baby deer and take three Russians prisoner – video

Operation Bambi: Ukrainian forces rescue baby deer and take three Russians prisoner – video
Operators from the 6th Rangers Regiment of Ukraine's Special Operations Forces (SOF) have taken three Russian service members prisoner and rescued a baby deer they spotted in the bushes during a raid on the Russian positions.

In the ensuing clash, Ukrainian troops killed one Russian service member and captured three others. They also seized weapons, communications equipment and documents.

articles.title: Ukraine Strikes NOVATEK Facilities in Ust-Luga
articles.body:
On August 14, Ukraine struck NOVATEK facilities in the Russian port of Ust-Luga, located in the Leningrad region.
The report comes from the General Staff of the Armed Forces of Ukraine.
NOVATEK, Ust-Luga is a production and transshipment complex designed for the fractionation and processing of stable gas condensate. Its capacity is nearly 8 million metric tons of raw materials per year.
This morning, news broke of a fire caused by an attack by Ukrainian drones, and preliminary assessments of the strikes have already emerged.
The attack damaged stable gas condensate fractionation units and the combined hydrocracking unit.
Ust-Luga is not merely a terminal for transshipping raw materials. Within the complex, stable gas condensate was processed into light and heavy crude oil, jet fuel, diesel, marine fuel components, and LPG.
A significant portion of the products obtained after refining was exported by sea. Thus, the complex allowed Russia not only to export raw materials but also to produce petroleum products with higher added value.
According to data for 2022, the complex produced approximately 6.8 million metric tons of commercial products. Of this total, about 4.2 million metric tons were light and heavy crude oil, and 1.05 million metric tons were jet fuel.
Another approximately 1.49 million metric tons consisted of diesel fuel and marine fuel components, while LPG production reached approximately 78,000 metric tons.
According to Militarnyi’s analysis, the cargo line of the port terminal located next to the complex was also damaged.
The combined hydrocracking unit is of particular importance. This process allows for the conversion of heavier oil fractions and residues into more valuable light petroleum products, notably kerosene and gasoil.
Therefore, damage to the fractionation and hydrocracking units affects not only individual production facilities but also the entire gas condensate processing chain.
Ust-Luga is one of the key elements of NOVATEK’s export infrastructure in the Baltic Sea, which ensured the processing of raw materials and the subsequent shipment of finished products by sea.

articles.title: Libya's Haftar played role in release of US hostage held by IS
articles.body:
Breadcrumb
Libya's Haftar played key role in release of US hostage held by Islamic State
A deal to free an American hostage held by an Islamic State affiliate in West Africa's Sahel region was brokered with the help of the eastern Libyan military commander Khalifa Haftar, four sources told Reuters.
The hostage, a pilot working for a Christian missionary organisation in Niger, was handed over to eastern Libyan authorities late Thursday, one of the sources said. Libya's role in the deal has not previously been reported.
Haftar's involvement in the freeing of a US hostage reflects how he has carved out a position as a major security broker in the Sahel region, and has used it as leverage to curry favour with the Trump administration.
The missionary, Kevin Rideout, worked for the evangelical agency Serving in Mission and was kidnapped in Niger in October. It was not clear what, if anything, was traded in exchange for his release. One of the four sources said the Libyan side had paid a ransom, without providing further details.
The State Department declined to comment. The White House did not respond to a request for comment about Haftar's involvement. In a social media post, Trump said the US looks forward to welcoming Rideout home.
The authorities in eastern Libya were not immediately available for comment.
Reuters reported last year that Rideout was seized by three unidentified men on his way to the airport in Niamey and taken to the western Tillaberi region of Niger, where Islamist militants linked to Islamic State and al Qaeda operate.
The US has made recovering Rideout one of its top priorities in the Sahel.
The Trump administration lifted sanctions on top Malian government officials earlier this year in an effort to secure overflight access to the country's airspace to hunt for the pilot.
For months, officials believed Rideout may have been moved to Malian territory.
The details of Rideout's handover to Libyan authorities and his journey to Libya were not immediately clear.
Two sources said the recent effort to secure his release from the Islamic State affiliate was led by Cherif Ould Tahar, a Malian Arab businessman with connections to regional armed groups and smuggling networks. Tahar could not immediately be reached for comment.

articles.body:
The ministry said its forces came across the two diplomats at a secret meeting while executing a judicial warrant to arrest the suspects. It said the diplomats had a long record of violations of Iranian law and diplomatic commitments, and were handed over after their identities were confirmed.

articles.title: Iran warns Trump against adventurism in Strait of Hormuz
articles.body:
Gholam-Hossein Mohseni-Eje'i, head of Iran's judiciary, said that the Strait of Hormuz is "an inseparable part of Iran's territorial and border domain" and warned that any "adventurism" in the waterway would be met with a decisive response, rejecting recent claims by U.S. President Donald Trump over the strait.
Writing on social media, Mohseni-Eje'i dismissed Trump's remarks as baseless, saying Iran is the rightful owner of the strategic waterway under international law and the principles of national sovereignty.

articles.title: Trump urges US to accept higher prices, escalates Iran rhetoric
articles.body:
Breadcrumb
Trump urges US to accept higher prices, escalates Iran rhetoric
President Donald Trump on Friday urged Americans to accept slightly higher gasoline prices as the cost of preventing Iran from obtaining a nuclear weapon and said he would soon declare the Strait of Hormuz a US territory.
The comments underscore the growing political risk for Trump as higher fuel prices collide with his campaign promise to lower energy costs, with Democrats already seeking to make the economic fallout from the Iran war an issue heading into the November midterm elections.
In a speech in Garden City, Trump said Americans who had to "pay a tiny little bit more for your gasoline" should remember that this was the cost of ensuring "a very evil country" could not have a nuclear weapon.
"What we're doing is a great service for the world, not only for ourselves ... and we're really doing a great job," said Trump, adding he would never apologise for attacking Iran.
Around roughly 20% of global oil and LNG shipments usually pass through the Strait of Hormuz and the potential for long-term disruption has pushed up oil prices.
"After we finish defeating Iran ... pretty soon I'll be declaring the Hormuz Strait a territory of the United States," said Trump, escalating his rhetoric over the vital waterway.
It was unclear how seriously Trump intended the remark or whether it represented a new policy position.
The remarks come as the Strait of Hormuz remains a critical pressure point for global energy markets.
Oil prices have risen this week, with Brent crude approaching $90 a barrel, while US gasoline prices have climbed to around $4 a gallon.

articles.title: Egypt political prisoners' families launch int'l rights group
articles.body:
Breadcrumb
Egypt political prisoners' families launch international rights group
Families of political detainees in Egypt have launched a new international association aimed at campaigning for prisoners' release and representing their relatives before Egyptian and international institutions.
The Families of Egyptian Detainees Association (FEDA) announced its formation on Thursday, saying it would seek practical solutions to what it described as a 13-year detention crisis and press for improved prison conditions and fair trials.
In its founding statement, FEDA said its main objective was to bring an end to "the tragedy that has continued for 13 years" by pursuing measures that could lead to the release of political detainees.
"Our hands are extended to everyone who can contribute to closing this painful chapter," the association said.
The group's launch coincides with the 13th anniversary of the Rabaa and Nahda massacres on 14 August 2013, when Egyptian security forces violently dispersed two sit-ins by supporters of ousted president Mohamed Morsi in Cairo.
Over 1000 were killed in the operations, a defining moment in the crackdown that followed Morsi's removal by the military the previous month.
FEDA said it intends to bring together families of Egyptian detainees inside the country and abroad, keep their cases on the domestic and international agenda and represent them before relevant bodies.
The association said it would use legal and political channels to seek prisoners' release and push for fair trials and detention conditions that comply with Egyptian law and international standards.
Its plans include approaching Egyptian and international institutions, political and religious leaders, and figures working in politics, media and human rights.
FEDA also intends to visit the United Nations and bodies dealing with detention and enforced disappearance, pursue legal cases over alleged abuses and organise solidarity events.
Egyptian authorities do not publish an official figure for the number of people currently detained on political grounds.
Previous estimates by rights organisations have put the number detained since 2013 in the tens of thousands.
Human Rights Watch estimated in 2017 that around 60,000 people had been imprisoned on political grounds since that year, although that cannot be treated as a current estimate of those presently held.
Rights organisations say political detention has affected journalists, activists, human rights defenders, protesters, academics and political opponents, as well as people detained over expression or political activity.
In its 2026 World Report, Human Rights Watch said thousands remained in prolonged pretrial detention or were serving sentences following trials it considered unfair, while arbitrary detention, enforced disappearance, torture and other forms of ill-treatment continued to be reported.
FEDA said detainees face problems including inadequate medical treatment, poor food and ventilation, overcrowding and restrictions on family visits and access to books, newspapers and news.
Human Rights Watch said detainees continued to be held during 2025 in conditions it described as amounting to ill-treatment, including denial of healthcare and prolonged solitary confinement, while dozens of deaths in detention were documented.
Egypt's government launched its National Human Rights Strategy in September 2021, pledging improvements to detention conditions, protection against torture and greater oversight of detention facilities.
The strategy also referred to expanding conditional release, presidential pardons and other measures aimed at reducing the prison population.
International rights organisations, however, have repeatedly said there remains a substantial gap between those commitments and practices on the ground.
FEDA said its establishment was intended to move families from individual campaigning towards a more organised effort, arguing that prolonged detention has imposed lasting social, economic and psychological consequences on prisoners' relatives.
The association stressed that it was not aligned with any particular political movement, saying its purpose was to represent detainees' families and work with Egyptian and international institutions to bring the political detention crisis to an end.

articles.title: Hezbollah: 'Lebanon-Israel deal puts undue pressure on army'
articles.body:
Breadcrumb
Hezbollah's Qassem says Lebanon-Israel deal puts undue pressure on army
Hezbollah chief Naim Qassem on Friday accused Lebanese authorities of subjecting the country's armed forces to undue pressure by implementing a framework deal agreed with Israel to end hostilities.
The June trilateral framework, to which the United States is also a party, involves the disarmament of the Lebanese militant group and a gradual withdrawal of Israeli forces from Lebanon's south, where it has occupied several areas.
It also includes the deployment of the Lebanese army to areas where Israel's military has pulled out, starting in test areas known as "pilot zones".
"How can you accept this ongoing humiliation of the Lebanese army, exposing it to bombardment and Israeli pressures, instead of acting as its protectors?" Qassem said in a speech.
In talks between Lebanon and Israel in Rome last week, both sides discussed which countries might participate in a committee tasked with verifying the Lebanese army's deployment in the pilot zones and clearance of Hezbollah weapons and infrastructure, a Lebanese presidency source told AFP.
"Israel is attempting to bind Lebanon to an inquiry committee that oversees the army's deployment, operations, and internal details. Where is the patriotism? Where is the dignity of the army that ought to be preserved?" said Qassem.
Hezbollah has repeatedly rejected the direct talks and refuses to surrender its weapons.
Washington on Tuesday announced it would sponsor a new round of negotiations between Israel and Lebanon in Rome in early September.
But Qassem reiterated the group's rejection of the framework deal and called on Lebanese officials to reverse it.

articles.title: Brazil’s Lula triggers reciprocity process against US tariffs in effort to show strength
articles.body:
Brazil’s Lula triggers reciprocity process against US tariffs in effort to show strength
SAO PAULO (AP) — Brazilian President Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva said Friday his government has triggered an economic reciprocity law mechanism against U.S.-imposed tariffs, saying the move was intended to show his nation must be respected.
In July, U.S. President Donald Trump imposed tariffs on hundreds of Brazilian exports, with duties reaching up to 37.5% in some products. The Trump administration has accused Brazil of unfair trade practices, but Lula has denied the accusations, insisting they are politically motivated ahead of the October election.
Lula is seeking reelection against Sen. Flávio Bolsonaro, a Trump ally who met with U.S. officials, including Trump, in Washington weeks before the administration proposed higher tariffs on Brazilian goods.
“Yesterday, we invoked the reciprocity law to show that we are not to be taken lightly,” Lula said in an interview with Brazilian podcasters. “We respect ourselves. I am very calm knowing what could happen, and I am prepared to debate the defense of Brazil anywhere in the world.”
Brazil’s Foreign Ministry said in a statement late Thursday it is requesting diplomatic consultations with its U.S. counterparts on the issue, as a sign of Lula’s aim “to privilege dialogue and negotiation in its international relations.”
The beginning of the proceedings does not necessarily mean Brazil will retaliate against U.S. tariffs.
“I don’t want any fight with the United States,” Lula said Friday. “Unfortunately, they are spreading falsehoods.”
Earlier this month, the U.S. State Department revoked the visa of Brazil’s ambassador to Washington in retaliation for Brazil’s denial of visas last month for two American diplomats who sought to visit ahead of the October election.
The U.S. government also has accused Brazil of stalling approval of Trump’s nominee for ambassador in Brasilia, while Brazilian officials say the U.S. should have first sought the government’s approval before submitting the nomination to Congress, as diplomatic protocol requires.
Since U.S. Secretary of State Marco Rubio revoked the Brazilian ambassador’s visa in response to Lula’s actions but did not order her expelled, U.S. officials have said the Trump administration does not want the dispute to escalate.
These officials, who have spoken on condition of anonymity to discuss internal administration deliberations, have said on multiple occasions that Rubio’s limited response was intentionally designed to give Lula time and space to back down.
At the same time, they have said that the U.S. will respond quickly should Lula’s government choose to escalate the matter and that declaring the Brazilian ambassador “persona non grata” and expelling her from the U.S. would be a logical next step.
Lula said once again Trump has treated him well, but warned any foreign governments “who come here to meddle in the election, will lose.”
___
Associated Press writer Matthew Lee contributed from Washington.
___
Follow AP’s coverage of Latin America and the Caribbean at https://apnews.com/hub/latin-america

articles.title: Torture 'ingrained' in post-Assad Syria, rights group says
articles.body:
Breadcrumb
Torture 'ingrained' in post-Assad Syria, rights group says
Torture, arbitrary detention and other serious abuses are continuing in Syria after the fall of Bashar al-Assad, with different security bodies and armed actors using many of the same methods that characterised the former regime, according to a new investigation by Syrians for Truth and Justice (STJ).
The report, published on 13 August and based on 19 interviews with survivors, relatives and witnesses and an examination of 14 cases between June 2025 and June 2026, documented severe beatings, electric shocks, mock executions, forced confessions, unofficial detention, denial of access to lawyers and deaths in custody.
STJ said the evidence does not point to a single, centrally directed torture apparatus comparable to Assad's vast detention system.
Instead, it warned that abusive practices are recurring across different security and armed bodies because the conditions that allowed torture to flourish have not been fully dismantled.
Bassam Alahmad, co-founder and executive director of STJ, told The New Arab that human rights groups had hoped some of the most notorious practices associated with the Assad era would disappear with the regime.
"We thought that some practices would at least stop after the fall of the Assad regime. One of them was torture, as well as forced disappearances and arbitrary detention," he said.
Alahmad, himself a former detainee, stressed that the scale remains very different from under Assad, when torture was systematic and widespread.
"I was myself detained. I knew how much - I would say more than 90 percent of people - were tortured. It was almost automatic," he said.
"Here, of course, it is not widespread like that, but the practice itself is ingrained."
STJ documented detainees being beaten with cables, sticks and rifle butts, subjected to electric shocks and threatened with execution. In some cases, detainees were held in unofficial locations, denied access to lawyers and moved between facilities without their families being informed.
From systematic torture to a recurring phenomenon
Alahmad described the pattern as a "phenomenon" - more than isolated incidents, but not a centrally organised policy comparable to Assad's torture system.
"The groups that were integrated into the government and the army brought this practice with them," he said. "It is not an order from the Ministry of Defence or Interior. It is not a practice coming from the top down."
He said the persistence of torture could not simply be explained by former Assad-era security personnel remaining in place, noting that Syria's new security bodies are largely staffed by members of armed groups that operated during the civil war.
Those practices were not confined to one faction, he added, pointing to previous allegations of torture involving Hayat Tahrir al-Sham, Syrian National Army factions and the Kurdish-led Syrian Democratic Forces.
For Alahmad, the central problem is impunity. "If you think that there is really accountability, you will not do this kind of work," he told The New Arab.
STJ also found indications that some detainees had been abused because of their communal or ethnic background.
Alahmad said the organisation had received reports involving Kurds, Alawites and Druze in which insults used during torture appeared to indicate a sectarian or ethnic motive.
"Some people were tortured and beaten because they are Druze or Alawite or Kurds," he said.
But he stressed that the abuses were not limited to minorities.
"There were also cases where Arab Sunni people were tortured, because there is a practice," he said.
Questions over accountability
The report comes amid scrutiny of detention practices after the case of Mohammad Ghamira, a former Syrian Civil Defence volunteer who was hospitalised in critical condition after being held at a police station in al-Haffa, rural Latakia.
Ghamira's family said he entered the station conscious and in stable health after being summoned over a financial complaint, but emerged several days later bleeding and seriously ill.
According to relatives, he was later found to have suffered a brain haemorrhage and remains unconscious in intensive care.
The Syrian Interior Ministry has announced an investigation into the incident, but Alahmad said such inquiries must be independent and transparent.
"I am afraid that this kind of announcement is more to calm down the people, because we didn't see a real investigation or attribution of the act to the people," he said.
"We are in the right direction that we do investigations, but we need these investigations to be transparent and independent."
He said accountability should extend beyond punishing individual officers and address how abuses can be prevented from recurring.
"Sometimes it's not about training," Alahmad said. "Sometimes it's just about a clear order that no one should be torturing like that."
For STJ, the danger is not that Syria has already recreated Assad's centralised machinery of torture, but that recurring abuses could become embedded in the new security order if they are tolerated or inadequately investigated.
The organisation called for all detention facilities to be officially registered, detainees to have access to lawyers and families, independent oversight of detention centres, transparent investigations into allegations of torture, and accountability for perpetrators regardless of affiliation.

articles.title: What to know about Luigi Mangione’s guilty plea in killing of UnitedHealthcare CEO Brian Thompson
articles.body:
What to know about Luigi Mangione’s guilty plea in killing of UnitedHealthcare CEO Brian Thompson
NEW YORK (AP) — Luigi Mangione’s guilty plea on Friday to federal stalking-to-kill charges raised immediate questions about why he decided to enter that plea, how it’ll affect his parallel state murder case and what his lawyers might do to prevent Mangione from spending the rest of his life in prison.
In a stunning turn, Mangione pleaded guilty in Manhattan federal court to a pair of stalking charges and admitted that he targeted and killed UnitedHealthcare CEO Brian Thompson as the executive walked to his company’s investor conference at a Manhattan hotel in 2024.
Neither Mangione nor his lawyers said why he pleaded guilty now, but they gave some clues.
Immediately after his plea, Mangione’s lawyers filed paperwork seeking to have the state case thrown out on double jeopardy grounds. That trial is scheduled to begin next month, but could be pushed back or canceled altogether depending on what the judge decides.
If it succeeds, Mangione’s defense team could concentrate on trying to convince the judge in his federal case, Margaret Garnett, to spare him from the life sentence that prosecutors say they intend to seek when he’s sentenced on Dec. 18.
Mangione was facing back-to-back trials and a pile of evidence
In their double jeopardy filing Friday, Mangione’s lawyers described him as a “pawn in parallel prosecutions,” and defense lawyer Karen Friedman Agnifilo accused state and federal prosecutors of “trying to punish him twice for the exact conduct.”
Indeed, Mangione remains scheduled to go to trial on state murder charges beginning Sept. 8. His federal trial — now moot because of his guilty plea — was set for January.
Complicating matters, anything said in federal court — including Mangione’s statements Friday admitting to killing Thompson — potentially could be used against him in state court, or vice versa.
But that’s not all. Prosecutors say they have a trove of evidence that proves Mangione’s guilt, including: Video of him shooting Thompson and tailing him the day before; Mangione’s DNA and fingerprints on items at or near the crime scene; testimony from shooting witnesses; a 3D-printed 9mm pistol that police found in his backpack when he was arrested that authorities said matched the gun used to kill Thompson; and a notebook found with Mangione at the time of his arrest in which he expressed a willingness to kill a healthcare executive.
The defense previously argued all the items in Mangione’s backpack were obtained in an unconstitutional search, but judges in both the federal and state cases disagreed.
Guilty plea allows defense to argue double jeopardy
Mangione’s guilty plea, just three weeks before jury selection in his state murder trial, appeared to be part of a larger defense strategy to swiftly resolve both cases, minimize his legal consequences and, perhaps, give him a chance to live some of his life outside a prison cell. Earlier plea talks broke down in June.
Within minutes of his plea, Mangione’s lawyers petitioned the judge in the state case, Gregory Carro, to throw out those charges on double jeopardy grounds. Instead of two trials — and two potential sentences that could run back-to-back — they are fighting for just one and are sure to argue he deserves a far lesser sentence than life in prison.
Manhattan District Attorney Alvin Bragg’s office, which is prosecuting the state case, will have a chance to respond to the defense’s double jeopardy motion before Carro rules. In a statement, the office said it would fight efforts to terminate the state case, in part because Mangione’s sentence in the federal case isn’t yet known. Thompson’s family members, in a statement, suggested they are also looking forward to the state case going to trial. Mangione has pleaded not guilty in the state case.
Compared with federal law and that of other states, New York has uncommonly strong protections for defendants facing multiple prosecutions — though they are not guaranteed.
Bragg’s office contends that the state charges, including murder and firearms offenses, involve different legal elements and criminal conduct than federal charges, which alleged Mangione traveled across state lines to stalk and kill Thompson.
However Carro rules, his decision will be subject to appeal, meaning a final answer on whether Mangione faces a state trial could take a while.
An opportunity to argue for less than a life sentence
Mangione’s lawyers previously fended off the government’s attempts to seek the death penalty. Now they’re fighting for a sentence that’s less than the life term U.S. Attorney Jamie McDonald said federal prosecutors intend to seek. Life is also the maximum punishment in Mangione’s state case.
Unlike other defendants, Mangione doesn’t have a plea deal with prosecutors. There were “no accommodations or concessions, and we are free to seek the maximum penalty under the law,” McDonald said.
Still, Garnett noted in court that the government’s calculation of federal sentencing guidelines would call for a sentence of 24 to 30 years in prison. Mangione’s lawyers can submit their own calculation and both sides can argue for greater or lesser punishment in submissions to the judge. Such filings typically chronicle the impact of a defendant’s crimes, as well as his history, upbringing and other aggravating or mitigating factors.
Mangione will also be interviewed by probation officers, Garnett said, adding that the report they produce will factor heavily in her sentencing decision. Judges are free to ignore sentencing guidelines, which are intended to reduce disparities in punishments levied for the same crimes.
Garnett told Mangione she is obliged to determine what she thinks is the correct guideline range and “more importantly what I think the appropriate sentence is in your case.”
“No one, not your lawyers, not the government’s lawyers, no one can give you any assurance of what your sentence will be since I am the one who will decide your sentence,” the judge said, “and I’m not going to do that today.”

articles.title: Drone threat halts Russia’s main Black Sea oil terminal, which normally ships 700,000 barrels a day
articles.body:
Drone threat halts Russia’s main Black Sea oil terminal, which normally ships 700,000 barrels a day
The Sheskharis oil terminal in the Black Sea port of Novorossiysk halted operations after a Ukrainian drone attack, sources told Reuters.
A tanker that had planned to dock at Sheskharis to take on oil turned around instead and headed for open sea early on August 14, the sources said, citing the threat of a drone attack.
The port then suspended both oil loading and crude intake at the terminal after its storage tanks reached capacity.
Sheskharis is Russia’s main oil-export terminal on the Black Sea, handling about 700,000 barrels of crude oil per day. Its shutdown adds to mounting pressure on Russia’s energy infrastructure, which has faced repeated Ukrainian attacks in recent months.
The suspension compounds the disruptions at Novorossiysk, one of Russia’s key export hubs. Three grain terminals there had already halted operations after an overnight Ukrainian drone strike on August 12.

articles.title: The Ceuta 'crisis' is the cost of deadly EU policies
articles.body:
Breadcrumb
The Ceuta 'crisis' is the cost of deadly EU policies
At least 141 have been reported dead, with many more missing, after an estimated 60,000 people attempted to enter Spanish territory from Morocco by swimming around the sea barrier separating the two from 29 July. The conditions under which the majority of those the Spanish government stated later left Ceuta “voluntarily” are still unclear, with civil society documenting testimonies of violence and coercion.
Those who remained in Ceuta faced dire humanitarian conditions, lacking sufficient food, water, and medical care as civil society reported a failure to provide their bare minimum for survival. Yet political discussion of the human toll among those who made the journey has been overwhelmingly absent.
Instead, politicians praise lawless returns while headlines proclaim an “invasion” of Europe via Ceuta, ignoring that it was Spanish authorities who deployed military personnel and equipment against individuals in need of urgent reception.
In addition to obscuring what happened to those who entered or tried to enter Europe beginning from 29 July, the “migration crisis” discourse overlooks how the long history of European border fortification, externalization, and expulsions in Ceuta and beyond has given rise to such events. 
Deadly history at the Spanish-Moroccan border
Although situated on the north-western African coast, Ceuta (Sebta) together with Melilla (Mlilia) have mainly been under Spanish control since the 15th-century Portuguese and then Spanish colonial expansions. With disputed status, their current borders are the product of mid-19th-century colonial military victories by France and Spain, which simultaneously ruled Morocco until the mid-20th century.
Since then, the enclaves remain military outposts, where, until recently, tributes to Franquism still stood. After Spain’s inclusion in the EU’s Schengen space in 1991, it erected border fences around the enclaves, dubbed the EU’s “only land borders with Africa,” illustrating how free movement for EU citizens came at the price of others’ immobility.
Due to their history and geographical position, Ceuta and Melilla are integral parts of North Africa. Until recently, locals could enter without visas and goods circulated without customs duties, making the enclaves an economic hub reliant on movement between Spain and Morocco.
Although onward travel to “mainland Spain” has been subject to border controls and visa requirements for non-EU citizens, the enclaves have also remained a symbol of Fortress Europe. Because the formal Morocco-Spain border crossing is largely inaccessible for the vast majority of people on the move in Morocco, particularly given racial profiling of those with Black skin, mass crossing attempts into Ceuta and Melilla have long been one of the only means for individuals to enter the enclaves and apply for asylum and other protections in Spain.
Yet since 2005, Spain has implemented what it calls “hot returns”—immediate, collective expulsion of persons not even identified—at its Ceuta and Melilla borders. Despite their non-compliance with national, European, and international law, “hot returns” were codified in national law in 2015, though only for people arriving by land, as confirmed by several national judgments, including, most recently, the Spanish Supreme Tribunal.
To deter those seeking entry and to effect their expulsions, Spanish and Moroccan violence has become a decades-long reality at these borders, epitomised by violent repression in Ceuta in 1995, the 2014 Tarajal Massacre in Ceuta, and the 2022 24 June Massacre in Melilla. Despite tireless advocacy, families and civil society on both sides of the borders have not seen accountability or justice for the many disappeared and killed during these violent expulsion operations, entrenching impunity at the border.
Reflections of Ceuta across and beyond Europe
Developments at the Spanish border have reflected the progression of European migration practice and policy more broadly. After the increase of arrivals to Europe in 2015’s “summer of migration” sparked political panic leading to border closures, their enforcement across the continent has relied largely not on the dignified and individualized processing of those continuing to flee to the EU, as required by European and international law, but instead on their immediate and often violent expulsions—commonly called “pushbacks”—operating entirely outside any legal protections.
In effect, “hot returns” spread from Ceuta and Melilla to the rest of Europe.
The backlash to migration also triggered reforms of the EU’s common asylum policy, which have been in effect since June of this year. Although praised by EU leaders, the new legislation has been heavily criticised by civil society for reducing rights protections afforded to those arriving by attempting to relocate much of Europe's asylum processing to its external borders—if not to third countries—and accelerate returns from its territory. This includes via country-level evaluations of safety divorced from reality: Within these efforts, Morocco has been designated as a safe country of origin for nationals arriving in the EU—a move ignoring detentions and violent repression there.
Although political leaders discussed the Ceuta events within an “instrumentalisation” framing, neither the new and regressive Crisis and Force Majeure Regulation to which this refers, nor any of the EU’s migration reforms, appear to have been applied in Spain’s response—confirming the long-standing criticism about their unworkable nature.
Indeed, one key focus of the reforms is this crisis regulation, which enables member states to derogate from ordinarily applicable asylum procedures in situations of so-called “instrumentalisation of migrants by a third country or a hostile non-state actor with the aim of destabilising” the EU or its member states. An emphasis on “instrumentalisation” traces back to Turkey’s 2020 opening of its border with Greece; in 2021, Belarus’s encouragement of asylum-seekers to travel to its borders with Poland, Latvia, and Lithuania was familiarly dubbed a “hybrid attack” on the EU by European Commission president Ursula von der Leyen.
As in Ceuta this past week, both instances resulted in heavy militarisation, deaths, and mistreatment of those who arrived at Europe’s borders, with little evidence of how Europe had been harmed other than through collective hysteria.
The repeated, deadly spectacle of border violence framed and responded to as an attack on Europe conceals an unacknowledged tension in the EU’s migration management logic: While advancing claims that the EU can be threatened by neighbouring states “instrumentalising” migration, the EU has simultaneously deepened its migration cooperation with neighbouring countries. This is particularly the case with countries in Africa, where funding is provided for increased border controls and returns in line with its own deterrence and expulsion policies.
Morocco is no exception, as affirmed by von der Leyen’s 3 August description that it remains an “important strategic partner” after the Ceuta events. Through these externalisation efforts, it is the EU that has been instrumentalising migration control, disregarding human lives, in exchange for development aid or other assistance to third countries—setting the stage for its further politicisation and abuse.
Last week’s events in Ceuta lay bare the failure of EU policies to reckon both with the continued human necessity of movement for survival and the local realities of communities on and around its borders. The history of its external borders with Morocco already made this clear. Yet they have further highlighted how the EU’s newest migration reforms remain both irrational, providing no solutions while fuelling human-made crises, and unsustainable, lacking the most basic humanity.
Hanaa Hakiki directs the Border Justice team at the European Center for Constitutional and Human Rights (ECCHR).
Delphine Rodrik is a senior legal advisor in ECCHR’s Border Justice team, where they support litigation challenging human rights violations at Europe’s borders.

articles.title: Former 80th Air Assault Brigade commander Ishkulov to lead Ukraine’s 11th Corps
articles.body:
Former 80th Air Assault Brigade commander Ishkulov to lead Ukraine’s 11th Corps
Colonel Emil Ishkulov, former commander of the 80th Air Assault Brigade and currently deputy commander of the 7th Air Assault Corps, will shortly take charge of the Ground Forces' 11th Corps, which is currently responsible for defending two key cities in Donetsk Oblast – Kramatorsk and Sloviansk.
Source: three Ukrainska Pravda sources within the defence forces, including senior officials
Details: Ishkulov will replace Brigadier General Oleksii Maistrenko, the current commander of the 11th Corps who has held the post for six months. The official reason for the change is not yet known.
However, Ukrainska Pravda sources within the 11th Corps say the decision is linked to the fact that Maistrenko's management approach "did not correspond to modern decision-making realities".
The 11th Corps is responsible for one of the toughest sections of the front – the Sloviansk and Kramatorsk sectors. This is the main front of Russia's advance in Donetsk Oblast.
According to one of Ukrainska Pravda's senior sources, Ishkulov's appointment will "significantly strengthen" these two sectors.
All of Ukrainska Pravda military sources rate Ishkulov's skills and management qualities fairly highly. Service members from the 80th Brigade who fought under his command describe Ishkulov as a very demanding commander.
Ukrainska Pravda has also learned that, in his new post, Ishkulov will need to work closely with the Third Corps, stationed in Lyman (Donetsk Oblast) and Borova (Kharkiv Oblast). The 11th Corps recently handed over two brigades that were under its operational command – the 81st and the 54th – to the 3rd Corps. They were positioned north of Sloviansk, bordering the 3rd Army Corps' sector.
Ishkulov and Biletskyi are believed to have maintained a good relationship since the time of the offensive near Bakhmut in the summer of 2023.
Why this matters: Newly appointed Commander-in-Chief Mykhailo Drapatyi has decided to "rehabilitate" Ishkulov following the Kursk operation, during which he refused to lead his 80th Brigade onto Russian territory – a decision that earned him the disfavour of former Commander-in-Chief Oleksandr Syrskyi and saw him moved to the post of deputy commander of the 7th Air Assault Corps.

articles.title: War in Ukraine: Deadly Russian air raid on Kramatorsk leaves 1 dead and 17 wounded
articles.body:
Emergency crews worked through the night on Friday to rescue residents trapped under rubble and extinguish fires after eight FAB‑250 guided aerial bombs hit the city, local authorities said. Several private homes and a garage caught fire, while an apartment building suffered extensive damage.
The strike caused sections of the ten‑storey apartment building from the first to the sixth floors to collapse, the emergency service said. Rescuers were filmed pulling a woman and a man from the rubble and helping residents leave damaged buildings. Firefighters also tackled flames at several sites across the city, while cars were damaged near the impact areas. The Donetsk regional prosecutor’s office has opened a war‑crimes investigation into the attack.
Kramatorsk has repeatedly come under Russian attacks during the war because of its proximity to the front line. The injured, aged between 47 and 85, were treated for blast and traumatic brain injuries, shrapnel wounds, cuts and abrasions, officials said.

articles.title: Judge moves Alex Murdaugh retrial from small county, but motion to toss out case will wait
articles.body:
Judge moves Alex Murdaugh retrial from small county, but motion to toss out case will wait
LEXINGTON, S.C. (AP) — The judge in Alex Murdaugh’s murder retrial decided Friday to move the case out of the rural South Carolina county where it consumed life for six weeks in 2023.
But left undecided is a defense request to throw out the whole case because Murdaugh’s lawyers said the chief state investigator lied to the grand jury that indicted their client in 2022 and another main investigator was fired for misconduct after taking a job at a different agency.
Murdaugh’s conviction and life sentence for killing his wife and son were overturned in May by the South Carolina Supreme Court after the justices ruled a court clerk may have influenced the jury.
Murdaugh shows up in coat and tie instead of prison jumpsuit
Murdaugh was in a coat and tie Friday after Judge Debra McCaslin ruled he didn’t have to wear a prison jumpsuit because he was not a security risk even though Murdaugh remains behind bars serving a 40-year federal sentence and a 27-year state sentence after pleading guilty to stealing about $12 million from clients and his family’s law firm.
The judge agreed Friday to move the retrial out of Colleton County, where the killings happened and the first trial brought throngs of media and true crime fans, overwhelming the few restaurants and hotels in the county of 40,000 people.
McCaslin said she had to move the trial because of all the publicity of the first trial, the circumstances of the court clerk tainting the first jury and the Murdaughs’ connections to the surrounding community, where his father, grandfather and great-grandfather were chief prosecutors and the family’s law firm dominated for a century.
The location of the retrial hasn’t been decided and Murdaugh’s attorneys called one of their own lawyers to the stand to testify about how Charleston County, where he lived, would be perfect.
The testimony lasted 30 minutes as annoyed prosecutor Creighton Waters asked about how expensive Charleston is and how difficult it is to find parking.
The judge said she wants to take her time and research hotels and courtroom availability for the retrial set to begin on April 5.
Arguments about dismissing the case are not heard
McCaslin didn’t hear arguments Friday about dismissing the case.
The defense has said it will provide more information in writing about why it believes the case should be dismissed because State Law Enforcement Division agent David Owen told a 2023 grand jury that blood was found on a shirt Murdaugh was wearing when a different agent determined no blood had been found.
Murdaugh’s lawyers are also concerned about former agent Ryan Kelly, who testified how investigators thought Murdaugh paid another man to shoot him in the head so his son could collect millions in life insurance money but the shot only grazed him.
After the trial, Kelly took a job with the Charleston County Sheriff’s Office but was fired for harassment and improper conduct. More details have not been released.
Murdaugh case continues to fascinate true crime fans
The true crime sensation continues to fascinate. Dozens of reporters, podcasters, bloggers and others were at the Lexington County courtroom to hear the latest in the case that combines money, violence, power and small-town Southern justice. Afterward, fans stopped defense lawyer Dick Harpootlian in the sweltering parking lot for selfies.
“The Murdaugh case is a total freak show,” Harpootlian said in the courtroom, arguing to move the case.
Prosecutors say Murdaugh shot his wife, Maggie, and younger son, Paul, who was 22, because he believed sympathy over their deaths would buy him time to fix his financial crimes. At that point in 2021, he was close to being exposed by both his law firm and the family of a teen who filed a wrongful death suit after Paul crashed a boat while drinking.
A jury convicted Murdaugh of two counts of murder in 2023. While admitting he is a thief, insurance cheat, bad lawyer and longtime opioid addict, he has adamantly denied the killings.
The judge decided other issues Friday, asking the defense to determine whether there is enough of the dwindling DNA material found under Maggie Murdaugh’s fingernails for both prosecutors and the defense to run additional tests.

articles.title: UK Charity Commission acts over Great Israeli Real Estate event
articles.body:
Breadcrumb
UK Charity Commission takes action after complaints over Great Israeli Real Estate event
The UK Charity Commission confirmed on Thursday that it formally engaged with the trustees of the Edgware United Synagogue after a barrage of complaints was received regarding the Great Israeli Real Estate event that took place in London on 14 June.
The event promoted the sale of properties in illegal Israeli settlements in occupied Palestinian territories, triggering protests at the time.
The Charity Commission said it exercised its statutory powers under section 15(2) of the Charities Act 2011 to issue regulatory advice and guidance concerning the charity's decision to host the event.
It added that the trustees of the Edgware United Synagogue must now take account of and act upon the guidance moving forward.
The development comes after the Commission said its statutory regulatory powers reflect its assessment that the issues raised by the complaints, such as that from the International Centre of Justice of Palestinians (ICJP), warranted formal regulatory engagement.
The complaint from the ICJP argued that the synagogue had allowed its charitable resources and premises to host a commercial event, where attendees were persuaded to buy properties in illegal Israeli settlements in the occupied West Bank.
The group also said that the event had gone ahead despite the trustees receiving detailed legal warnings before it took place, raising concerns over trustee governance, the discharge of trustees' legal duties, due diligence, the use of charitable assets, and reputational risk.
Another key concern about the event was the obligation of trustees to act exclusively in the best interests of their charity, while maintaining public trust and confidence.
The ICJP argued that by allowing the event to proceed, the trustees failed to consider the legal warnings and obligations, despite being made aware of the issues.
A statement from the ICJP, however, said that the Commission’s response was not sufficient, noting the serious nature of the matter.
The group said that they had submitted thorough evidence which showed the event raised serious concerns under both international law and UK laws.
“Where a charity permits its premises and resources to be used in connection with conduct that raises such serious legal concerns, the Charity Commission should take robust regulatory action to uphold charity law and protect public trust and confidence in the charitable sector,” a statement from the ICJP said.
The organisation called for a more adequate response and called for the Charity Commission to show that it is ready to use all of its powers in cases where charities risk being connected to serious breaches of law.
“Failing to do so risks undermining public confidence in charity regulation and sending the wrong message to trustees about the standards expected of them under charity law,” the ICJP said.

articles.title: Colombia Seeks to Acquire L 410 NG Aircraft to Replace Its C-212 Aviocars
articles.body:
The Colombian Army plans to purchase two Czech L 410 NG light transport aircraft manufactured by Aircraft Industries.
This was reported by the Spanish publication Infodefensa.
The L 410 NG is a twin-engine turboprop light transport aircraft designed to carry up to 19 passengers or up to 2,300 kg of cargo. Its maximum takeoff weight is 7,000 kg.
The Ministry of National Defense of Colombia has allocated approximately $33.1 million for the purchase.
The new aircraft are intended to replace three CASA C-212 Aviocars, which Colombia received in 2003 as a gift from the Spanish government as part of a military aid program. These aircraft are scheduled to be decommissioned.
The Assault Aviation Division, which will receive the aircraft, was established in 2010 through the merger of the Special Forces Brigade and the Counter-Narcotics Brigade—along with a Special Air Operations Battalion.
In addition to the C-212, the division also operates Cessna C-208 Caravan and Antonov An-32 aircraft, as well as UH-60 Black Hawk, Sikorsky S-70i, and Mil Mi-17 helicopters.
The L 410 NG retains short takeoff and landing capabilities. It requires approximately 600 meters for takeoff and about 590 meters for landing. This allows the aircraft to operate on short and unpaved runways, which is particularly important given Colombia’s rugged terrain.
The L 410 NG is a modernized version of the Let L-410 Turbolet. It is equipped with GE H85-200 engines and state-of-the-art Garmin G3000 avionics. Thanks to larger fuel tanks, the flight range has increased from approximately 1,400 to 2,600 km, and the payload has increased by approximately 500 kg. The aircraft has a service life of up to 30,000 flight hours.
The Czech Republic recently exported the L 410 NG to Thailand, Kazakhstan, Senegal, and Chile.
The aircraft have been entirely designed by Aircraft Industries in Kunovice with 617 Czech companies involved in their production.
The company is part of the Czech Omnipol Group, which, incidentally, manufactures the Senator armored vehicles in partnership with the Canadian company Roshel.

articles.title: West Bank settler attacks continue despite international uproar
articles.body:
Breadcrumb
Israeli settler attacks in West Bank continue despite international outrage
Israeli forces and settlers continued their assault against Palestinian communities across the occupied West Bank on Friday despite mounting international condemnation over the siege of homes in Qusra and escalating attacks elsewhere.
In Qusra, south of Nablus, settlers remained near Palestinian homes for a sixth consecutive day, while Israeli forces prevented foreign and Israeli solidarity activists from reaching besieged families with water and other basic supplies.
The siege has drawn unusually sharp criticism from Washington, with White House officials pressing Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu to publicly condemn the settlers after learning that one of the affected homes belongs to a Palestinian American.
US Ambassador to Israel Mike Huckabee -- a supporter of the settler movement -- described those responsible as "Israeli terrorists" and their actions as "criminal", while France condemned what it called the "occupation" of Palestinian homes and called on Israeli authorities to arrest and prosecute those responsible.
Amid the criticism, Israeli Defence Minister Israel Katz ordered the military to prepare a plan to transfer civilian law enforcement in the occupied West Bank to the police.
"The army's role is to combat Palestinian terrorism ... and not chase hilltop youth," Katz said, using a term commonly applied to hardline young settlers involved in establishing unauthorised outposts and attacks on Palestinians.
Under the proposal, Israel Police would establish a dedicated force to handle civilian matters in the occupied territory.
Settlers returned on Friday morning to an outpost near Palestinian homes in Qusra, erecting a canopy in the presence of soldiers. Border Police later dismantled it, but the settlers remained nearby.
The confrontation has centred on the Ras al-Ain area west of Qusra, where settlers established an outpost between three Palestinian homes belonging to the families of brothers Rizq and Youssef Hassan and Qusay Abu Rida.
Residents have been prevented from moving freely and accessing basic necessities, while settlers last month cut water and electricity supplies to three neighbouring homes, according to the UN Human Rights Office.
Mohammad Joudat, a media activist from Qusra, told The New Arab that foreign and Israeli solidarity activists attempted on Friday to bring water and other supplies to the besieged families.
"Israeli forces arrived at the scene, prevented them from reaching the homes and completely removed them from the area," Joudat said.
Israeli forces entered Qusra on Thursday and evacuated the three homes before gathering their residents in one of them.
Local reports said the army subsequently informed residents of 16 homes that they would have to evacuate so they could be used as military positions.
The UN Human Rights Office said settlers had consolidated control over the area west of Qusra since an outpost was established there in November 2025.
Residents have since faced home invasions, physical assaults, theft, vandalism and arson, including an attack on a mosque, it said.
The UN office said the latest actions, carried out with Israeli support or acquiescence, were making life "intolerable" for Palestinian families and were clearly aimed at forcing them from their homes and land.
Taybeh faces continued attacks
The events in Qusra come amid a wider escalation in settler attacks across the occupied West Bank, including in Taybeh, the territory's last entirely Christian Palestinian village.
Israel declared Taybeh a closed military zone earlier this month, saying the measure was intended to protect residents following repeated settler attacks.
But Ihab Hassan, a Palestinian Christian activist, told The New Arab that attacks had continued despite the closure, while journalists, foreign activists and other outside observers faced restrictions on entering the village.
"No, the Israeli army is not protecting the residents. I say this based on what is actually happening on the ground," Hassan said.
"Israeli settler attacks on the village have continued even after it was declared a closed military zone. The difference now is that journalists, foreign activists, and other outside observers face restrictions on entering."
Hassan said international and Israeli activists had previously provided a protective presence in Taybeh, sometimes placing themselves between settlers and Palestinian residents.
"Restricting their access while settlers continue to reach and attack the village has left the community even more isolated and vulnerable," he said.
Hassan said the situation reflected a broader pattern across the occupied territory.
"In some cases, the army says it will 'remove' the settlers, but the fact that an army claims it cannot remove settlers who are besieging Palestinian families speaks for itself," he said.
He argued that settlers were also seeking to exploit the current political environment to seize land and establish realities that would be difficult to reverse.
"Once families are driven from their homes, land and property are taken over, and new facts are established on the ground, reversing them becomes extraordinarily difficult, even under a future Israeli government that might take a different approach," Hassan said.
"For Taybeh, this is therefore not simply about individual attacks," he added.
"It is about whether the last entirely Christian Palestinian village in the West Bank can remain on its land."

articles.title: Blackout hits four Central Asian countries at once
articles.body:
Blackout hits four Central Asian countries at once
Power outages struck Kyrgyzstan, Kazakhstan, Tajikistan, and Uzbekistan simultaneously on the afternoon of August 14.
In Bishkek, residents of several districts began reporting power outages around 3 p.m. local time (noon Moscow time), according to the outlet Kaktus.media. Kyrgyzstan’s Energy Ministry stated it was aware of the problem but could not yet identify what had caused it.
Power went out shortly afterward in four districts of Almaty and 10 districts of the surrounding Almaty region, the Kazakhstani news outlet Tengrinews reported. Local energy officials blamed the blackout on an accident involving overhead power lines.
Eyewitnesses said the Almaty metro stopped running, traffic lights went dark, and mobile phone service was disrupted. Water supply was also affected, which the outlet attributed to pumping stations losing power. Kazakhstan’s Energy Ministry announced at 3:40 PM Moscow time, approximately an hour after the blackout, that power workers had begun restoring power.
Residents of Dushanbe, along with several other cities and districts in Tajikistan, also reported power outages, the Tajik news outlet Asia-Plus reported. The Ministry of Energy and Water Resources stated it could not yet determine the cause of the blackout but denied that an accident at the Nurek Hydropower Plant, the country’s largest power station, was responsible.
Power outages also hit several regions of Uzbekistan, including the southern Surkhandarya region. Uzbekistan’s Energy Ministry stated the problems stemmed from “an accident in the power grid of a neighboring country.”
